Experts said the new measures should be judged against more modest benchmarks than a full reversal of Singapore’s fertility decline.

Kalpana Vignehsa, senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, said no advanced economy had sustainably restored replacement-level fertility through policy and success should instead be measured by whether such initiatives helped fertility rates stop falling or decline more slowly.

“On that score, this package is more promising than its predecessors. It shifts from one-off incentives towards sustained, universal support,” Vignehsa said.

Among the policy shifts, childcare leave will now be linked to the number of children a parent has.

Currently, every working parent has six days of leave if their youngest child is six years old or younger and two days if their youngest child is aged seven to 12.

This will be increased to eight days of leave for one child, aged up to 12, 10 days for two children and 12 days for three or more children.

While the government and employers currently share the cost of child-related leave, the former will cover the expenditure for all statutory child-related leave, up to a reimbursement limit.

Wong said the government also aimed to reduce full-day childcare fares to S$150 (US$118) a month and infant care fees to S$300 at government-supported schools. Currently, families can pay nearly S$600 a month for full-day childcare and more than S$1,000 monthly for infant care.

First-time applicants for the build-to-order scheme, which enables Singaporean families to buy public housing flats directly from the government, will also get an additional ballot chance for every child they have or are expecting, according to Wong.

Every Singaporean child would receive almost S$70,000 in direct financial support over the years by the time they turned 17, Wong added.

Vignehsa noted that fertility decisions rested on confidence that care would be affordable, careers would survive parenthood, there would be enough time in the week to parent, and that support would not disappear after infancy.

“This package builds that confidence more credibly than a larger baby bonus would have,” she said. “The effects will likely be gradual and most visible among couples deciding on a second or third child, rather than [resulting] in a dramatic TFR rebound.”

Still, Vignehsa said “two scarcities” remained unaddressed: “the income and career losses that accompany caregiving, and the sheer shortage of time and energy in Singaporean working life”.

She suggested making flexible work and reasonable hours a durable, protected feature of working life, offering caregiving compensation and looking upstream at rising singlehood as other methods to slow the fertility rate decline.

Danyya Ateera, 34, a health and safety officer, who has two children aged two and five, told This Week in Asia that no additional financial benefit or childcare leave could make her want more children.

“No incentive can make me change my mind, although an understanding workplace can lighten the load a bit,” she said, noting that she often felt guilty for taking time off work during busy periods even though her children needed her.

For Valerie Ong, 33, who has a two-year-old and is expecting a second child, the need for a bigger home is a key reason she intends to stop at two.

On the reduced childcare fees, Ong, who works in advertising, said, “It’s a very tangible cost that families feel. If you give me a S$10,000 lump sum, I just think it’s just cash assistance, but if you lower my school fees, mentally, it changes my opinion of the cost of having a kid.”

While having S$70,000 spread across 17 years would help offset costs such as childcare, enrichment and insurance, Ong said the money would not be viewed as funds to upgrade to a bigger property in land-scarce Singapore. “The sum is too small to even come close.”

Wong on Sunday touched on larger families wanting bigger homes that cost more and said he had asked National Development Minister Chee Hong Tat to consider additional housing support for larger families.

Ong, however, said for couples who decided not to have children at all, no amount of cash incentives or cost-covering from the government would help since they would always have more money as DINKs (dual income no kids).

Tan, 31, is one such couple who is married with no children. She told This Week in Asia that while the new measures showed having children could be affordable, there were other trade-offs to consider.

“It does sound like a lot of money [to support parents having children] but there’s also other factors to consider like the time costs and giving up our lifestyle now to have a kid,” said Tan, who declined to give her full name.

“There are also the expectations we have for ourselves of what we want to give our kid if we have one.”

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s anti-corruption fight became Xi Jinping’s most important policy
item.description:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies.

In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”.

At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians.
item.content:encoded:
The South China Morning Post has launched a major data project diving into President Xi Jinping’s signature anti-graft campaign. In the first part of a series accompanying the data project, Phoebe Zhang looks at how the campaign became one of the Communist Party’s most important policies.

In the early years of President Xi Jinping’s first term, when graft fighters were taking down senior officials in ways that raised eyebrows, Chinese authorities constantly had to remind the public that the anti-corruption campaign was not “just a gust of wind”.

At that point, Beijing had already locked up dozens of senior officials, including Zhou Yongkang, a former member of the Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee, the highest echelon in China’s political hierarchy. Before his downfall in 2013, Zhou had been one of China’s most influential politicians.

Concerns were so widespread that the anti-corruption push would be a flash in the pan, especially at the local level, that Wang Qishan, then the party’s top anti-corruption chief, warned that local governments might fall back on temporary “movement-style” crackdowns.

A decade later, few need convincing as the anti-corruption fight expands, netting record numbers of senior officials and unearthing new types of graft involving cryptocurrency schemes and clandestine proxies.

A new analysis by the South China Morning Post found that the campaign has widened since its inception. Last year, anti-corruption agencies handed down punishments to 983,000 people, with the fallout ranging from mild warnings to investigations and criminal prosecution. The number of senior officials taken down last year was three times that of 2013.

The SCMP’s data bank project also found that from 2013 to 2025, 60 per cent of senior officials felled by China’s anti-corruption drive were serving in regional governments. The campaign has hit provincial administrations particularly hard, with resource-rich areas – notably Jiangxi, Liaoning, Shanxi and Hebei provinces, as well as Inner Mongolia, autonomous region – recording the highest number of dismissals.

What began as a crackdown on economic graft has evolved into a systemic overhaul of bureaucratic conduct. While bribery remains the main legal charge, the definition of corruption has expanded to include party discipline and adherence to policy directives.

By now, most experts agree that the anti-corruption campaign is among Xi’s most important policies, and one that is key to his vision of China’s future and the party’s ability to rule for generations to come.

And the party has shown no interest in pulling any punches.

During a January meeting of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the party’s top anti-graft body, Xi declared that “the situation in the fight against corruption remains grave and complex”, urging officials to come up with new methods to discover, identify and tackle all types of wrongdoing.

Just last month, China’s top leadership announced that party governance would be the focus of the fifth plenary session of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee, expected to be held in October. This meeting is likely to be the party’s most important gathering ahead of its 21st national congress in autumn of next year. The five-yearly party congress is likely to feature a leadership reshuffle and the endorsement of a fourth term for Xi.

In a Xinhua report on the coming plenary session, the Politburo said party self-governance “faces new circumstances and challenges” and called for “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party” – a phrase that typically means fighting corruption and tightening party discipline.

No end point

While generations of Communist Party leaders have pledged to uproot corruption, Xi has tried to convince the country from the outset that his fight is different.

In 2013, at the second plenary session of the party’s 18th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), Xi pledged to fight “tigers and flies at the same time” – targeting not only high-ranking officials but also misconduct at the grass-roots level – to underscore a policy of “no forbidden zones, full coverage and zero tolerance”.

Soon, Beijing introduced a set of “eight-point austerity rules” to restrict party cadre behaviour. These include banning the use of luxury cars and gifts, banning red carpets, floral arrangements and grand receptions during inspections, simplifying meetings, reducing unnecessary documents and limiting overseas visits.

The rules are still in effect today.

The anti-corruption campaign has deepened and broadened to cover all policy areas and sectors, including security, finance, education and the graft fighters themselves. In its first three years, it took down top leaders in all 31 provincial-level jurisdictions. The campaign has also hit the military’s top brass, especially in the past two years.

The push has become more institutionalised as well. In 2018, the National Supervisory Commission (NSC) was created and merged with the CCDI, giving the party’s anti-corruption campaign a legal basis.

Beijing has sought to supplement laws with party regulations. More than 70 per cent of the Communist Party’s regulations have been enacted since 2012.

China has also overhauled its corruption-fighting agencies to reflect a “vertical management” style, giving more oversight to higher authorities.

It has reinvented the inspection regime, inherited from Imperial China but largely inactive in the years before Xi, so inspectors dispatched from Beijing look for signs of corruption at the local level.

Over the past 14 years, Xi has repeatedly emphasised that his anti-corruption campaign has no end point, warning that no official should harbour any illusions of impunity.

At the 20th party congress in 2022, Xi said the anti-corruption fight should “never rest, not even for a minute”.

Staying disciplined

Corruption is the “greatest threat” facing the party, Xi said in a speech at the 19th party congress in 2017.

At times, he has argued that purging corruption is crucial for the Communist Party to escape China’s “historical cycles” of dynastic rise and collapse, and ensure its longevity.

Xi has said that corruption hinders governance and economic development. “If corruption is allowed to spread, it will eventually lead to the destruction of a party and the fall of a government,” he has warned.

Li Jian, a former researcher with the Publicity Department of the Central Committee, wrote in January that the reason that the party could not afford to lose the fight against corruption was because graft harmed the party’s vitality and ability to fight.

“[Corruption] seriously undermines fair and just market rules, distorts the efficiency of resource allocation, erodes the fruits of reform and development, and damages the business environment as well as social fairness and justice,” Li wrote. He concluded that there was a need to create a “sound political environment and a level playing field for high-quality development”.

“Combating corruption is like sailing against the current – if you do not advance, you will fall back,” said Zhiqun Zhu, a professor of political science and international relations at Bucknell University.

“Long-term goals such as rejuvenation of the Chinese nation or unification with Taiwan cannot be achieved any time soon, but the anti-corruption campaign has yielded concrete results, with a cleaner government, a more professional and efficient bureaucracy, and a more loyal and dedicated leadership team,” said Zhu, who is also director of Bucknell’s China Institute.

Alfred Wu, associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the National University of Singapore, said Xi’s views on corruption were shared by his predecessors, though they never pushed the fight to the same level.

“Jiang Zemin had repeatedly said that ‘anti-corruption is a serious political struggle that matters to the life and death of the party and the nation’, while Hu Jintao said at the 18th party congress that failure to tackle the issue could prove fatal to the party,” he said, referring to China’s previous two presidents.

Beijing has also made the enforcement of its strategies part of the anti-corruption campaign.

The latest revision of party disciplinary regulations explicitly prohibits failing to implement the “new concept for development and high-quality development” – Beijing’s term for its new growth model, coined after Xi came to power.

This violation has been mentioned in the investigation findings of a handful of disgraced senior officials, including Lan Tianli, the former party secretary of Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, who was investigated last year.

Devendra Kumar, an associate fellow at the Centre of Excellence for Himalayan Studies at Shiv Nadar University, said the corruption-fighting efforts under Xi were ultimately about discipline.

“In this context, anti-corruption in China cannot be understood in the narrow sense of deviations from institutional rules and laws,” he said.

“Rather, it is fundamentally about ‘discipline’, which encompasses not only compliance with regulations but also officials’ political disposition and, increasingly, aspects of their family life, including whom they associate with, where family members work, and where they travel.”

Kumar added that the campaign was aimed at enforcing the party’s agenda and preferred modes of thinking through measures such as the campaign on the correct view of political performance, which began in March.

With local governments across China preparing for a leadership shuffle, Xi said a “correct view” of performance was particularly vital to ensure new appointments prioritised long-term public benefit over short-term vanity projects.

According to Xinhua, local party leaders were tasked with the “top priority” of implementing top leadership’s decisions with “unwavering focus”.

Party discipline also figures heavily in “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new branch of the Chinese leader’s political thought unveiled in June. Its key tenets include insistence on “a centralised, unified leadership of the party Central Committee” as well as “full and rigorous party self-governance” and ensuring that “officials do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”.

Kumar added that there were similarities between Xi and his predecessors’ signature policies in that they all aimed to extend party rule and impose discipline.

For example, he said, Mao launched the “continuous revolution” – an ideological extension of the civil war the party won in 1949 – to prevent the party from becoming a stagnant bureaucracy. Xi, by contrast, sees bureaucratisation as a key remedy, with anti-corruption as a tool to fix the problems arising from the party’s organisational structure, according to Kumar.

Communist Party institutions lack mechanisms such as public oversight and transparency to foster bottom-up accountability. As a result, he said, top-down methods of enforcing discipline and accountability were necessary for maintaining order and preventing deviations from established regulations and norms, even during periods of weak leadership.

Xi laid bare some of those concerns in the report he delivered at the 20th party congress in 2022.

He said that China had made great achievements as a result of reform, opening up and socialist modernisation, but “a number of prominent issues and problems – some of which had been building for years and others which were just emerging – demanded urgent action”.

Among them, there were a “lack of clear understanding and effective action as well as a slide towards weak, hollow and watered-down party leadership in practice”, according to the Chinese leader. He added that despite repeated warnings, ills including pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance persisted.

Another problem Xi saw as serious was “privilege-seeking mindsets and practices”, with some “deeply shocking cases of corruption”.

“The intensity with which Xi has pursued disciplinary campaigns must be understood in context,” Kumar said.

“When Xi came to power, party institutions were not sufficiently effective in ‘caging’ cadres in their day-to-day functioning, and cadres’ ideological commitment was also considered weak.”

He noted there were structural reasons for the campaign to continue, as it had become part of Xi’s broader agenda of revitalising the party, both ideologically and institutionally, and the anti-corruption campaign and institutional changes of the past decade had embedded a “disciplinary regime” into the party’s day-to-day governance.

“Consequently, we should expect an intensification of anti-corruption efforts in the run-up to the 21st party congress,” Kumar said.

item.title: [SCMP] Brazil presidential debate zeroes in on Chinese investment and US tariffs
item.description:
Brazil’s presidential candidates opened the televised campaign season on Sunday with a debate that turned repeatedly to the country’s position between Washington and Beijing.

The exchange comes in an election cycle already shaped by American tariffs, a visa dispute over election monitoring and the Lula government’s warming ties with China.

Ronaldo Caiado, Augusto Cury and Renan Santos took to the debate stage in Sao Paulo but the lecterns reserved for President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema remained empty.
item.content:encoded:
Brazil’s presidential candidates opened the televised campaign season on Sunday with a debate that turned repeatedly to the country’s position between Washington and Beijing.

The exchange comes in an election cycle already shaped by American tariffs, a visa dispute over election monitoring and the Lula government’s warming ties with China.

Ronaldo Caiado, Augusto Cury and Renan Santos took to the debate stage in Sao Paulo but the lecterns reserved for President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and former Minas Gerais governor Romeu Zema remained empty.

Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro, who are leading in every published poll, refused to take part, with the Brazilian president telling a podcast in July he would skip debates if the exercise meant listening to nonsense.

Flavio Bolsonaro has tied his attendance to Lula’s, and Zema withdrew hours beforehand, saying the event had “lost its purpose”.

A senator for Rio de Janeiro and the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio became a candidate in December after being named by his father as his heir. Jair was sentenced to 27 years in jail for plotting a coup and masterminding a plan to assassinate Lula after losing his re-election bid in 2022.

The Band network has opened the televised campaign in every presidential race since 1989, the first direct vote after two decades of military rule. Broadcasters treat the event as the moment that sets the tone for the season.

US-China issue

Foreign policy rarely takes up much room in Brazilian presidential debates, which tend to be dominated by security, jobs and inflation. The absence of the two front-runners left the others time for subjects that usually stay at the margins.

Washington imposed a 25 per cent tariff on most Brazilian goods on July 22, capping a Section 301 case that ran for a year. It covered digital payment rules, ethanol market access and illegal deforestation. A separate forced labour investigation proposes a further 12.5 per cent duty.

The trade dispute has run alongside an argument over the vote itself, which Brasilia treats as a matter of interference.

Last month, Brazil denied visas to two US State Department officials who planned to question electoral authorities. And this month, Lula said he would withhold agreement for US President Donald Trump’s nominee as ambassador until the vote was over.

Meanwhile, Beijing has moved in the other direction, offering Brasilia support as Washington escalated.

President Xi Jinping telephoned Lula on July 26, four days after the tariffs took effect, and said China opposed external interference. The two governments agreed to widen cooperation on artificial intelligence, satellites, critical mineral processing and fertiliser trade.

In the debate studio, a radio journalist asked Augusto Cury how he would manage Washington during the second Trump term. The psychiatrist and author, who is running for Avante, argued that the tariffs answered American fiscal pressure rather than any dispute with Brazil.

“We cannot be subservient, put 25 per cent, plus 12.5, 37.5 per cent, and damage our export list,” he said. Cury said he would foster equally good relations with China while pushing Brazil out of its raw material role.

Caiado, the former Goias governor running for the PSD, or Social Democratic Party, attributed friction with the Trump administration to Lula’s electoral calculations.

“Lula is desperate to create this impasse because he saw the presidents of Canada and Australia winning, so he provokes Trump all the time,” he said.

Caiado said the foreign ministry had become a mouthpiece for the governing Workers’ Party. He promised to restore its ability to negotiate for a country he said retained leverage in energy, grain and fresh water.

However, it was Renan Santos who drew more attention than his two rivals on stage, despite never having held elected office.

The 42-year-old co-founded the Free Brazil Movement that organised the protests that preceded former president Dilma Rousseff’s impeachment in 2016. Polling has kept him third for most of the year – at between 5 and 9 per cent – but an AtlasIntel survey in July put him first among Brazilians aged 16 to 24, with 38 per cent.

Supporters and opponents call him “the Brazilian Bukele”, a label he encourages by citing controversial Salvadorean president Nayib Bukele – the self-proclaimed “coolest dictator in the world” – when talking about his war on crime.

Like Bukele, Santos’ platform pairs mass incarceration and militarised policing with wide deregulation of the economy.

On arriving at the studios, Santos was asked how he would handle warming between Lula and Trump as well as their divergence over Chinese investment.

“It seems that the sovereignty debate of Lula and Flavio involves choosing who your guardian will be,” he said. “One wants to choose China, the other wants to choose the United States. And that is not what makes a nation sovereign.”

Inside the studio he pressed the same charge against the governing party in language aimed at its trade record rather than its diplomacy.

“Right now we look at the Workers’ Party [Lula’s party] project wanting to put Brazil on its knees before China, without training a qualified workforce,” he said. “What matters to Lulism is that we keep buying the finished product from China while we sell ore or sell our grain.”

Kim Kataguiri, a federal deputy and one of Santos’s main campaign coordinators, said the position amounted to pragmatism rather than an alignment of any kind.

“He means that Lula, in exchange for nothing or for very little, automatically aligns with China,” Kataguiri told the South China Morning Post at the studios.

Kataguiri drew a sharper line on the other side, separating the American state from the administration that currently runs it.

“With Flavio, it is not even in relation to the United States, it is specifically in relation to the Trump government,” he said.

“It is not an alignment with the nation, with the American state, but with a figure, and a figure who, by all indications, will have difficulty electing a successor.”

He said Brazil should set terms for both the US and China instead of picking one, starting with what Beijing brings to the table.

“China wants space inside Brazil, so let it offer investment, let it offer technology, let it offer defence partnership,” he said, naming AI and rare earth processing, sectors he said Beijing led Washington, and added that Brazil could import that technology through strategic partnerships.

The same demand applied to the Americans, which he said had a shrinking commercial presence in Brazil.

“They do not want us to make more trade partnerships with China, so let them offer more partnership,” Kataguiri said. “American investment in Brazil only falls. The United States took Brazil as a given for the past 20 years and neglected our relations.”

Lula tells Trump real target is China

While the three candidates argued in the Sao Paulo debate, Record TV aired an exclusive interview with Lula recorded that morning at his official residence in Brasilia.

Presenter Mariana Godoy asked what had been settled with Trump on two subjects: the tariffs on Brazilian goods and cooperation against organised crime.

Lula described a call with the US president on Friday that ran about 80 minutes in which he reportedly told Trump the grounds for the new sanctions were false, citing record low deforestation and Lula’s own history of fighting forced labour, then placed the pressure elsewhere.

“Underneath it all, what he was really getting at was China,” he said.

Lula said he offered Trump a joint task force on critical minerals and rare earths, with one condition.

“Only this time we are not going to be an exporter of raw material. We want to transform it here, to make mobile phones, to make electric batteries, to make chips,” the president contended.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines stakes claim as Latin America’s Asean gateway
item.description:
The Philippines is positioning itself as Latin America’s bridge to Southeast Asia, testing whether shared history and culture can translate into hard trade figures as Asean and the Mercosur bloc look beyond their traditional partners.

Manila’s Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro made the pitch during visits to Brazil and Chile from August 10 to 13.

“Upon this human foundation, commercial bridges thrive: the Philippines stands as the premier strategic gateway for Latin American firms expanding into Asean’s US$4-trillion market,” she told an audience in Chile, referring to the two regions’ shared Spanish colonial history, Catholic faith and people-to-people ties.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines is positioning itself as Latin America’s bridge to Southeast Asia, testing whether shared history and culture can translate into hard trade figures as Asean and the Mercosur bloc look beyond their traditional partners.

Manila’s Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro made the pitch during visits to Brazil and Chile from August 10 to 13.

“Upon this human foundation, commercial bridges thrive: the Philippines stands as the premier strategic gateway for Latin American firms expanding into Asean’s US$4-trillion market,” she told an audience in Chile, referring to the two regions’ shared Spanish colonial history, Catholic faith and people-to-people ties.

Lazaro also floated the idea of expanding logistics links – citing the regional presence of Philippine port operator International Container Terminal Services – as a way to cut costs and shield supply chains from global shocks via direct trans-Pacific shipping routes.

The pitch lands in a crowded field, however: Singapore remains Southeast Asia’s dominant commercial, financial and logistics hub, while Vietnam and Indonesia have attracted growing interest from companies looking to diversify supply chains.

It also comes as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and Mercosur – a South American trade bloc whose members include Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and Uruguay – look for new partners amid US tariffs, energy insecurity and wider geopolitical uncertainty.

The two blocs do not have an existing free-trade agreement with each other and most trade is still conducted bilaterally. Combined two-way trade totalled a modest US$33.3 billion in 2023, the latest year for which figures are available.

Moves are being made to strengthen ties, however. Brazil has approved negotiating mandates to negotiate preferential trade deals with Indonesia and Vietnam. The South American nation also completed domestic approval of the Mercosur-Singapore Free Trade Agreement earlier this month.

“US tariffs have already motivated Mercosur to accelerate the trade agreement with the European Union,” said Alberto Maresca, a doctoral fellow at UNU-CRIS and Ghent University, and a visiting researcher at the Getulio Vargas Foundation’s School of International Relations in Brazil.

Maresca said Brazil was leading the push for closer ties with Southeast Asia, adding: “The need for economic and political diversification, motivated by Trump’s foreign policy, would be an important catalyst for a Mercosur-Asean agreement.”

Darynaufal Mulyaman, a political economist and assistant professor of international relations at the Christian University of Indonesia who studies both blocs, said the two regions were being pushed to spread risk more widely.

“States are no longer operating under the assumption that supply chains and partnerships will remain open and stable indefinitely,” he said. “That assumption breaking down forces both Asean and Mercosur to hedge rather than concentrate their dependencies on a narrow set of traditional partners.”

States are no longer operating under the assumption that supply chains and partnerships will remain open and stable indefinitely

Darynaufal Mulyaman, political economist

The Strait of Hormuz crisis continued to threaten Asia’s energy supplies, while Taiwan Strait tensions “threaten to disrupt the semiconductor and manufacturing chains that both Southeast Asia and, indirectly, Latin America depend on”, Mulyaman said.

“These are not abstract risks any more,” he added.

Both regions had good reason to diversify trade partners “at a time of heightened geopolitical competition, growing protectionism and uncertainty around traditional markets”, said Ariane Costa, deputy director of the Brazilian Centre for International Relations’ geopolitics programme.

Common histories

Cultural familiarity could give the Philippines an edge in attracting Latin American companies, analysts say, even if Manila cannot match Singapore’s infrastructure or financial depth.

“The Philippines certainly shares cultural similarities with Latin America and Mercosur due to the common histories that both countries and regions share with Spain,” Rodolfo Caffaro Kramer, president of the Mercosur-Asean Chamber of Commerce, told This Week in Asia.

“Naturally, these cultural similarities help foster trade, and in this regard, the Philippines is the Asean member with the closest cultural ties to Latin America.”

Free-trade agreements that reduce tariffs, cut red tape and harmonise regulations were “always welcome”, Kramer said.

Costa said the Philippines could still carve out a role by leaning on its geography, US ties, English-speaking business environment and growing links with other Asian markets.

“For Latin American companies seeking to enter Asean, the Philippines could therefore become an important entry point into specific sectors and value chains rather than a direct substitute for Singapore,” she said.

Other observers were more cautious, saying the Philippines could not rely on cultural similarities alone to strengthen economic ties.

“Filipino society does carry cultural affinities that make the idea of a gateway sound natural on paper,” Mulyaman said. “The real test becomes whether the country is competitive enough to open up genuinely attractive conditions for Latin American investors and traders.”

Compared with “capital rich Singapore” and “Vietnam’s aggressive catching up posture”, Manila still needed to do more before the gateway framing became “more than aspiration”, he added.

Pragmatic priorities

Closer ties would give both blocs “more agency in shaping the rules and institutions of the international economic system”, Costa said, strengthening the negotiation position of the Global South.

But she stressed that this “should not be construed as Mercosur choosing Asean and the Global South instead of Europe or North America”, adding: “The objective should be to avoid excessive dependence on any single market or geopolitical axis.”

Observers say the most promising areas for cooperation include food, agricultural technology, electronics, biofuels, critical minerals, infrastructure, logistics, energy and manufacturing.

“Mercosur has a great opportunity to become a large-scale food producer to supply Asean and help it achieve food security,” Kramer said.

Maresca added that Asean technology exports could help Mercosur reduce its reliance on Chinese and US imports, while Costa said Southeast Asia could offer new export markets for higher-value Mercosur goods and services.

However, any deeper relationship is likely to emerge gradually rather than through one sweeping bloc-to-bloc agreement.

“What is still missing is a broader strategic architecture connecting these initiatives,” Costa said, noting that internal differences, regulatory barriers and sensitivities over competition could slow progress – especially among South American sectors wary of Asian competition.

“Trade relationships require logistics, information, financing and networks, not only preferential tariffs,” she said.

“For these reasons, I would expect the relationship to develop incrementally: first through bilateral agreements with key Asean economies, followed by greater trade facilitation, investment and regulatory cooperation.”

item.title: [SCMP] The African firms adopting Chinese AI as US-China rivalry intensifies
item.description:
The United States may want the world to choose sides in the AI race with China, but in Africa, many businesses are pursuing a more pragmatic strategy: using Chinese models where they offer better value or flexibility, while keeping their options open.

For example, when African insurtech platform Curacel expanded the range of artificial intelligence (AI) models powering its internal infrastructure, it did not look only to Silicon Valley.

Instead, the Nigeria-based firm – which provides AI-powered claims and fraud-detection infrastructure to African insurers and fintech companies – added GLM-5.3, a Chinese model developed by Beijing-based Zhipu AI, alongside models from Western providers.
item.content:encoded:
The United States may want the world to choose sides in the AI race with China, but in Africa, many businesses are pursuing a more pragmatic strategy: using Chinese models where they offer better value or flexibility, while keeping their options open.

For example, when African insurtech platform Curacel expanded the range of artificial intelligence (AI) models powering its internal infrastructure, it did not look only to Silicon Valley.

Instead, the Nigeria-based firm – which provides AI-powered claims and fraud-detection infrastructure to African insurers and fintech companies – added GLM-5.3, a Chinese model developed by Beijing-based Zhipu AI, alongside models from Western providers.

Henry Mascot, chief executive and co-founder of Curacel, said Chinese models delivered comparable results at lower cost on high-volume tasks such as coding, data extraction, classification and customer support, although Western systems remained stronger on the most demanding reasoning and reliability-sensitive work.

“In our experience, the leading Chinese models have closed much of the performance gap,” Mascot said.

He said Curacel’s multi-model set-up allowed it to use GLM-5.3 selectively.

“We can route suitable workloads to it based on quality and cost without moving the entire stack or locking ourselves into one vendor,” Mascot said. “We have also used lower-cost [Chinese] models within client deployments.”

Curacel’s approach reflects a broader shift, with models such as DeepSeek, Qwen from Alibaba, the owner of the South China Morning Post, and Moonshot AI’s Kimi challenging established systems from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic.

Many Chinese models make their weights – the files that allow companies to adapt them and, with sufficient infrastructure, run them locally – available for download.

Their growing use in Africa coincides with Beijing’s efforts to expand its role in the continent’s digital infrastructure, technical training and AI governance.

Huawei Technologies is one example of how Chinese companies are combining AI models with the infrastructure needed to run them.

In May, its South African cloud business introduced a “model as a service” or MaaS platform, providing pay-per-token access to DeepSeek, Qwen and GLM, together with development and deployment tools.

China last month launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), with Beijing presenting its open-weight technology as an alternative to the largely proprietary systems offered by leading American companies.

The contest extends beyond models to semiconductors, critical minerals, cloud infrastructure and the rules governing AI. African businesses may choose technology according to price and performance, but governments could face growing pressure to align with Washington or Beijing.

That pressure is becoming more explicit. A draft State Department communication reviewed by Reuters on August 14 warned that countries joining Waico could be excluded from the US-led Pax Silica coalition.

Michael Michie, co-founder of Nairobi-based EverseTech – an AI consultancy that also builds AI systems for banks, government agencies and other African organisations – said Chinese models had begun to advance more quickly.

“A year or so ago, you might have expected to wait quite a long time for a Chinese model release that represented a major step forward. Now we are seeing meaningful improvements within six months or less,” Michie said.

EverseTech has moved some of its clients to Chinese models. A legal-sector client switched because of the lower cost per million tokens. Another, which relied heavily on retrieval-augmented generation – a process in which an AI system searches company documents before producing an answer – moved after EverseTech found that a Chinese model could convert the documents into searchable numerical representations faster and more cheaply, Michie said.

“For most customers, the question is no longer simply, ‘Which model is the most powerful?’ It is, ‘Which model gives me the capability I need at a price that makes commercial sense?’” he said.

Price is far from the only consideration. In Uganda, the developers of Sunflower – an AI model providing farmers with weather updates and agricultural advice in over 30 local languages – built the system on Qwen3 after finding it handled Ugandan languages better than models from Meta Platforms or Google.

Djamo, an Ivory Coast fintech company serving francophone Africa, assigns models according to the job at hand. Co-founder and CEO Hassan Bourgi said a lightweight Chinese model could handle a simple customer service task such as closing spam requests, while a more advanced model might be needed for complex work such as writing or reviewing code.

“It’s getting commoditised at some point for the simple stuff,” Bourgi said. “But when it’s very complex, I think the Americans are still a bit ahead today.”

Bernard Momanyi Nyagaka, co-founder of Sanifu AI, said open weights could allow banks and fintech companies to run models within their own infrastructure instead of sending sensitive information to an outside service. Sanifu helps internal teams build AI agents and data applications that automate manual work.

“Open weights mean you can self-host, fine-tune and keep sensitive data – bank records, KYC [know-your-customer] documents – inside your own infrastructure, rather than sending it to a third-party API [application programming interface],” Nyagaka said.

However, self-hosting requires computing capacity and technical expertise. Open-weight models may reduce reliance on a model developer, but dependence can shift to the cloud platforms, chips and technical support needed to run them.

Nyagaka advised that sensitive data should be kept local, regardless of geopolitics. “For banking, data sovereignty should be a design principle, not a vendor feature. Whatever model you use, the architecture should ensure regulated data doesn’t leave your controlled environment,” he said.

And while lower prices can make a model attractive, companies must also consider the cost of leaving the provider later.

Michie said: “The strategic mistake would be designing the institution so that five years from now, it has no realistic ability to move away from that model or provider.”

He said organisations should examine data-portability rules, termination rights and ownership of organisational data before committing to a provider.

Curacel limits that risk through a model gateway – a single interface that can route tasks to Chinese, American, European or self-hosted models. It also tests models against its own workloads rather than relying only on published benchmarks. “That makes switching a routing decision instead of a product rewrite,” Mascot said.

Nyagaka argued that open-weight Chinese models could, in some cases, create less dependence than proprietary Western services because companies could retain and host the model weights themselves. “The lock-in risk is highest with closed, hosted APIs of any origin,” he said.

But some tech executives have rejected the idea that African businesses must choose between Chinese and American AI.

“I would push back on the idea that Africa is merely a testing ground for US-China competition,” Mascot said. “African companies are active buyers. They will choose the technology that solves the problem at the right price, regardless of where it was built.”

That pragmatism, according to Michie, should ultimately give African firms more room to manoeuvre.

“Africa’s strongest position in the US-China technology competition is not choosing one side,” he said. “It is building enough capability and leverage to work with both and eventually contribute more of our own technology to that ecosystem.”

item.title: [SCMP] A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
item.description:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.

As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets.

Earlier this month, Chinese renewable energy company Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online in Ulanqab. The AI computing facility has, at its heart, a 120,000-square-metre AI data centre, roughly the area of 20 standard football pitches, according to a company statement.

Designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators, the campus has a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts, a scale that would make it one of the world’s largest AI computing facilities.

For comparison, Colossus 2, the massive US-based AI data centre run by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to a ranking by consultancy Epoch AI.

Envision selected the Ulanqab location because it could pair computing infrastructure directly with renewable power, with the Galaxy Campus partly powered by Envision wind farms, according to the firm.

Ulanqab accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s, according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

“Much of that wind once simply blew past, wasted,” said Yang Wenlong, a project director at Envision Group. “Now it can be turned into electricity for computing, and then into tokens.”

About 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s energy was powered by green electricity, including solar power, Yang noted.

A decade-long pivot

Ulanqab’s shift from raising cattle and potato harvesting to the AI frontier has followed a decade-long path.

In 2013, Huawei Technologies began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab.

Short video giant Kuaishou initiated construction of a data centre in 2020, and completed the first phase of a centre designed for 300,000 servers several years later.

Traditional data centre operators VNET, Centrin Data and Chindata have since added green, AI-focused computing projects in Ulanqab, and Hangzhou-based AI model start-up DeepSeek was reportedly set to add one gigawatt of computing capacity in the city earlier this year.

As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, according to local government figures.

The city has a combined 12.5 gigawatts of capacity under development or planned, three times the 4.2 gigawatts projected for Johor, the southern state of Malaysia that has emerged as one of the largest data centre sites in the Asia-Pacific region, according to recent research by investment bank Goldman Sachs.

“We are no longer selling computing power; we are selling tokens,” said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data management bureau, referring to the industry’s preferred measure for the units of text processed by AI models.

China’s appetite for those tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025, before exceeding 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data.

This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them. For Ulanqab, the wind blowing across the grasslands is no longer merely an energy resource – it helps to power an AI query.

And every AI token comes with a cost.

The power economy

“Every one million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data.

In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power.

Rates vary by supply arrangement, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (US$0.05) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can account for 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant.

At full utilisation, a one-gigawatt AI computing centre might consume as much as 8.76 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. Cutting the electricity cost by just 0.1 yuan per kilowatt-hour might reduce a centre’s annual power bill by about 876 million yuan.

For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is no marginal advantage – it is a central part of the business model.

But it is only half the equation. The electricity consumed by computing equipment ultimately becomes heat that has to be removed.

That is how Ulanqab’s cold, dry climate provides another advantage. With an annual average temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius, the city can use outside air as a natural cooling resource for much of the year, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and leaving more electricity available for computing.

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes directly to computing, while a higher figure indicates more power is consumed by supporting systems such as cooling and power conversion.

Leading data-centre clusters in the region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of close to 1.5, meaning that more of each watt reaches its chips.

A difference of only a few cents can translate into hundreds of millions of yuan in savings at gigawatt scale. Those efficiencies matter because the amount of electricity consumed by computing has been rapidly rising.

China’s data centres consumed about 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.6 per cent of national power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA).

By 2030, annual consumption by the sector was expected to reach about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times 2025 levels, and account for roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use, according to Wang Hongzhi, director of the NEA.

A coordinated system

The race to secure electricity for AI infrastructure is not unique to China. In the US, the rapid expansion of AI data centres has raised concerns about whether existing power grids can keep pace with demand, with some projects facing delays because of a bottleneck in securing enough electricity.

This is in contrast to Ulanqab, where AI giants and tech behemoths are betting that its wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a cheaper and more sustainable foundation for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

For China, the challenge is not only generating enough electricity, but also ensuring that electricity supply and computing capacity grow in tandem.

In 2026, China’s Government Work Report called for the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply for the first time, reflecting Beijing’s push to better align its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure with the country’s power system.

The concept, known as “computing-power and electricity coordination”, aimed to bring together electricity generation, grid capacity, energy storage and computing resources so that renewable power could be used more efficiently to support growing AI demand.

Jiang Yi, spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, described the new power grid as providing stable, clean electricity, the computing network as the “brain” directing intelligent power-grid scheduling and renewable energy consumption, and the communications network as the “highway” supporting cross-regional computing.

That vision goes beyond simply building more data centres. It requires linking electricity, computing and communications infrastructure into a more coordinated, national system.

For Ulanqab, that could make its advantages more valuable. Its wind farms provide renewable electricity, data centres then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia.

But China’s computing boom has created another challenge: not all that capacity is being used.

While demand for AI computing is surging in some of the country’s biggest technology centres, large amounts of capacity elsewhere remain underused, leaving servers, power infrastructure and expensive data centre facilities running below their potential.

Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) puts the gap in stark terms. In 2025, China’s intelligent-computing centres had about 3.8 billion card-hours of intelligent-computing capacity available, but only about 1.4 billion card-hours were actually used, putting utilisation at just 36.8 per cent.

CAICT has called for closer coordination between computing supply and demand, including better scheduling of computing resources and more precise matching between users and available capacity.

The mismatch reflects the geography of China’s computing buildout. Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates, while much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based.

Moving up the value chain

For Ulanqab, the next challenge is therefore not simply building more servers, but making sure those servers are connected to real demand.

The city is now seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan for 2026-28, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens.

The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, focusing on green computing for large AI model training and inference, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent.

The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models.

For a user sitting thousands of kilometres away, an AI query may take only seconds to answer.

Behind that response, however, is a chain of infrastructure stretching back to places such as Ulanqab: servers drawing electricity, cooling systems removing heat and wind turbines turning the movement of air across the grasslands into power.

The next time someone asks a chatbot a question, part of the answer may begin with the wind passing through the grasslands of Inner Mongolia – transformed first into electricity, then computing power and finally into the words that appear on a screen.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but how long will the trend last?
item.description:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.

The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.
item.content:encoded:
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.

In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.

The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.

Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting open spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales.

Tuen Mun Town Plaza went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.

“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the plaza.

“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

What appeared to be a desperate measure by Hong Kong’s retail and catering sectors – still struggling with the trend of residents heading to mainland China for cheaper shopping and dining options – turned into an initial success.

Chhoa said the shopping centre had witnessed a “noticeable” 20 per cent surge in holiday foot traffic following the promotion, and a 10 to 15 per cent rise in weekday attendance.

All in the game

At Hanamaruken, a ramen shop inside the plaza, co-founder Jelly Tong said her team upgraded the basic Beyblade provided by the landlord to a high-performance model to better compete with visiting players after recognising the game’s potential to boost business.

“Word then spread in their Beyblade chat groups that our store had an exceptionally strong set-up, and some kids ended up bringing six or seven friends over to challenge us,” Tong said. “Afterwards, they stayed here to eat and discuss our custom gear.”

The commercial benefits have extended beyond restaurants and toy retailers to high-end luxury tenants such as Lukfook Jewellery. A regional manager said that setting up an in-store battle station helped break down traditional stereotypes surrounding luxury retail.

“We saw many new faces coming in after matching with our staff to browse our products and some actually made transactions,” said Patrick Ng Pui-kuen, the brand’s New Territories West district manager, who oversees the branches in Tuen Mun.

Among dozens of enthusiasts gathered at the shopping complex were 24-year-old warehouse worker Liu Chun-yin and his friend.

“Sometimes I show my spinning top at the nearby ice cream shop here to get special offers or battle against the staff at the tea shop to win a discount,” Liu said.

His friend, a recent Beyblade convert, recalled a visit where he stayed at the venue from 2pm until 9pm, spending seven hours straight battling fellow players and purchasing food and drinks in between matches.

At the D-Park residential and shopping complex in Tsuen Wan, dedicated free-play zones equipped with rows of desks have also drawn parents with young children alongside seasoned adult hobbyists.

Andy Yip, a 34-year-old civil servant from Kowloon East, made a trip to Tsuen Wan with his 11-year-old son and other family members, knowing there would be players at the venue.

“Before my son picked up the hobby, we spent most of our weekends in mainland China, but now we stay in Hong Kong more to accompany him, as he wants to play Beyblade with others,” he said.

Yip added that these outings were typically paired with dining and retail shopping, noting that he typically spent HK$1,000 (US$128) on dinner after his son played at D-Park, while their family members browsed at nearby shops during matches.

At the Pioneer Centre shopping centre in Prince Edward, management has introduced a few Beyblade stadiums to attract a steady stream of parents and children, accompanied by a spend-to-draw promotion offering exclusive models of the tops as prizes.

Eric Cheng, senior leasing manager at the mall, said the set-up and promotion in August had driven a 5 to 10 per cent increase in foot traffic compared with the same period last year, while sales at electronic goods and food and beverage businesses had jumped by 15 and 20 per cent, respectively.

“Compared with other intellectual property photo spots or traditional pop-ups, Beyblade’s interactive nature brings us much higher foot traffic,” Cheng said.

“Visitors at photo spots often leave after taking pictures, while playing Beyblade at the mall gets them to stay longer.”

Cheng said that longer stays could translate to higher spending as shoppers sought food and beverage options in between battles.

Only a short-term cure?

But according to one economist, the Beyblade trend is a temporary solution and not a cure-all for the city’s broader retail sector challenges.

Professor Terence Chong Tai-leung, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance, said shopping centres were ideal venues for Beyblade matches, which required space, and operators could set up play zones at a low cost.

“On a micro level, it drives temporary food and beverage spending as visitors have a reason to come,” Chong said, noting that overall the retail sector has still failed to show significant growth over the past year.

But he stressed that such initiatives were not enough to counter broader macroeconomic headwinds or the flow of residents across the border, noting that price remained the most significant factor driving consumer behaviour.

To stay relevant in the long run, local shopping centres should rethink their structural function, shifting from traditional sales hubs towards specialised themed venues or showrooms for physical products, he said.

“Most successful malls in Hong Kong have distinct themes, and if you want to attract people, you have to concentrate,” he said. “For example, becoming the definitive hub for sneakers so that people will visit whenever they want to buy sneakers.”

Showrooms would also allow customers to preview products before purchasing them online, he said.

“Due to structural shifts in shopping habits, consumer needs that used to require a mall visit can now be easily met through various online platforms,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] SpaceX’s Starlink blackout punishes Myanmar civilians, not just cybercriminals
item.description:
SpaceX discontinued its Global Roam service for existing customers as of Monday. The US company offered no specific reason beyond regulatory compliance, but few would question the move, given the need to clamp down on the increasing number of cybercrime networks that tap into its Starlink services globally.

Yet in Myanmar, the Starlink move is a double-edged sword.

The country’s civil conflict has cut many people off from conventional digital communications. For conflict-affected communities, SpaceX’s decision could mean being disconnected from the internet.
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX discontinued its Global Roam service for existing customers as of Monday. The US company offered no specific reason beyond regulatory compliance, but few would question the move, given the need to clamp down on the increasing number of cybercrime networks that tap into its Starlink services globally.

Yet in Myanmar, the Starlink move is a double-edged sword.

The country’s civil conflict has cut many people off from conventional digital communications. For conflict-affected communities, SpaceX’s decision could mean being disconnected from the internet.

The move thus risks reinforcing the long-standing strategy of Myanmar’s military – and the current military-backed regime – governing through information control and the disruption of humanitarian services. The regime’s head recently noted that Starlink connections were being used by the online scam industry.

What he failed to mention was that many parts of Myanmar, including those held by anti-government forces, rely on Starlink to access the internet. Nearly 40 per cent of Myanmar’s townships now experience intermittent or total internet shutdowns every month.

Since the 2021 coup, the military has weaponised internet access, imposing mobile-network shutdowns and internet blackouts in conflict-ridden areas across the country. As the ensuing civil war has damaged telecommunications infrastructure, communities have been further isolated.

An estimated 13 million people – nearly a quarter of Myanmar’s population – rely on Starlink for digital access because no viable alternative exists in conflict zones.

Across much of Sagaing, Kachin, Karenni, Chin and other contested regions, healthcare providers, community-based organisations, schools and local administrative bodies depend on Starlink terminals to coordinate emergency medical referrals, organise humanitarian relief, deliver remote education and issue security warnings.

At least 6,000 schools run by local authorities and communities mostly operate online due to the ongoing civil conflict. Thousands of healthcare facilities in mixed-control and conflict areas also rely heavily on Starlink technology for daily coordination and operations.

For the relatively low price of around US$120 per month, one terminal can accommodate about 100 users. Most are humanitarian or community-based organisations and residents in conflict zones.

Myanmar is not officially licensed for Starlink operations. Formal regulatory approval would be required from the Myanmar authorities – something the military is not inclined to do, given Starlink’s use by both scam centres and opposition groups. Many terminals have reportedly been registered through other countries. All of which means the end of Global Roam has huge implications for the millions who depend on the roaming satellite service for emergency healthcare support, education and essential digital connectivity.

When the internet goes dark in a conflict zone, fear spreads faster than facts. Violence and human rights abuses become harder to document, verify, investigate and hold to account. In locations such as Saw township, where communities have faced military air strikes and bombing in recent months, the absence of reliable information has allowed rumours to spread rapidly. Villagers have fled in panic, sometimes towards danger. Satellite internet access enabled emergency medical teams and humanitarian workers to reach victims and provide immediate first-line support.

With Global Roam’s discontinuation and stricter guidelines for international use across other Roam tiers, local communities and humanitarian organisations in Myanmar are looking for alternatives.

A community worker in Myanmar’s dry zone said locally built mesh or radio networks could offer a temporary means of communication, but no alternative could match Global Roam’s affordability, portability, ease of deployment or scale.

Other options exist, in theory, such as geostationary-orbit satellites or an upgrade to Starlink’s Global Priority tier. But in practice, they are not realistic. High prices and limits on data usage put them out of reach for financially struggling local community organisations and people living in conflict zones.

There is another dimension here. Since 2025, Starlink has reportedly been under investigation by the US Congress for providing internet access to scam centres in Myanmar. This led to the shutdown of more than 2,500 terminals seemingly associated with scam compounds. Even before the recent policy change, users in Karenni (Kayah), Rakhine and parts of Sagaing had experienced Starlink access blockages as a result of crackdowns on scam operations.

Over the past five years, cybercrime syndicates along the Thai-Myanmar border have proliferated, using satellite internet to evade law enforcement and sustain billion-dollar scam networks targeting victims worldwide, despite crackdowns. SpaceX’s recent policy change shows that the company and US lawmakers are stepping up their response to criminal enterprises exploiting satellite technology.

But scam syndicates are not ordinary users. Local insiders anticipate that groups with the financial resources have already shifted to higher-priced connectivity options, including Starlink’s more expensive global plans, or switched to in-country internet services after relocating from the border areas to the inland Myanmar.

This is not the first time they have survived crackdowns. In 2025, China teamed up with the Thai and Lao authorities to launch a massive multinational operation against cross-border scam networks in the Thai-Myanmar border area.

Thailand has also cut off scam centres from landline internet, fuel and electricity. Last year, Starlink shut down devices used by the scam compounds. Yet the criminals adapted, shifting from industrial-scale operations to smaller ones, moving inland and changing their targets from Chinese nationals to Americans. These centres grew exponentially in 2025 and 2026.

More than 300 civil society organisations operating in Myanmar have urged the US government, SpaceX and the international community to consider establishing a “targeted restrictive mechanism” that denies scam centres access to the internet while preserving civilian connectivity.

Myanmar’s tech dependency dilemma represents a stark reality: the scam economy and humanitarian services both require internet access, but cutting off one could impose a far heavier burden on the other.

The question, therefore, is not whether governments and technology companies should combat cyber-enabled crime. They should. Rather, the question is whether they can do so without unintentionally undermining humanitarian operations and cutting off civilians from the internet.

Su Mon Thazin Aung is a Fellow with the Myanmar Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. She is also an Adjunct Assistant Professor at the Department of Southeast Asian Studies, National University of Singapore. This article was first published by the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg

item.title: [SCMP] Bites to bytes: Thai street food app feeds into hunger for authenticity
item.description:
Bangkok’s best street food has always existed on a kind of mental map for Thai food writer Choltanutkun Tun-atiruj.

It is built from habit, cravings and neighbourhood rhythms: the office crowds, the schools, the university nearby and the vendors selling everything from moo ping (grilled pork skewers) and sticky rice to pad thai and kuay teow reua – a bowl of rice noodles in dark broth flavoured with cow or pig’s blood, then topped with meat and spices.

“I can’t tell you my favourite because I rotate between vendors, depending on what I’m craving that day, but ever since I moved to this area a few years ago, I’ve never had to order anything on [food delivery and ride-hailing super-app] Grab ever again,” said Choltanutkun, who lives in Sukhumvit in the heart of the Thai capital.
item.content:encoded:
Bangkok’s best street food has always existed on a kind of mental map for Thai food writer Choltanutkun Tun-atiruj.

It is built from habit, cravings and neighbourhood rhythms: the office crowds, the schools, the university nearby and the vendors selling everything from moo ping (grilled pork skewers) and sticky rice to pad thai and kuay teow reua – a bowl of rice noodles in dark broth flavoured with cow or pig’s blood, then topped with meat and spices.

“I can’t tell you my favourite because I rotate between vendors, depending on what I’m craving that day, but ever since I moved to this area a few years ago, I’ve never had to order anything on [food delivery and ride-hailing super-app] Grab ever again,” said Choltanutkun, who lives in Sukhumvit in the heart of the Thai capital.

Officials are now trying to turn mental maps like hers into a more formal one.

The Thai Street Gold Star app, developed by the Office of Small and Medium Enterprises Promotion and Suan Dusit University, was launched in late July. It is being rolled out across Bangkok, Pattaya in Chonburi province and Chiang Mai.

The app aims to boost the visibility and reach of food vendors while supporting efforts to lift the sector to international standards. Users can search for approved vendors, browse menus and find directions to each stall.

To receive certification, vendors must meet requirements covering food hygiene and sanitation, the identity and memorability of their dishes and customer service standards.

The use of digital technology alongside higher standards would improve operators’ competitiveness, generate income for small and medium-sized enterprises, stimulate tourism and help establish Thailand as a global gastronomy and wellness-tourism destination, said deputy government spokeswoman Lalida Persvivatana.

Aphisavadh Sirivadhanawaravachara, a researcher on hospitality management and tourism in Thailand, said the app had potential to elevate the sector by increasing vendors’ visibility and creating new marketing opportunities.

“It should not be viewed simply as a way to regulate or relocate vendors, but as an opportunity to create an ecosystem that helps vendors develop their businesses, build their brands, access new markets, and connect more effectively with tourism,” Aphisavadh said.

Thailand had an enormous advantage in the diversity of its local cuisine, he said, suggesting that the app could eventually showcase the distinctive food, ingredients, culinary traditions and experiences of each region.

Food and lifestyle writer Sansern Srisawat said the app could help locals and tourists navigate the myriad food stalls around the country.

“Nowadays, I see people using Google Maps as a guide, but it isn’t designed specifically for food,” he said. “It will help customers make decisions and trust those vendors more.”

It could also serve as an alternative marketing avenue for vendors facing lower profits after signing up for food delivery platforms to reach more customers, Sansern said.

Big money

For many tourists, Thailand’s street food is a major reason to visit the country. Government figures put the value of the country’s street food market at more than 261 billion baht (US$7.9 billion).

But researchers say its importance goes far beyond tourism.

“Street food is not a tourist attraction added on top of Thai cities; it is how urban Thailand feeds itself every day,” said Weerapak Samsiripong, a researcher for the Institute for Population and Social Research at Mahidol University.

Weerapak, whose research spans street food and urban security in Thailand, said many locals relied on street food, but it was especially important for lower-income populations, accounting for two-thirds of their household food budget.

That made the app design important, he said, particularly because Thailand already had several street food certifications. “Gold Star will be most useful if it is aligned with the existing standards … It can become the unifying mark this landscape needs.”

But he said gaps remained in the level of support, communication and practical guidance that some vendors received, especially when policies were carried out at the local level.

Street food policy needed to involve vendors, Aphisavadh said, pointing to the apprehension of those operating in unauthorised areas. “Of course, regulations and public order are important. But we can also look at these situations as opportunities rather than simply problems,” he said.

Weerapak said policymakers needed a clearer picture of the sector itself, adding that government figures on street food income accounted only for the “visible” parts of the sector, while the contributions of vendors operating without fixed addresses remained unknown.

“Without knowing how many vendors there are, where they operate and what they need, it is difficult to design support that actually fits them,” he said.

Lost in translation

The local government’s recent attempt to manage kerbside stalls by moving vendors into designated market areas has also raised concerns that the city could lose some of the charm that has made it popular among visitors.

“Unless you go somewhere like Chinatown or Khao San Road … there are fewer vendors than from a few years ago. Many street vendors have been moved or organised away,” Choltanutkun said.

While she appreciated Bangkok’s cleaner footpaths, especially in areas such as Sukhumvit, Choltanutkun said street food vendors brought “so much charm and character to the city”.

Sansern said he still wanted to see long-standing vendors “thrive while staying true to their originality”, rather than transforming themselves into stalls in large department stores or tourist-heavy areas.

But it did not have to be an either-or solution, Weerapak said, because Thailand did not need to choose between preserving the charm of its street food stalls and making them more organised.

“Good street food management is not about banning or permitting; it is about the balance between control and support,” he said. “Street food policy works best when economic promotion, tourism, city orderliness and health are pursued as one synergistic package rather than separately.”

Aphisavadh added that the initiative had the potential to preserve and elevate Thai street food culture, provided it helped vendors become more professional while protecting their authenticity.

“If we can achieve that, the Thai Street Gold Star app could become much more than an app for finding street food,” he said. “It could become a strategic tool for Thai street food development, culinary tourism and local economic development.”

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s Anwar traded reform for power. Now Umno wants it all
item.description:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.

The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.
item.content:encoded:
The roar from thousands of People’s Justice Party (PKR) delegates gathered at a grand convention centre in Melaka last weekend exuded all the confidence expected of a party leading Malaysia’s government.
