The past three years have been the culmination of more than two decades of struggle for PKR, with it finally achieving its long-held goal of installing leader Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and wielding the power to push through reforms.

Yet beneath the confident facade lurks a ruling party now scrambling to find its way.

PKR’s victory in the 2022 general election came at the cost of the very reforms it had promised to deliver, as Anwar had little choice but to negotiate compromises with erstwhile rivals, including former ruling party Umno, to steady his administration. Those trade-offs did not go unnoticed.

Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, of which PKR is a founding and principal member, has suffered a series of bruising defeats across three state elections since November – and whatever platform the prime minister gave a once-deflated Umno has turned the party into the greatest threat to his rule.

Staring down the possibility of being turfed out of Putrajaya after just one term, PKR members are left wondering how to reverse the trend, especially as surging Malay nationalist sentiment carries a resurgent Umno forward.

“The delegates are all confused. They need clear direction,” a senior party leader told This Week in Asia, speaking anonymously due to the sensitivity of the matter.

“Before, it was about coming to power and raising Anwar as prime minister. Now what?”

Senior members who attended last weekend’s congress pointed to a disconnect between Anwar, his party’s top leadership and the rank and file, who have been left without a common purpose to rally around.

That gulf became apparent during Anwar’s opening speech at the congress last Saturday.

Delegates gave only a lukewarm response as their party president and prime minister listed out, at length, his administration’s successes in bolstering growth and investment numbers.

It was only when Anwar touched on the multibillion-ringgit scandal at the Tabung Haji pilgrim fund – made public last month – that the crowd roared to life, with some delegates passionately demanding retribution against Umno, the party in power when the alleged offences occurred.

That reaction offered the clearest indication yet that the prime minister and PH need to coalesce around a clear message if they hope to slow Umno’s momentum, and that of its nascent partnership with the opposition Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS).

“You see Umno and PAS talking about uniting the ummah [Muslim faithful], and claims that [PKR coalition partner] DAP is out to wrest power from the Malays. It’s simple messaging that people can easily understand,” the senior PKR leader said.

When comparing investments and other economic indicators, Anwar scored higher than past leaders, he said. “But the people here don’t understand all that. You need to present things using simple language.”

House of cards

The problems trace back to November 2022, when Anwar was named prime minister by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah on condition that he form a unity government that included allies and rivals alike, to avoid a hung parliament.

The arrangement threw a lifeline to Umno, which had just suffered its worst electoral outing, winning fewer than 30 of parliament’s 222 seats.

From there, Anwar has been accused of setting aside his reform agenda and steering his government rightward, mirroring the previous Umno administration’s penchant for cracking down on sexual minorities and free speech in a bid to win over a Malay-Muslim majority suspicious of his motives.

Despite growing outrage from long-time supporters, the prime minister enjoyed a period of relative political stability over the first half of his five-year term, as economic growth and foreign investment hit record highs.

But that proved to be merely the calm before the storm.

The first salvo was fired in the Sabah state election last November, when Anwar’s PH coalition was all but wiped out. Hardest hit was the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the largest party in Anwar’s federal coalition, which lost every seat it contested.

Over the past two months, PH’s tenuous grip on power has truly sunk in, as it suffered back-to-back defeats at the hand of fellow federal partner, Umno.

Umno cruised to an extended supermajority in the southern state of Johor in July, then struck an informal alliance with Islamist rivals PAS to wrest control of Negeri Sembilan state from PH earlier this month.

The losses in the three state elections were the first tangible signs that Anwar and PH were in real trouble, after years of complaints from civil society groups and PH’s own support base about the lack of reforms following decades of promises.

Wong Chen, a three-term MP who quit PKR this month after being unceremoniously removed from a government post and cut off from his constituency fund, said the current trend pointed to PH losing the next national poll, which must be held by February 2028 at the latest.

If they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support

PKR defector Wong Chen on his former party

Wong, who later joined fellow former PKR leader Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama party, said the recent string of electoral losses proved that Anwar’s personal popularity was not enough to guarantee PH’s survival against Umno and PAS.

“They have to start accepting the fact that if they don’t quickly reform in the last few months that they have, then they won’t even be able to win enough support to be a strong opposition,” Wong said.

The losses did trigger a response from Anwar. Last weekend, he pledged that the government would proceed to repeal the controversial University and University Colleges Act 1971 – which student activists have long said stifles freedom of speech and expression – and fulfil promises to impose a two-term limit on the prime minister and separate the powers of the attorney general and public prosecutor.

But those pledges may amount to little if they only translate into legislative change, according to Timothy Wong, a senior analyst with government affairs consultancy BowerGroupAsia.

“There needs to be real action behind institutional reforms rather than relying solely on legislation to convince the majority,” he said.

“They will need to do more to convince a politically fatigued electorate, especially urban and middle-class voters who are feeling increasingly disenfranchised by the country’s politics.”

Complicating matters further is Anwar’s continued reliance on Umno, which long-time Malaysia watcher James Chin says has every reason to sabotage the prime minister’s reform push, leveraging its cabinet positions – and the budgets that come with them – to bolster its own electoral chances.

“If you want to do real deep reforms, you have to inform the cabinet. And of course Umno, which has a lot of ministers in cabinet, will try to sabotage it or not agree to it, so you’re stuck,” said Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

“He [Anwar] knows deep down inside that Umno is plotting to win the next election and replace him as prime minister.”

Cracks in PH

Anwar caught a break, of sorts, last weekend, when delegates at DAP’s own convention voted decisively to remain within the governing coalition, after months of speculation the party might walk away.

But that lopsided vote belied the seething dissent within DAP’s ranks over how Anwar has managed the ruling coalition – especially his perceived favouring of Umno.

“Instead of bringing the coalition partners together, what has he done? He has divided us, pitted one against the other and empowered Umno. We cannot afford to ignore that,” DAP leader Sangeet Kaur Deo told her party’s convention.

“We cannot run away from the fact that today, under our government, Malaysia is more divided on racial lines than ever before. We cannot deny that there are scandals relating to corruption that have escalated during the time that we have been in power.”

Within PKR itself, the complaints are just as pointed. Some argue Anwar’s political instincts have curdled into self preservation.

His decision, in closing the party congress last Sunday, to announce an extra 222 million ringgit (US$54.6 million) in annual constituency allocations for MPs – money used for everything from pothole repairs to cash handouts for the needy – struck many grass-roots members as besides the point.

It did nothing to address the growing anger over stalled reform, critics say – with no explanation offered either for why three PKR MPs seen as loyal to Rafizi had their own allocations slashed.

Rafizi quit PKR after losing the deputy presidency to Anwar’s daughter, Nurul Izzah, in a contest he claimed was rife with nepotism.

Nurul Izzah has since stepped back too, beginning what the party has called a “leave of absence” to pursue her studies after serving her final days as her father’s deputy at the congress.

The extra funding fits a pattern: over the past two years, Anwar has pushed to increase cash handouts and maintain costly fuel subsidies despite the strain on public coffers, in a bid to win broader support.

One grass-roots leader offered a warning from history. “You can’t keep giving people freebies and expect them to love you. Look at what happened during BN’s time,” he said, invoking the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition that lost power in 2018 at the height of the 1MDB corruption scandal despite its own cash-handout scheme. “They still lost. We are doing exactly the same thing now.”

These internal rifts may not trigger an outright collapse of PH, but analysts warn that pressure from DAP and PKR supporters will keep mounting as long as Anwar prioritises political stability and his relationship with Umno over the reform agenda.

“The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out as an electoral alliance,” said public policy adviser Kamles Kumar, associate director for Malaysia at strategic advisory group Asia Group Advisors.

“If electoral losses continue, the question will increasingly shift from whether PH can stay together to whether staying together still benefits each component party.”

And the next test for PH is not far off. The Melaka state election, which must be called by February next year, is already looming and the Umno-led BN – which holds 21 of the state assembly’s 28 seats – has signalled its terms for any future deal: PH can have a shot at the seven seats BN does not currently control, but nothing more.

The bigger danger is not PH formally breaking apart, but becoming increasingly hollowed out

Kamles Kumar, public policy adviser

According to one Melaka-based PKR grass-roots leader, the party leadership is seriously considering the offer, even if it means accepting a subordinate role to Umno.

Yet this appears badly out of step with sentiments on the ground. “The top are talking about negotiating with BN, but we’ve already seen what happened in the two past state elections. On the ground, people are already sharpening their knives,” the insider said.

“As far as the grass roots are concerned, we have two choices. Fight and lose, or not do anything and die [politically].”

Anwar has promised party delegates he will listen: to their opinions, their suggestions and even their criticism.

For a party that spent 20 years fighting to put him in power – and is now watching that power slip through its fingers – the question is no longer whether he hears them.

It is whether, after everything, just listening will be enough.

Additional reporting by Iman Muttaqin Yusof

item.title: [SCMP] As natural disasters rage, does China’s ‘top-down’ climate model provide a way forward?
item.description:
A punishing drought is draining Europe’s great rivers, pushing the Loire, the Danube and the Rhine towards record lows.

At the Kaub gauging station, the reference point for shipping on the Rhine – Germany’s economic artery – the water level fell to 17cm (6.7 inches) this month, a low unseen since measurements began in 1880.

Meanwhile, wildfires are burning across southern Europe, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of thousands and producing the defining image of a European summer in which disaster has come to feel as seasonal as the holidays.
item.content:encoded:
A punishing drought is draining Europe’s great rivers, pushing the Loire, the Danube and the Rhine towards record lows.

At the Kaub gauging station, the reference point for shipping on the Rhine – Germany’s economic artery – the water level fell to 17cm (6.7 inches) this month, a low unseen since measurements began in 1880.

Meanwhile, wildfires are burning across southern Europe, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of thousands and producing the defining image of a European summer in which disaster has come to feel as seasonal as the holidays.

But this is not a story unique to any one continent or hemisphere. In recent weeks, smoke from intensified Canadian wildfires drifted down the American east coast, leaving New Yorkers struggling to breathe, while China has battled a prolonged heatwave and persistent floods while bracing for what could be the strongest El Nino cycle in the past 150 years.

The cascade of crises has revived an old question: how should societies adapt to a rapidly changing climate? It is one the world’s three leading economies are answering very differently.

The green transition is no longer something [China] needs external pressure to pursue. It’s a basic national development strategy

Jiangwen Guo, Chatham House

The results, analysts warn, are just as disparate. China’s government can set long-term plans and back them with public money and strong execution.

The United States leans heavily on its private sector, with little public effort to match. Europe sits uneasily between the two: its public institutions short of long-term vision and money, its private sector short of awareness.

“Compared with the Western system, China’s greatest advantage in these areas is its very strong capacity for top-down implementation,” said Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow in the Environment and Society Centre at Chatham House.

“That is the root of all of this.”

Governments everywhere face the same three challenges on climate adaptation, according to Guo.

The first is that adaptation is hard to quantify. Cutting emissions produces a number, so investors can see what their money bought; protecting a city against future heat does not, and public attention fades with the weather.

Each heatwave, wildfire or flood in Europe makes the threat feel real, she said, and once it passes, the scar is easily forgotten.

The second is that risk is intensely local, which makes region-by-region risk assessment an indispensable first step. China’s 2035 adaptation strategy, published in 2022, devotes a full chapter to it, an advance on its predecessors.

The third is that adaptation cuts across regions, industries and government departments, making coordination extremely difficult, especially when it is already a lower priority for many.

China faces all three, Guo said, but was likely to implement solutions better than most, with the central government recognising the need for climate adaptation and willing to invest in it.

“Across China, the green transition is no longer something the country needs external pressure to pursue. It’s a basic national development strategy,” she said.

That strategy carries benefits as well as drawbacks. China’s rapid production of solar panels, for instance, brought prices down and encouraged widespread adoption – but the abundant supply has proven difficult to stem, with fierce intra-industry competition driving down prices and leading the country’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to deem the phenomenon an issue that must be “comprehensively addressed”.

European analysts said crucial elements were missing from the continent’s efforts to adapt to the rapidly changing climate.

“The economic and political mindset of our current leaders tends towards letting the market decide rather than planning for the long term,” said Clement Caudron, a project lead at The Shift Project, a Paris-based climate think tank.

France was not putting enough resources into its climate efforts, while the absence of a long-term vision and sufficient, stable public funding made it hard for businesses and ordinary people to plan ahead, according to Caudron.

Budget constraints were also limiting the government’s ability to launch major public investment programmes in strategic sectors, Caudron explained. Climate, he said, was often among the first items to be sacrificed in budget negotiations.

The Fonds Vert (Green Fund), a French government fund created in August 2022 after a summer of heatwaves to help local authorities pay for environmental infrastructure – including climate adaptation – has seen the money available for new projects fall from €2.5 billion (US$2.9 billion) in 2024 to €1.15 billion in 2025, and €837 million in this year’s budget.

“Exceptions do get made in major crises – during Covid, we allowed ourselves to spend public money to support the economy and stave off a collapse – which proves we can do it when we want to,” Caudron said.

“But for the climate, the emergency is evidently not deemed sufficient to justify the same.”

Similar challenges were present at the EU level, according to Antoine Oger, executive director of the Institute for European Environmental Policy think tank.

He said climate adaptation required systematic efforts and significant investment in near-term budgets, but the effects might only be felt in the long term, which are not in sync with politicians’ short-term mandates.

“For them it’s not particularly enticing to make some decisions that will have impact in 20 years from now, from a purely political perspective,” he said.

The EU also struggles with its complex governance system that makes the massive, coordinated effort necessary for harmonised climate adaptation policies difficult, according to Oger.

Where Brussels is hemmed in by electoral cycles and shared competences, Beijing can plan in decades, Oger said, crediting this area as one where China’s system had the edge.

“There are, of course, different governance layers in China, but this is a much more integrated system to deal with this sort of long-term change … The five-year planning is much better than an electoral cycle, from a governance perspective,” he said.

Oger said he was not arguing for the EU to adopt China’s model, which had problems of its own. But, he added, a system built around a stable, coherent and long-term outlook was better equipped for a slow-moving, systemic challenge like climate change. “That is just a fact.”

The EU also lags on private-sector awareness, an area where the United States offers a model, according to Thibault Laconde, founder of Callendar, a French firm that helps companies adapt to climate change.

Since the Los Angeles fires and a run of severe droughts, many American companies have moved to protect themselves against future extreme weather, he said. Corporate awareness, in his view, may matter more for adaptation than public awareness did.

“If you’re a company, you do not need an incentive to do it. It’s in your own interest to make sure your factory or your infrastructure can keep operating reliably,” Laconde said.

But the private sector-driven model in the US also had its own limitations – in particular, a lack of “patient capital” provided by the government – to help companies overcome their short-term impulses in their long-term investments, according to Todd Tucker, director of industrial policy and trade at the Roosevelt Institute.

The United States still did not have a national plan for climate adaptation, and most states lacked one too, wrote Madison Condon, a professor at Boston University School of Law, in a report published by the institute in July. Both China and the EU have adopted blueprints.

And there are some gaps in this realm the private sector cannot fill. When Washington moved to dismantle the National Centre for Atmospheric Research, American insurance actuaries formally objected, Condon noted, arguing the centre’s continuity was “not only a scientific necessity, but an economic one” for an industry that depended on its data to price climate risk.

Even in those areas where commercial providers present alternatives, opting for the private-sector option carries risks.

The US state of Connecticut licensed climate-risk scores from a private firm, an approach Condon warned left the government endorsing black-box models whose inputs and methodology it did not control, adding that publicly maintained models could serve as a check on private-sector data.

Regardless of the system, the increasing urgency of the need for climate adaptation is clear, and the costs of inaction are climbing, according to the UN Environment Programme.

Climate-related extreme events cost the world an estimated US$140 billion a year between 2000 and 2019, per the programme’s latest Adaptation Gap Report, an annual figure projected to reach between US$1.7 trillion and US$3.1 trillion by 2050, depending on how much the planet warms.

“Budgets may be tight. There may be many competing priorities. But the smart choice is to invest in adaptation now,” wrote the programme’s executive director Inger Andersen in the report, “to minimise loss of life, to soften damage to infrastructure and, ultimately, to protect economies from the stronger climate impacts that are approaching over the horizon”.

item.title: [SCMP] Wall Street helped build modern China. But is it now being cast aside?
item.description:
For decades, Wall Street titans – from former Goldman Sachs chief Henry Paulson to Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio – were hailed as “old friends of China”, feted by senior officials and granted rare access to the country’s top leadership.

Today, while American financiers continue to visit China and maintain commercial links, those private meetings with the top leadership have largely diminished, even as Beijing gradually opens its capital markets.

The shift has raised a crucial question for global investors: can Wall Street maintain its bridge to Beijing amid a changing US-China relationship?
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Wall Street titans – from former Goldman Sachs chief Henry Paulson to Blackstone co-founder Stephen Schwarzman and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio – were hailed as “old friends of China”, feted by senior officials and granted rare access to the country’s top leadership.

Today, while American financiers continue to visit China and maintain commercial links, those private meetings with the top leadership have largely diminished, even as Beijing gradually opens its capital markets.

The shift has raised a crucial question for global investors: can Wall Street maintain its bridge to Beijing amid a changing US-China relationship?

“The decline of such roles suggests they have stopped being useful,” said Christopher Marquis, Sinyi professor of Chinese management at Cambridge Judge Business School.

“China’s economy no longer needs foreign bankers’ capital and expertise the way it did 20-plus years ago.”

The “honeymoon period” for Wall Street and Beijing dates to China’s reform era in the late 1990s and 2000s, when Beijing relied heavily on foreign financial expertise to modernise its economy.

That era was epitomised by the 1995 establishment of China International Capital Corporation, the country’s first joint-venture investment bank, launched with Morgan Stanley to restructure state enterprises and build capital markets.

Goldman Sachs was another major beneficiary, paying US$2.58 billion for a stake in the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China in 2006 – then its largest-ever principal investment – and helping underwrite some of the country’s largest overseas listings. Others, including Morgan Stanley, built similarly close ties with Chinese banks and companies.

The partnership yielded massive returns. Alibaba Group Holding’s US$25 billion debut on the New York Stock Exchange in 2014 became the largest initial public offering in history at the time, paving the way for a wave of tech listings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

At the same time, Chinese capital was flowing into global markets. The China Investment Corporation, Beijing’s sovereign wealth fund, ploughed a combined US$8 billion into Blackstone and Morgan Stanley in 2007 alone, opening another channel of engagement between Wall Street and Beijing.

“The relationship was two-way, mutually beneficial and trusting during those years,” said Kevin Chen Kaifeng, chief economist at Horizon Financial in New York.

“Almost all of those driving factors are now gone,” he added, citing the slowdown in Chinese listings in US markets, Wall Street’s exit from major stakes in Chinese state-owned banks, and declining Chinese investment in the US.

Regulators on both sides have added friction.

Nasdaq’s tighter rules have piled pressure on Chinese issuers already facing strict US audit scrutiny, while Beijing requires mainland firms to clear rigorous national security and data privacy reviews before listing abroad.

Only two mainland Chinese companies completed US debuts in the first half of the year, raising a combined US$59.5 million – the weakest half-year showing in five years in terms of both deal count and proceeds, according to a June report by accounting firm EY.

Chinese authorities have also tightened controls on cross-border capital flows by cracking down on unauthorised offshore brokerages, expanding outbound investment rules to individual residents, and applying a 20 per cent tax on offshore family trusts and insurance structures.

“The two-way streets of deals dried up on both ends,” Chen said.

Wall Street’s leverage has waned in another way.

Marquis said its traditional role as an advocate for market access had also lost much of its currency. Banks once lobbied heavily for policies that kept the pipeline of China deals open, but with Washington’s bipartisan hawkish turn on China, that advocacy carried far less weight than it once did, he said.

I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers

Christopher Marquis, Cambridge Judge Business School

During the 2018 US-China trade war, top Wall Street executives – traditionally Beijing’s strongest allies in Washington – attempted to leverage their political access to broker a truce, only to find their lobbying efforts powerless in the face of US President Donald Trump’s tariff and export ban agenda.

“No amount of Goldman or Blackstone advocacy can soften export controls or investment restrictions,” Marquis said. “Wall Street can no longer deliver its half of the bargain.”

The retreat also reflected a shift in Beijing’s own financial priorities, analysts said.

Today, Beijing is pursuing national self-sufficiency to insulate its economy from geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and the risk of decoupling from the United States and its allies, with technology innovation as a central priority.

China’s top leadership has repeatedly stressed that finance should “serve the real economy”, part of a stated ambition – formalised in this year’s five-year plan – to build China into a “financial powerhouse” on its own terms. The policy is explicitly distanced from the profit-driven model long associated with Wall Street.

Finance had been defined “as an arm of state power rather than a sector to be developed with foreign help”, Marquis said.

Yet the market has not shut. At least seven foreign firms, including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase, now wholly own mainland securities brokerages after Beijing removed foreign-ownership caps in 2020.

A high-profile business delegation – including Schwarzman, BlackRock’s Larry Fink, Goldman’s David Solomon, and Citi’s Jane Fraser – accompanied Trump on a state visit to Beijing in mid-May, where President Xi Jinping assured executives that China would expand access for foreign capital.

While some financiers continued to maintain strong links with China, analysts said those individual relationships were unlikely to restore Wall Street’s former role.

“I don’t foresee future ‘old friend of China’ roles for Wall Street bankers,” Marquis said. “There may still be a legitimate, narrower commercial role … but they should treat access for what it is: conditional and transactional.”

Chen struck a more hopeful note, arguing the bridge could be rebuilt if China reopens its financial markets further to foreign institutions and Chinese investment in the US recovers.

“The future depends on whether China can open up institutions, and revamp Chinese investments in the US,” he said. “If this happens, the future of the Wall Street bridge is bright.”

item.title: [SCMP] How to be a good tourist; a guide for the modern traveller
item.description:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.
item.content:encoded:
From Tenerife to Thessaloniki, demonstrators’ chants and roadside graffiti alike say, “Tourists go home”, although sometimes in rather stronger language.

Around the world, the residents of “must-see” destinations can no longer see each other for the crowds, and increasingly view tourists less as benefactors and more as a bane. Local authorities are responding ever more robustly to their complaints.

To drink alcohol in certain Amsterdam streets now attracts a fine of €95 (US$110), while in the village of Varenna, on Italy’s Lake Como, it’s twice as much for wearing swimwear away from the beach.

Not far away, in seaside Portofino, the introduction of no-loitering zones has effectively put an end to selfies, unless you’re a professional narcissist and the income to be expected from sponsors or followers is greater than the potential €275 (US$317) penalty for blocking traffic.

However, much of the globally growing ill will is not about bad behaviour but merely about numbers.

Destinations that have seen many long-term rental properties turned into more profitable short-term accommodation for tourists are introducing strict regulations (British Columbia) or banning Airbnb and its ilk altogether (Barcelona).

Local satisfaction is crucial to success, but if the visited are unhappy, so are the visitors.

Tourists discover soaring head taxes, 90-minute queues and compulsory advance-purchase tickets with a timed entry, and that the quiet stroll between two pretty mountain villages they have come back to enjoy for a second time now has an entrance fee and one-way-only traffic, and yet is still a conga line.

Individual residents, municipal authorities and national tourism bureaus alike declare that they don’t dislike tourists, and don’t want to discourage them, but they do want to choose the visitors they get.

An official online Tokyo travel guide, How to stay safe and be respectful in Tokyo at night, has little to say about safety in what anyway ranks as one of the world’s least dangerous cities. Instead, it explains how not to offend locals by littering, or by drinking or smoking in public.

But if the Japanese are too polite to say straight out, “Don’t come unless you obey the rules”, José Antonio Donaire, Barcelona’s commissioner for sustainable tourism, feels no such restraint. He wants to restrict visitors to no more than the 15.7 million the city hosted in 2025, and he wants half of those to be cultural tourists – presumably people who swoon at the sight of Joan Miro’s surrealist art or Antoni Gaudi’s soaring Sagrada Família rather than their 15th Estrella Damm lager of the day.

In terms of accommodation capacity, all tourists may be equal, but some are more equal than others. These regulations, fines and fees suggest a definition of good tourists: it’s those who stay longer, spend more with local businesses, respect the needs of residents, do not congregate all in one spot and neither dive into historic fountains (€500/US$576 fine in Rome) nor indulge in drunken caterwauling at 3am (€140/US$161 in Amsterdam).

However, concentrating on attracting good tourists will still not solve the problem of volume, and some destinations are looking to spread the load.

Japan has offered some international visitors free domestic flights to destinations beyond the well-worn Tokyo-Kyoto-Osaka trail that two-thirds of them take.

Spain’s new policy is to encourage visitors to avoid the summer peak, and to look beyond the supply of sun, sea, sand and potential sexual partners along its crowded Mediterranean beaches towards the equally sun-baked sleepy villages of the interior. These are all sugar-cube houses, crumbling castles and excellent walking among hills hatched with olives and vines, where good tourists eat local dishes, rather than fish and chips or pizza.

All these schemes ignore the jumbo jet in the room, though. If we don’t want a future in which the world’s major cities are to be toured by boat rather than by hop-on, hop-off bus, there must be a reduction in the emissions that make such catastrophes ever more likely.

One per cent of fliers produce 50 per cent of airline emissions, so the rest typically urge the elite to cut back first. But the good tourist understands that simply to board a plane is to be a member of an elite. Eighty per cent of the world’s population never takes to the air, so perhaps halving your own flying is not an unreasonable idea. This would reduce emissions, although the only true ecotourism is just staying at home.

In China and Europe, extensive rail systems offer less damaging ground-level travel as an easy substitute. Or there’s the option to halve the number of trips but stay for twice as long. The good tourist leaves the rentals to the locals who need the space and opts for a hotel instead.

Good tourists also avoid getting bogged down in the slough of meme-driven, artificial-intelligence-derived ignorance that is most online travel commentary. That leads to the taking of well-trodden paths between sights ranging from those of genuine cultural and historical significance to those merely of social-media-driven popularity, where the idea of being there, and being seen to be there, is more important than the actual experience.

Today, social media merely ensures that a location may go from overlooked to overwhelmed in the blink of a smartphone’s camera shutter, the image repeated in increasingly dishonest “I was here, too” postings.

The hydroelectric project next to the cliffside temple is cropped out, the sky is edited into an improbable blue and the camera angle narrowed to exclude the hordes of others taking the near-identical shot. The resulting image is of perfect beauty in tranquil solitude while the reality is anything but. And the blame cannot be laid solely at the perfectly pedicured feet of influencers. Every step you take, every post you make, people are watching you.

The good tourist travels flexibly, and keeps quiet about new discoveries. But if you follow the crowd, then it’s unsurprising that crowds are what you find.

As the late Irish travel writer Dervla Murphy told The Guardian newspaper in 2009, “Choose your country, use guidebooks to identify the areas most frequented by foreigners – and then go in the opposite direction.”

Of course, if significant numbers go in the opposite direction, there will no longer be an opposite direction, although when there are no longer “hidden gems” to be found “off the beaten track”, this will at least result in a merciful release from cliché.

There was a time when travel writing was not all how-to guides, or thinly disguised advertising, but written by a tiny number of people who ventured abroad to be a substitute for those who couldn’t.

It’s time to lead the way by sometimes going nowhere, perhaps instead sitting down with a well-informed account from the past of somewhere you might go in the future. Or might not.

Travel less, but travel better.

item.title: [SCMP] US economist Barry Eichengreen on reality of de-dollarisation and next currency reshuffle
item.description:
Barry Eichengreen is a leading American economist and one of the world’s foremost experts on international monetary systems. He is a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since 1987. He served as a senior policy adviser at the International Monetary Fund in 1997-98.

Here, he discusses why today’s “de-dollarisation” talk is different from past episodes, how close the world is to a reshuffling of the international monetary system, and what it will really take for the yuan to close the gap.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Barry Eichengreen is a leading American economist and one of the world’s foremost experts on international monetary systems. He is a professor of economics and political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he has taught since 1987. He served as a senior policy adviser at the International Monetary Fund in 1997-98.

Here, he discusses why today’s “de-dollarisation” talk is different from past episodes, how close the world is to a reshuffling of the international monetary system, and what it will really take for the yuan to close the gap.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

Since last year, discussions about “de-dollarisation” have resurfaced with renewed intensity. In your view, how much of this reflects a genuine structural shift? And what, if anything, makes the current moment different from previous episodes of dollar scepticism?

My view is that a genuine structural shift is finally getting under way against the backdrop of some long-standing concerns about the US dollar – for example, concerns about the high level of public debt in the United States and whether the growth of the debt is sustainable or not.

If there are chronic debt problems, will they have negative implications for the stability of the dollar and the value of foreign central banks’ holdings of US Treasury securities? Those concerns are long-standing, and people have been pointing to them when asking whether the era of dollar dominance may be coming to a close – they have been pointing to them for a long time.

What is new and different, however, are two sets of questions that we did not use to ask about the United States and the dollar, but everyone is asking now.

First, the strength of US political institutions. The dollar’s stability and confidence in the greenback rest fundamentally on the rule of law, separation of powers, the independence of the central bank and the control of corruption.

People are beginning to ask whether those institutional arrangements are more fragile than previously assumed. This has begun to undermine the feeling of security among foreign central banks, governments and other investors holding financial portfolios heavy in dollars.

Second, new questions are being asked about US geopolitical alliances. We know from history that central banks, governments and others prefer to hold and use the currencies of their alliance partners, because those partners are viewed as reliable stewards of their reserve holdings. If one is in an alliance with the United States, moreover, holding and using US dollars is a show of good faith in the country.

However, US President Donald Trump has raised questions about the continued commitment of the United States to Nato and to its other security arrangements. That has led the Europeans and others to ask: Do we really want to be so reliant on the US and the dollar in this geopolitically uncertain world, or should we look to alternatives, including relying more on our own currency – the euro, in the European case?

So, I think questions about both US alliances and the strength of US institutions are new and different, and they imply that the prospects for the dollar may be different going forward as well.

It will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot

Some argue that the US dollar-centred monetary order that emerged after Bretton Woods may be nearing its end, giving way to a more multipolar system. Do you share that view? And what role do you expect the yuan to play in whatever comes next?

I have long shared that view. In 2011 – prematurely, perhaps – I published a book called Exorbitant Privilege about the rise and fall of the dollar.

My forecast then was that we would be moving gradually towards a more multipolar monetary and financial system, less centred on the dollar – a more multipolar monetary system that better matched our more multipolar global economy. We have moved in that direction as predicted, but more slowly than I expected.

The persistence of dollar dominance is very strong because so many banks, firms and governments use dollars, which creates network effects that lock in the use of the dollar.

So, I’ve been surprised in the last 15 years that we haven’t moved towards that multipolar system more rapidly. But that movement may now accelerate.

I think China’s currency will, over time, come to play a more consequential global role. But the important point to emphasise is that the yuan is starting out very, very far behind the dollar.

Hence it will take years, maybe even decades, for China to close that gap with the United States and the dollar – unless the US shoots itself in the foot and confidence in the dollar is abruptly lost.

We have seen progress in the yuan’s international use, from broader participation in China’s payment systems to growing panda bond issuance. Do you believe China is now in a particularly important window for advancing yuan internationalisation? How would you characterise the recent progress?

The US-Iran war is affording China additional opportunities to increase the use of its currency in global oil and gas trade, and to do more settlements with the energy exporters from the Middle East in its own currency.

And now, those energy exporters are likely happy to take yuan in payment. They can use those yuan to buy the services of Chinese construction companies and Chinese exports of solar panels, batteries, electronics and other advanced technologies.

The war in the [Persian] Gulf has, I think, accelerated the tendency for other central banks and governments to look for alternatives to the dollar, and in this way created a window for China.

Starting from ground zero 15 years ago, China has made impressive progress. But you have to put that in context, where the dollar still accounts for nearly 60 per cent of the foreign exchange reserves of central banks around the world, and the yuan accounts for 2 per cent.

And one sees the same thing along other dimensions, such as turnover in global foreign exchange markets, where the dollar is 10 times as important as the yuan.

I think China has been making rapid progress, for example, in transactions through China’s Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). Those transactions had been growing at a 30 or 40 per cent annual rate – really fast, starting from basically nothing 10 years ago.

But that growth slowed sharply in 2025. This slowdown suggests that there still are important obstacles to the yuan’s internationalisation. So I would say: impressive progress, but still, the dollar remains in a different league than China’s currency.

China has developed the requisite financial and technological infrastructure. China is, in a way, ahead of the United States in terms of the digital financial revolution. But it has to create confidence among bankers that the markets and platforms on which the yuan can be traded constitute a safe, secure and reliable way to make payments. Creating confidence in a new, novel payments platform takes time. More time will be required.

The US correspondent banking system clears many more transactions per day than CIPS does. And it will take, as I said before, probably decades before that gap is closed.

Looking ahead, what do you see as the next steps for yuan internationalisation? Do you believe Beijing ultimately envisions the yuan on par with the US dollar, or as one of several major currencies in a more multipolar world?

China needs to continue to enhance the liquidity of its financial markets. If people are going to make payments using the yuan, they are going to have to hold balances in the currency, so they have the money ready to make those payments.

The kinds of securities that foreigners can hold in China are limited by regulation and capital controls. The availability of financial derivatives to hedge the risk of exchange rate changes – those markets are limited in China.

So China needs to move slowly but surely to liberalise access to those financial markets, increase the liquidity of its markets, and – where markets barely exist, as in the case of derivatives – to build them out.

I want to be clear here: China should move slowly but surely in this direction. It should not move quickly and abruptly, since doing the latter could create financial risks.

Back in 2015, China began to move rapidly to relax its capital controls. Money flowed out of the country, the stock market crashed and the authorities reversed course. This episode was a reminder that slow but steady wins the race, and that moving abruptly is not a good idea.

Regarding how Beijing envisions the path, the answer is not entirely under Beijing’s control. Whether the dollar remains the leading international currency – and for how long – depends first and foremost on Washington.

What Beijing can do is think about what the best Chinese policy is under different scenarios: under the scenario where the dollar remains sound and stable, and banks, governments, and others around the world feel comfortable in holding and using it; or, if there is a crisis of confidence in the dollar caused by the United States itself, how quickly China can ramp up its alternative, namely, own-currency settlement.

Beijing should be doing scenario planning, rather than having a blueprint for what they think will happen next.

In the event of a crisis of confidence in the US dollar, are widely discussed alternatives such as the euro and the yuan truly ready to step in as viable substitutes?

None of the alternatives, including the euro and the yuan, are ready to substitute for the dollar. What they can do is supplement the dollar on the margin. But they lack the scale as international currencies, and they have shortcomings.

In the case of China, it is the lack of access to domestic financial markets and the limited liquidity of those markets. In the case of Europe, it is the absence of a stock of safe and liquid assets for international investors to hold and use. Consequently, neither the euro nor the yuan can replace or substitute for the dollar any time soon.

While on some dimensions, like the use of currencies as reserves by central banks, the dollar has lost some of its global market share, the euro has gained none of that market share. The yuan has gained only about one-quarter of what the dollar has lost. The other three-quarters have been gained by non-traditional reserve currencies: the South Korean won, the Australian dollar, the Canadian dollar, the Danish krone, the Norwegian krone.

So far, you and I have been talking about the currencies of big economies. Traditionally, there has been an association between the widespread international use of a currency and the size of the issuing economy. Big economies engage in more foreign trade and foreign investment, so it makes sense that their currencies would be the dominant units in international transactions.

But we now live in a digital world where it is easier to buy, sell, hold and trade the Australian dollar, the Swedish krona, and so forth. These non-traditional reserve currencies are the currencies of small, open, well-managed, inflation-targeting countries. They are becoming more attractive in international use. They too lack the scale to replace the dollar, but they can help to supplement it on the margin.

What role do you see Hong Kong playing in the next phase of yuan internationalisation? As Beijing builds up Shanghai’s offshore financial capabilities, do you see the two cities as increasingly competitive?

Hong Kong in the next phase will play the same role that it has played in the previous phase – as a kind of sandbox, or pilot scheme, for yuan use, where Chinese authorities experiment with and observe the effects of different financial innovations.

This will continue to be the case. If you believe having markets and financial derivatives is important for the use of China’s currency, those markets will be developed, in part, in Hong Kong. And if they work smoothly there, they will be brought onshore.

Hong Kong now has a stablecoin ordinance and has issued two stablecoin licences to a couple of big banks. We don’t know whether stablecoins will become important going forward. I, for one, doubt that they will. But Hong Kong can be a place where banks and others can experiment with the payments technology provided by stablecoins.

And if that turns out to be important, it’ll be easier for China to catch up, because Hong Kong will already have provided evidence about how that new payments technology works, how it should be regulated, and so forth.

As for the competition between Hong Kong and Shanghai, economists generally think that competition is good. Competition forces banks, regulators and others to step up their game to avoid losing market share. So that is what Hong Kong will have to do.

Hong Kong has anchored its currency to the US dollar for more than four decades. If the world becomes more multipolar over time, do you believe the arrangement will still make sense? How do you see Hong Kong’s role evolving in a less US dollar-centric world?

The dollar peg has served Hong Kong well. It has had more advantages than disadvantages because the global economy has been dollar-dominated. Hong Kong links directly into that because markets for financial instruments denominated in US dollars are so big. This enables Hong Kong banks to act as global banks, because they have a big global market out there that they can service.

If people grow more sceptical about the US dollar and move away from it, the global system will become less dollar-centric. At that point, the advantages to Hong Kong of being linked to the US dollar obviously become less.

Hong Kong authorities ought to quietly engage in the same kind of scenario planning for different outcomes, depending on what kind of policies – stable or unstable – are followed in the US, so they can respond appropriately. But I would emphasise that they should do their scenario planning quietly.

As stablecoins and central bank digital currencies gain traction around the world, do you see them as game-changers that could disrupt the current monetary hierarchy, or will they simply reinforce the existing status quo?

If you look at the long sweep of history, you see that financial and payments technology is always changing. We moved from doing transactions using lumps of gold and silver, to tokens and coins, to bank money and bills of exchange, and so forth.

We are in another one of those periods where financial and payments technology is changing rapidly. An important new technology is blockchain, or distributed ledger technology. I am convinced that distributed ledger technology will be used to make cross-border payments going forward.

The question is: what kind of units run on those new payment rails? Will they be stablecoins on the one hand, or central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits on the other hand? And depending on the answer to that question, in what currency will they be denominated? In US dollars, or something else?

The US has taken a bet on stablecoins. If privately issued stablecoins become the dominant unit that runs on those payment rails, it is likely to cement the international role of the dollar, because 99 per cent of stablecoins are linked to the US dollar. And again, the US has a big head start in going down that road.

On the other hand, both the euro area and China are looking at central bank digital currencies and tokenised commercial bank deposits. If that turns out to be what runs on these new payment rails, it won’t be the dollar but the euro and the yuan that dominate in the future.

So you have to ask, will we be relying more on private digital money, which is what the US is aiming for, or publicly issued and regulated digital money, which is what China and Europe are developing?

The arrow of history points towards public provision of the public good of stable money. In the past, we tended to have lots of private issuers of banknotes and coins. Gradually, governments have taken over that function as a public utility. In effect, they have monopolised it. So if I have to bet on one outcome or another, I would bet on central bank digital currencies and tokenised bank deposits.

Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy

Gold has outlasted every major currency in history. As central banks buy gold at the fastest pace in decades, are we witnessing a return of the world’s oldest monetary asset? What role do you see it playing in the future international monetary system?

I do not think gold will play a big role in the future. Central banks that inherited very dollar-heavy reserve portfolios in the past want to diversify. One direction they can diversify towards is by using some of their dollars to buy gold. We’ve seen a little bit of that on the margin.

If you are a country like Russia that is subject to sanctions, then buying gold is a way of protecting your reserves from being frozen by foreign authorities. You can buy gold, bring it home and vault it in St Petersburg or Moscow. We’ve seen examples of that kind of behaviour in the last decade and a half.

But it is important to note, number one: all the gold purchases that we’ve seen in the last 15 years have been by emerging markets that did not inherit a lot of gold from the past. Advanced countries that inherited gold from the Bretton Woods period and the earlier gold standard period have not added to their reserves.

And number two, it is important to note that most of the increase in the share of gold in central bank reserves has been due to the run-up in the price, and not active purchases.

We may see a little bit more of that behaviour, because every global investor wants a commodity play in their portfolio. Holding a little bit of gold is a way for central banks to acquire that exposure and a bit of additional diversification.

Many speak of a “multipolar” monetary system. In practice, how would such a system function? Would it inevitably require greater coordination among major economies, and is meaningful monetary cooperation still possible at a time of growing geopolitical fragmentation?

In practice, a multipolar system would be one in which several currencies play consequential international roles – in which several currencies are used in cross-border payments and are regarded as stable stores of value by international investors. Multiple central banks would act as international lenders and liquidity providers of last resort.

Just as a diverse ecosystem is good for planet Earth, a multipolar monetary system would be good for the global economy. If there were a shortage of liquidity, and one central bank fell down on the job – for instance, if the Federal Reserve were dominated by isolationist governors – then central banks in China and Europe could step up. When foreign central banks needed liquidity, they would turn to Beijing and Frankfurt, as well as New York and Washington.

However, we are in a world now where coordination is difficult to achieve, partly because the current US administration makes it difficult to coordinate – or to use another word, cooperate – smoothly with other governments.

The best we can do is hope that the central banks and governments responsible for these different currencies follow sound and stable policies, so that the exchange rates between their currencies remain relatively stable.

If they each understand that they have some responsibility for the stability and liquidity of the global system, they can act individually to help to stabilise the system.

If the issuers of the currencies that are internationally used all follow sound and stable policies, that would be better than our current dollar-dominated system.

Note, however, that my previous statement had a lot of sentences that began with the word “if”.

Consider, for example, the Federal Reserve and the dollar currency swap lines that it provides to other countries. By and large, it only provides them to friendly governments – countries that are geopolitically aligned with the United States – rather than providing them more widely.

On the other hand, the People’s Bank of China swap lines are very diverse. It provides them to politically aligned countries in Asia, but it also provides them to the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and others. I worry about whether the US model of only providing liquidity to the country’s friends is compatible with global stability.

Looking back through history, are there any precedents for a multipolar monetary system, or are we entering an entirely unprecedented paradigm?

One that is relevant to us today is the gold standard period before 1913, when currencies were linked to gold, but gold was not really used for international transactions. Gold is very heavy and risky to ship internationally, so currencies were used for payments.

The British pound sterling, the French franc, and the German mark – all three of them were widely used for cross-border transactions in that system before 1913. The system worked smoothly because the policies of the issuing central banks and governments were sound and stable.

A very different precedent would be the 1920s and 30s, when both the US dollar and the British pound sterling were used internationally. In the 1920s, the two currencies were equal in importance. But neither the issuing central bank nor government followed sound and stable policies. Both the US and the UK had crises of one sort or another in the early 1930s. There was flight from the two international reserve currencies. As a result, that system worked very poorly.

We have seen multipolar systems before. Whether they work well or poorly depends on the stability of the underlying policies.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘No bandwidth left for the family’: why many Singaporeans want to be child-free
item.description:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.
item.content:encoded:
As Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong prepares to unveil plans to ease the strain on families during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday, a new survey points to a difficult question behind the city state’s record-low fertility rate: what if a substantial share of residents no longer want children at all?

Nearly one in four Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 surveyed by YouGov in July said they had no children and did not intend to have them in the future.

Zahir Latif and his fiancée are among them.

For eight years, the couple have returned to the same question: should they have children? Each time, the conversation has ended in the same place.

They worry about money, time and the fear of losing themselves, Zahir, 42, said. The unstable income that comes with freelance work – he is a content creator and his fiancée is a writer – has also made parenthood feel incompatible with the life they have built.

Taking on a stable 9-to-5 job could mean giving up any semblance of work-life balance, he added.

“Besides money, time is something Singapore struggles to give back to its citizens,” he said. “If you want to get enough sleep, your day is pretty much over in a few hours after work.”

The couple’s decision reflects one of the most striking findings of the survey, based on responses from 496 Singaporean adults aged 18 to 44 collected in July: 23 per cent said they did not currently have children and did not plan to have them in the future. A 2023 YouGov poll found the proportion was 25 per cent among 1,023 respondents aged 18 to 55.

The limits of policy were also evident, with 30 per cent of Singaporeans aged 18 to 44 saying there was nothing the government could do to make them more willing to have children.

Lower-cost preschool and childcare was the policy most likely to encourage parenthood, cited by 35 per cent of respondents in that age group, while improved work-life balance through national initiatives and increased cash incentives were each mentioned by 31 per cent.

The findings showed that giving Singaporeans their time and lives back was as critical as providing financial support, said Vincent Chua, an associate professor of sociology and anthropology at the National University of Singapore.

Singapore’s economic system had made work and raising a family “mutually exclusive” activities, Chua said.

“Modern capitalism demands maximum extraction of labour – not just in terms of hours, but in cognitive focus and emotional energy, and raising a family is an intensive, non-market activity requiring immense emotional and physical bandwidth,” he said.

“In a highly competitive society, there is simply no bandwidth left for the family.”

Zahir said that any scenario they had considered involving children usually meant moving abroad, where cost and time pressures were less intense. “Unless Singapore changes its work culture, no amount of money can change our minds.”

Singapore’s resident total fertility rate fell to a record low of 0.87 in 2025, even after years of state support aimed at making parenthood more affordable and manageable.

Those measures include baby bonus cash gifts, grants and co-matching for children’s savings accounts, healthcare support for newborns, preschool subsidies and lower fee caps at government-supported childcare centres.

In April, Singapore also expanded its shared parental leave scheme from six to 10 weeks, increasing the total government-paid parental leave to 30 weeks for eligible parents.

Officials have repeatedly said the challenge goes beyond money.

In April, a work group chaired by Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah was formed to tackle the declining birth rate, with a mandate to review support across marriage and parenthood.

Last Saturday, Indranee told local media that the team had been receiving feedback from Singaporeans, with a full report expected early next year.

“What is clear is that many do aspire to get married and have children,” she said. “But at the same time, they do encounter challenges including the cost of raising children, the need for time with family, caregiving arrangements and housing.”

Prime Minister Wong earlier this month acknowledged the growing barriers faced by those navigating parenthood.

“Across the world, family life is coming under greater strain. Expectations have risen, and parents feel pressured to give their children the best possible start in life. At the same time, many are caring for ageing parents while balancing the demands of work,” he said during his National Day message on August 8.

The government was taking a fresh look at issues such as the cost of raising children, access to affordable childcare and other ways to lighten the load on families, he added.

Wong is expected to speak about the plans in more detail during his National Day Rally speech on Sunday.

Focus on family well-being

Even so, analysts say Singapore’s fertility challenge should not be read as beyond repair, but as one that may require a broader definition of success: making family life more sustainable for those who already have or still want children, rather than relying only on incentives to lift birth numbers.

“I would not call it hopeless,” said Tan Poh Lin, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies, of efforts to raise Singapore’s birth rate. “However, I do view that the demographic transition has now entered a new phase where more simply do not want children regardless of circumstances.”

Singapore was likely to shift its focus to improving family well-being throughout parenthood and expected measures would include enhancements to cash gifts and childcare leave to benefit families with older children, Tan added.

“Apart from more financial and workplace support, what is needed by families is a greater sense of economic security, including access to upskilling opportunities and employment support,” she said. “What is needed is the right environment, crucially a sense of stability and security.”

To have generous family-friendly policies like those in Nordic countries, Chua said society must accept a high-tax social model.

While the Nordic model was enticing, he added that it might not be replicated easily in Singapore due to its work culture.

“Workers who actually utilise such generous leave would likely face career discrimination and employers might simply self-censor and avoid hiring married couples with young children altogether,” he said.

Tax manager Debbie Lin has been wrestling with whether to have a second child. While her heart is set on giving her daughter a sibling, she vividly remembers the sacrifices she had to make for motherhood.

Lin rejoined the workforce in February after putting her decade-long career on pause for two years to focus on raising her daughter. “When I look at peers who are continuously employed, I estimate that I am now around 30 to 40 per cent behind some of them in terms of salary and career progression,” she said.

Companies needed to be encouraged to adopt family-friendly policies, Lin said, to dispel fears prospective parents might have about opportunity costs to their careers.

“A family-friendly policy that employees are afraid to use is not really a family-friendly policy,” she added.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organiser, former leaders guilty of inciting subversion
item.description:
The now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and two of its former leaders have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

In a 216-page judgment delivered at West Kowloon Court on Friday, three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution did not permit Western-style democracy.

They found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government demonstrations.
item.content:encoded:
The now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil and two of its former leaders have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law by advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.

In a 216-page judgment delivered at West Kowloon Court on Friday, three High Court judges ruled that any attempt to overthrow or undermine the Communist Party of China’s leadership could constitute a subversion offence because the country’s constitution did not permit Western-style democracy.

They found the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung had incited public hatred towards the party by likening Beijing’s crackdown on protesters in 1989 to local authorities’ suppression of the 2019 anti-government demonstrations.

While stressing it was not unlawful for the alliance to organise vigils to mark the crackdown, the panel said the defendants had used the annual event to attract new supporters and instigate them to take action to oust the ruling party.

“[The defendants] did not genuinely and honestly believe that their words and deeds were not in breach of the national security law. They just refused to pull back from the brink and were bent on embracing the alliance’s resistance line to the very end.”

Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee will hear oral mitigation arguments on August 28 before delivering the sentences.

Beijing’s national security office in Hong Kong said the defendants should be harshly punished for severely undermining the city’s fundamental interests and endangering the state’s constitutional order.

A government spokesman praised the verdict as a reasoned judgment, while accusing “external forces” of making “blatant and persistent” attempts to vilify local authorities through political manoeuvres and misleading statements.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said that anyone who tried to “shift the goalposts” or cover up their crimes with “clever words and flattery” would not escape justice.

Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said the verdict highlighted the importance of the Chinese constitution in the city’s constitutional order and offered clearer guidelines for law enforcement.

Police Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-wah, of the force’s national security department, declined to say whether future discussions of the 1989 crackdown would constitute an offence. He said event organisers had to comply with relevant laws.

Former lawmaker Lee and Chow, a barrister, have been remanded in custody for nearly five years. A fourth defendant, former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, has also been detained for more than four years and is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to the offence in January.

Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said she was “very angry” over the ruling because she felt the judges did not give sufficient consideration to the defence’s arguments and evidence.

Chow’s mother said she hoped that “flowers of all colours can blossom”.

The court heard that putting an end to “one-party dictatorship” was among the alliance’s five operational objectives, which also included vindicating the 1989 protest movement and building a democratic China.

The trial centred on Article 1 of the Chinese constitution, which was amended in 2018 to describe the party’s leadership as the “defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics”.

The judges noted that the article effectively required the country to be run solely by the party as a socialist state. The role of other “democratic” parties, they said, was restricted to taking part in the “patriotic united front” under the party’s leadership.

The defence contended that all the alliance’s objectives were a legitimate exercise of fundamental human rights.

Lee testified that the one-party system was incompatible with the constitution’s preamble, which provides for “multiparty cooperation and political consultation” under the party’s leadership.

Chow argued that pursuing democratic change in society should not be considered illegal in the first place.

The judges rejected their assertions, saying the defendants did not simply seek more diverse political participation on the mainland but hoped to overthrow and undermine the party.

They said Lee, Ho and Chow had all along been hostile towards the regime and refused to make any compromise.

The defendants never saw any opportunity for a peaceful dialogue with central authorities or any chance that Beijing would agree to amend the constitution again, the judges added.

Set up after the 1989 crackdown, the alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to mark the event and call for accountability and democratic reforms across the border. The event had been the only large-scale public gathering on Chinese soil to remember the 1989 crackdown.

Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

Inciting subversion in Hong Kong carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment under the national security law. Any company or organisation that commits an offence under the law can be handed a fine of an indefinite sum.

In a statement, UK Foreign Office Indo-Pacific minister Rosie Winterton said the verdict was “further demonstration that acts of remembrance in Hong Kong are now treated by the authorities as threats to national security”.

An EU spokesperson said: “The conviction … confirms the continuing deterioration of the freedoms of expression and assembly and a further shrinking of the space for independent civil society in Hong Kong.”

The foreign ministries of France and Germany also issued a joint statement saying the countries “deeply regret” the guilty verdict and called for the immediate release of Chow, who was awarded the Franco-German Prize for Human Rights and the Rule of Law in 2023.

The Australian government said it was “deeply concerned” by the verdict, while calling on Beijing to “cease suppression of freedoms of expression, assembly, media and civil society” and to repeal the national security law.

US Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes called for the defendants’ immediate release, arguing that the vigils sought only to remember the past and honour the lives lost in the Tiananmen crackdown.

Additional reporting by Leopold Chen and Connor Mycroft

item.title: [SCMP] More Hong Kong consumers allege coercive beauty sales in wake of Opatra crackdown
item.description:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.
item.content:encoded:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.

Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.

Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.

Following the arrest of two managers at the Hong Kong operator of UK-based beauty chain Opatra London over coercive sales practices, its company secretary resigned, while customs officers continue investigating six customer complaints involving disputed sums between HK$1,800 (US$230) and HK$100,000.

Customs said that the number of complaints had risen to 25 as of Thursday and an investigation was under way.

Opatra’s headquarters in the United Kingdom said on Friday that it and the Hong Kong distributor had agreed to suspend operations.

The brand’s four Hong Kong branches – two in Sha Tin, one in Yuen Long and one in Causeway Bay – have suspended operations since the controversy flared up about a week ago.

Now, more victims have detailed alleged aggressive sales tactics they have encountered while shopping for beauty products.

For 22-year-old university student John*, it took just a few seconds to be dragged into what he described as a “beauty trap” on the busy Hankow Road in Tsim Sha Tsui in May.

Outside a Lionesse shop, John said he was approached by a saleswoman who handed him a “free sample”.

He said the woman told him he had “dark eye circles” before applying an unidentified skincare product directly to his face. Concerned about a possible skin reaction and caught off guard by the ambush, John said he agreed to enter the shop.

Once he was seated, John said staff applied another liquid, claiming it was a HK$1,560 deep cleanser. They then showed him the “dirt” removed from his skin in a mirror in an attempt to persuade him to buy the product, he said.

John said he was then hurried into signing an electronic form, with the signature box enlarged to the point that he could not read the contract terms, including a “no refunds” clause.

Instead of handing over the product, the saleswoman then directed him to a free facial and bombarded him with questions about his age and employment status, along with two other staff members, John said.

Under pressure, he agreed to purchase a HK$30,000 annual facial package, but explicitly requested an instalment plan capped at HK$2,500 a month due to his credit card limit, he said.

John alleged that one of the salesmen took his card and made multiple attempts to process transactions exceeding HK$2,500.

Bank records showed five unsuccessful attempts, he said, for HK$30,000, HK$8,440, HK$5,000, HK$7,500 and, finally, HK$2,500. He said the bank immediately blocked the card because of the suspicious activity.

He said he ultimately paid HK$2,500 via PayMe to a merchant named “Vertex Innovations Limited” so he could leave the shop.

When he sought a refund through the Consumer Council, Lionesse’s management denied allegations of high-pressure sales practices, arguing that the open shop environment meant he could have “left immediately”, John said.

The company said the failed transaction records reflected standard authorisation procedures between the bank system and the merchant terminal and did not constitute improper sales practices. It declined to provide a refund, instead offering to exchange products of the same value.

In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, Apex Retail, which manages Lionesse in Hong Kong, declined to comment on individual allegations or circumstances that did not involve identifiable customer matters.
