Recalling the experience, John said: “I’m just a student. The incident put immense psychological pressure on me and forced me to waste a lot of time organising bank records, payment details and relevant documents to file a complaint.”

He added: “I never intended to get involved in beauty services, but this experience made me realise how dark and manipulative beauty sales could be.”

He is now seeking a chargeback of HK$4,060 from the bank.

Company registration records show the directors of Apex are Ozel Barnos, Eli Vaknin, Sagi Vardi, Yogev Itzhak Vardi and Yinon Avraham Vardi.

The company website, which has become inaccessible, said it started as an Israeli family business and now had about a dozen shops in the city, under the brands of Earth, Napara, Privilege Boutique, Avinichi, Dualsonic and more.

Another firm to come under scrutiny was The Mineral Boutique, a brand under Beauty Express Group that has at least five branches in major shopping centres.

A 42-year-old clerk surnamed Wong alleged that similar tactics were used when a saleswoman applied a product directly onto her skin without permission at the Log-on shop in Festival Walk, Kowloon Tong, in June.

Wong said the saleswoman claimed the product could only be removed using a specialised device inside the counter area.

Once inside, Wong alleged, staff repeatedly grabbed her hand when she tried to pull away and cornered her while attempting to sell her high-value products, alongside a store manager.

Wong said that when she tried to leave, the saleswoman replied: “What is there left to think about? You’ve already seen the results.”

Wong said the remark prompted her to leave immediately and then file a formal complaint with City’super, the parent company of Log-on.

In a response to Wong, City’super said it had investigated the incident, reiterated that aggressive sales tactics were strictly prohibited and offered her a gift box.

City’super told the SCMP that it had received two customer “comments” about the counter’s services in the past year, as well as “a limited number of comments or complaints” over the past five years.

It said all cases had been investigated and handled through established procedures.

Asked whether such complaints influenced lease renewals, City’super declined to comment on specific contractual arrangements.

“We evaluate business relationships and commercial arrangements based on a range of factors including compliance with applicable laws and regulations, operational requirements, customer feedback and other relevant considerations,” it said.

Beauty Express Group declined to comment on the complaint, citing a lack of sufficient information to identify the customers involved.

It told the SCMP that it did not tolerate aggressive sales practices, non-consensual physical contact or any conduct that compromised a customer’s ability to make a free and informed purchasing decision.

The group’s directors include Aviad Ben Ezra and Baruch Szerer. Other brands under the group include Telosin, Premier by Dead Sea, Gratiae and more.

Lawyer Eric Chan Pak-ho said the tactics used on the student could constitute an offence under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. However, the key question was whether sales staff had used “harassment, coercion or undue influence” to persuade John to agree to each purchase.

Chan added that concealing no-refund policies could increase the company’s legal liability.

Under the law, practices that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice or conduct and cause them to make a purchase they would not otherwise have made are considered an offence.

Commercial lawyer Kenix Yuen Pui-kwan said that applying beauty products to a consumer’s skin might not, in itself, breach the ordinance.

“However, if that conduct forms part of a broader sales strategy involving harassment, coercion or undue influence, it may be relevant,” Yuen said.

Depending on the nature of the physical contact, other criminal issues could also arise, she cautioned.

Dr Amos Cheung, a clinical psychologist registered with the Hong Kong Psychological Society, said falling victim to high-pressure sales tactics did not mean a person lacked intelligence.

Such tactics were carefully engineered to exploit human vulnerability and bypass rational reasoning, he said.

Offering free samples could make shoppers feel indebted and reluctant to refuse invitations to enter a store, while applying products to someone’s face without consent could also help identify customers who were more susceptible to manipulation, he said.

Sales representatives could exaggerate imperfections in shoppers’ appearance in ways linked to their self-esteem and sense of self-worth, pushing them towards “emotional reasoning”, Cheung said.

“Such feelings of fear, anxiety and restlessness could impact your rational reasoning process and push you into a state of emotional reasoning,” he said.

He added that compliments could also lower customers’ guard by making sales staff seem friendly and trustworthy.

“If you are unsure about a store’s sales tactics, do not visit it alone,” he said.

“It’s important to be alert to words intended to trigger unnecessary anxiety, shame and panic, and prepare your response, such as ‘I never purchase out of impulse. I will think about it.’ Then, leave immediately.”

*Name changed at interviewee’s request

item.title: [SCMP] Despite US sanctions on Xinjiang cotton, China’s textile industry weathers the storm
item.description:
When the US government announced the addition of 43 Chinese companies to an import blacklist in late July over allegations of forced labour in the country’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region – including several household food and apparel brands – the local reaction to the news was surprisingly calm.

“It felt like a sudden batch of companies was added out of nowhere … but it shouldn’t have much of an impact on the sector,” said the owner of a cotton-ginning mill in southern Xinjiang, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

This was a far cry from the panic triggered four years ago, when Xinjiang cotton became a geopolitical flashpoint between Washington and Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
When the US government announced the addition of 43 Chinese companies to an import blacklist in late July over allegations of forced labour in the country’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region – including several household food and apparel brands – the local reaction to the news was surprisingly calm.

“It felt like a sudden batch of companies was added out of nowhere … but it shouldn’t have much of an impact on the sector,” said the owner of a cotton-ginning mill in southern Xinjiang, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

This was a far cry from the panic triggered four years ago, when Xinjiang cotton became a geopolitical flashpoint between Washington and Beijing.

Back in June 2022, the mill owner was sitting on a massive stockpile of unsold cotton, anxious about falling trading prices and losing his downstream buyers to the effects of the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act (UFLPA) – a US law that effectively bans American imports of all products with inputs from Xinjiang.

“At least for Xinjiang cotton, I feel the industry has weathered the storm,” he said. Now, the local processing rates of cotton products are “remarkably high” – around 30 to 40 per cent – and development across the entire cotton textile supply chain is booming, he added.

“From spinning and weaving to printing and dyeing, companies are steadily expanding their scale,” the mill owner said.

His change in attitude might also be a snapshot for a broader change in the global political landscape. After significant export diversification efforts and a shift in the balance of power between China and the US – especially since last year’s sweeping trade war – Chinese industries seem to be reacting to US sanctions with greater resilience and confidence.

However, analysts and industry insiders said this was no time to relax. Despite the goodwill generated by the summits held or planned between the two countries’ leaders this year, they said the risks for Chinese firms were only bound to increase amid lingering bilateral tensions.

Its most significant impact has been reshaping how US fashion companies manage sourcing, compliance, and supply chain transparency

Sheng Lu, University of Delaware

The US broadens its list

Passed by the US Congress and signed into law in 2021, the UFLPA establishes a “rebuttable presumption” that all goods from the region involve forced labour – a charge Beijing consistently denies – and specifically bars listed companies from exporting their goods to the US unless they can provide clear and convincing evidence to the contrary.

The latest additions to the list, which took effect on August 3, represent an expansion of 30 per cent – the largest single increase in the list’s history – bringing the total number of companies to 187. Sectors covered include gold, pharmaceuticals, aluminium, garments and food, according to the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

A few industry leaders in the cotton, textile and apparel sector in China were included on the list, including Henan Tongzhou Cotton and Fujian Septwolves.

Septwolves said the company was “shocked and saddened” by its inclusion on the list, and that the company’s core business was focused on the domestic market, so its operations would be unaffected. Tongzhou Cotton has not replied to requests for comment from the South China Morning Post.

In a statement, China’s Ministry of Commerce called the additions “completely lacking in factual basis” and described the move as an “act of economic coercion”, saying it “would do whatever was necessary to protect the rights and interests of Chinese firms.”

The country’s National Textile and Apparel Council also issued a statement saying that there was “no ‘forced labour’ of any kind” in Xinjiang’s cotton and textile sector, adding that cultivation and harvesting were largely automated, with over 90 per cent of the region’s cotton harvested by machine.

“The US action gravely damages the order and stable operation of global textile supply chains,” the council said. “Xinjiang produces approximately one-fifth of the world’s cotton, and China accounts for nearly one-third of global textile and apparel exports.”

According to figures from China’s National Bureau of Statistics, the region produced 6.17 million tonnes of cotton in 2024, up 20.2 per cent from the 5.13 million tonnes recorded in 2021, the year the UFLPA was approved.

In its statement, the textile council called upon international apparel brands to “respect the facts” regarding Xinjiang’s development, cautioning them to “keep commercial operations from being coerced by politics, and avoid becoming tools of anti-China forces in the US.”

Re-sourcing textile resources

Years after taking effect, the UFLPA had yet to cause an immediate or complete decoupling of the US-China textile and apparel trade, said Sheng Lu, a professor in the department of fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware. China is still regarded as indispensable for textile raw material sourcing among US importers, he added.

“The impact of the UFLPA has been more nuanced than many initially expected,” Lu said. “Instead, its most significant impact has been reshaping how US fashion companies manage sourcing, compliance, and supply chain transparency.”

According to US Department of Commerce data, in value terms only 6.4 per cent of US cotton apparel came from China during the first five months of 2026, down from 9.9 per cent a year earlier and 21.9 per cent in 2019, marking another record low, Lu said.

That said, Lu added he did not expect the latest expansion of the UFLPA entity list would trigger another mass relocation of apparel sourcing.

“Many leading US fashion companies reported sourcing only a single-digit share of their total apparel volume or value from China and appear to have already reached their desired level of exposure to China,” he said.

“Rather than continuing to accelerate their exit from China, these companies are increasingly focused on optimising their broader sourcing portfolios while maintaining limited sourcing from China, which continues to offer strong manufacturing advantages in areas such as small minimum order quantity, flexibility and agility, and vertical integration.”

China’s industry adapts

A general consensus among Chinese textile exporters is that a workaround for dealing with the UFLPA has been gradually established: use foreign cotton when traceability is required, and Xinjiang cotton otherwise.

Some industry insiders said most traceability only existed on paper, leaving an ample grey area in which to manoeuvre.

One sales manager at a major textile manufacturer in eastern China said the UFLPA had been like a hammer hanging over the company’s head, but there was never a clear timeline as to when strict enforcement of the policy would actually begin.

It was a big headache for the company, which exports sofa covers to the US, when the policy was first implemented in 2022, the manager said, adding that some downstream clients began to ask for traceability documents for the raw materials, having to prove that their products did not use Xinjiang cotton.

But all of the company’s products were made with cotton from the region, the manager said, attesting to the material’s quality. His American clients tended to steer clear of products containing cotton, because “they don’t want to get mixed up in politics,” he added.

“So, we try to avoid promoting cotton goods and focus on other fabrics instead.”

Fang Huiling, senior analyst at Shanghai-based Orient Futures, said field surveys across Xinjiang and other provinces showed that Chinese cotton growers had found ways to circumvent the US sanctions by diversifying export destinations and separating production lines for export and domestic markets.

“After years of sustained sanctions by the US, domestic companies have become accustomed to the situation and built greater resilience. That’s why I believe the impact [of the latest UFLPA sanctions] on China is limited,” Fang said.

I honestly feel like this is the toughest year of my 11-year career in the industry

Hua, textile factory owner

Instead, they might even inflict greater pain on US cotton growers than those in Xinjiang, Fang said. American agricultural products were easy targets for Beijing during trade tensions with Washington, she said, adding that as one of its countermeasures during last year’s trade war, China imposed an additional 15 per cent tariff on US cotton.

“China is the world’s largest textile producer and was once the top purchaser of US cotton,” Fang said. “Chinese buyers have gradually diverted their purchases away from the US towards countries like Brazil, weighing heavily on American cotton growers.”

However, not all industry insiders were so optimistic.

“Imported cotton is more expensive – sourcing from places like Brazil or Myanmar costs about 2,000 yuan (US$297) more per tonne once you factor in shipping, customs clearance, and other fees,” said Hua, who owns a textile factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province that mainly serves overseas clients, adding this difference included the costs incurred from preparing and providing traceability information to the US.

“But it’s not just a matter of price; the main issue is quality,” said Hua, who preferred to go by a surname. “Imported cotton has higher defect rates than Xinjiang cotton.”

While costs have gone up, Hua’s American clients were not accepting price increases, he said, adding the appreciation of the yuan continued to squeeze his profit margins.

“I honestly feel like this is the toughest year of my 11-year career in the industry.”

In tall cotton – for now

But even with the ups and downs of the US-China relationship, which have affected the enforcement of certain trade measures more generally, making sure that UFLPA is being complied with has always been patchy, according to Nick Marro, global trade lead at the Economist Intelligence Unit.

“This could reflect a lack of expertise or personnel on the US Customs side, but also a lack of very strict guidance coming from the policymakers themselves,” Marro said.

But Hua said he would not dare test the leniency of US law enforcement, since getting caught would mean substantial fines and the seizure and eventual forfeiture of the entire shipment.

More than 24,300 shipments with a total value of almost US$1 billion had been blocked since the act came into force, according to DHS.

“Everyone fears that the ban on Xinjiang cotton is just the beginning – what we’re all really worried about is whether the US might eventually impose a complete ban on textile exports down the road,” Hua said.

For the sofa cover exporter in eastern China, orders from the US have been resilient this year – a relief after last year’s tit-for-tat tariff war that once brought bilateral trade to a near standstill.

“Unless some unforeseen policies come out, things generally look fairly optimistic for now,” the manager said.

But manufacturers in Xinjiang have long ceased pinning their hopes on the mercy of the US.

“The Chinese government should just move the headquarters for all those must-have goods the US relies on China for to Xinjiang,” the cotton mill owner said. “That way, if you want to buy them, you have to buy from Xinjiang.”

As an example, he cited rare earth elements – the valuable minerals crucial to hi-tech and defence supply chains.

item.title: [SCMP] China is using Jiang Zemin centenary to signal political continuity
item.description:
The centenary of Jiang Zemin’s birth, marked on August 17 with a memorial in Beijing attended and addressed by President Xi Jinping, was more than an occasion to commemorate a former Chinese leader. It was also an exercise in political history: a moment to locate Jiang, the era he led and the reform legacy associated with him within the broader story of the Communist Party of China’s evolution and China’s modernisation.

That is what makes the event politically significant. The question is not simply why China is commemorating Jiang so prominently. It is why the leadership has chosen this particular historical moment to reaffirm his place in the country’s political narrative and what that says about how Beijing views the road from reform and opening up to Chinese modernisation today.

Xi’s speech placed Jiang squarely within the history of the party, describing him as the core of the party’s third-generation central leadership and as a principal founder of the important notion of the “Three Represents”. It also highlighted Jiang’s contributions to reform and opening up, socialist modernisation and China’s development.
item.content:encoded:
The centenary of Jiang Zemin’s birth, marked on August 17 with a memorial in Beijing attended and addressed by President Xi Jinping, was more than an occasion to commemorate a former Chinese leader. It was also an exercise in political history: a moment to locate Jiang, the era he led and the reform legacy associated with him within the broader story of the Communist Party of China’s evolution and China’s modernisation.

That is what makes the event politically significant. The question is not simply why China is commemorating Jiang so prominently. It is why the leadership has chosen this particular historical moment to reaffirm his place in the country’s political narrative and what that says about how Beijing views the road from reform and opening up to Chinese modernisation today.

Xi’s speech placed Jiang squarely within the history of the party, describing him as the core of the party’s third-generation central leadership and as a principal founder of the important notion of the “Three Represents”. It also highlighted Jiang’s contributions to reform and opening up, socialist modernisation and China’s development.

The formulation matters. It presents Jiang neither as an isolated political figure nor simply as the representative of a bygone era. Instead, it places him within a chain of political leadership and national development stretching across several decades.

For China’s leadership, historical continuity has considerable political importance. The reform era was not a single event but a succession of experiments, adjustments and institutional changes undertaken by different generations of leaders. Jiang’s years in national leadership, particularly during the 1990s and early 2000s, coincided with one of the most consequential transformations in modern Chinese history: the consolidation of the socialist market economy, the acceleration of economic globalisation, the development of Pudong, the restructuring of state-owned enterprises and China’s accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO).

Those developments fundamentally altered China’s relationship with the global economy. China moved from being a relatively marginal participant in international production and trade to becoming an increasingly central manufacturing and trading power.

Therefore, to commemorate Jiang today is also to acknowledge that contemporary China did not emerge fully formed. Its present economic strength is the cumulative product of decades of institutional experimentation, reform, opening up and policy continuity.

Reform is China’s past – and also its future

This point carries particular resonance in 2026.

China is entering the 15th five-year plan period in an international environment radically different from that of Jiang’s era. Strategic competition between China and the United States has intensified. Trade protectionism has returned with force. Technology restrictions are reshaping supply chains, while geopolitical tensions are encouraging some governments to reconsider the assumptions of economic globalisation.

Against this backdrop, reaffirming the legacy of the reform era is not necessarily nostalgia. It can also be read as a statement of direction.

China’s message is that reform and opening up remain part of its historical trajectory, even though their content and methods must evolve with changing circumstances. The external environment might have changed dramatically, but Beijing is not presenting modernisation as a retreat from the world.

That is one reason the Jiang commemoration has relevance beyond China’s domestic political history. Jiang’s tenure is closely associated with China’s deeper integration into the global economy. WTO accession, expanding foreign trade, rising foreign investment and the development of global industrial linkages helped lay foundations for the China that exists today.

At a time when decoupling and de-risking have become prominent concepts in international policy debates, recalling that history sends a message that the country continues to see openness as an important component of development.

A legacy of experimentation

A centenary is not an ordinary anniversary. It creates a natural historical checkpoint. Jiang was born in 1926; his centenary arrives at a moment when China is again confronting major questions about economic transformation, technological development, national security and its relationship with the outside world.

Such moments encourage governments and societies to not just revisit the past but extract meaning from it. The political value of historical memory lies precisely here. By determining which achievements are emphasised and how they are connected to the present, political leaders can help establish a framework through which the past is understood.

The Jiang commemoration thus functions as a form of historical integration. It reinforces the idea that the party’s governing experience should be understood cumulatively rather than through a succession of political breaks.

This does not mean every policy of the Jiang era is being endorsed wholesale, and neither does it suggest China intends to reproduce the circumstances of three decades ago. The world economy, Chinese society and China’s position in the international system have all changed profoundly.

Rather, the lesson is that continuity does not require repetition. The reform and opening up of the 1990s cannot simply be copied in the 2020s. However, the underlying principles of experimentation, institutional adaptation, engagement with the global economy and the pursuit of modernisation can be reinterpreted for a new era.

That might be the most important political significance of remembering Jiang at 100. By placing Jiang within the uninterrupted historical development of the party and the country, Xi’s commemoration reinforces a political narrative of succession without rupture, reform without abandonment and modernisation without historical amnesia.

Political continuity, not nostalgia

The message emerging from Beijing is that today’s China is the product of accumulated experience; that reform and opening up remain embedded in the country’s modernisation story; that different generations of leadership are being presented as contributors to a continuous national project; and that the lessons of earlier periods remain relevant as China navigates a more contested international environment.

In that sense, the most revealing question surrounding Jiang’s centenary is not simply how Xi evaluates Jiang. It is how the present leadership uses Jiang’s legacy to explain the relationship between China’s reform past, its modernisation present and its uncertain future.

The answer appears to be clear: China does not intend to return to the Jiang era. It intends to carry forward what it regards as the useful historical experience of that era while adapting it to new conditions.

That is not nostalgia. It is political continuity and, at a time of profound global change, a deliberate statement about where China believes its modern history came from and where it intends to go next.

item.title: [SCMP] China becomes first nation to recover orbital launch rockets with 2 distinct paths
item.description:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.
item.content:encoded:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.

The Zhuque-3 is China’s first commercial rocket to both reach orbit and have its first stage recovered.

LandSpace also became the fourth entity – after US companies SpaceX and Blue Origin, and state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) – to achieve controlled recovery of a reusable vehicle from an orbital launch.

Like SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Blue Origin’s New Glenn, the Zhuque-3 uses landing legs to recover its rockets.

But last month, China was the first to recover a booster on an orbital launch with a different technique, after the first stage of CASC’s Long March 10B was recovered using a unique sea-based net capture system.

SpaceX’s Super Heavy booster, which is also made of stainless steel, is awaiting US Federal Aviation Administration approval for its first recovery flight to send the Starship into orbit.

The Super Heavy will also attempt a non-leg-based orbital recovery, using mechanical “chopstick” arms mounted on a tower to catch the booster.

Wednesday’s milestone is just the start of China’s reusable rocket recovery efforts, while the US already has hundreds of successful booster recoveries and reuses under its belt.

The 66-metre (217-foot) Zhuque-3 rocket, powered by liquid methane and oxygen, lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in the Gobi Desert at 7.35am on Wednesday, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The rocket delivered a Honghu-3 internet satellite into its designated orbit, while its first stage returned to Earth and touched down vertically at a recovery site in Minqin county, Gansu province, about 390km (242 miles) southeast of the launch pad.

“This mission marks China’s first successful recovery of a first-stage reusable launch vehicle using landing legs, and also China’s first successful land-based recovery of a first-stage orbital-deployed launch vehicle,” LandSpace said.

“LandSpace will continue to advance the iteration and engineering verification of reusable technology, helping my country further improve its low-cost, high-frequency and highly reliable space transport capabilities,” the company added in a social media post.

Dong Kai, the rocket’s deputy chief designer, told the LatePost news outlet on Wednesday that LandSpace aimed to reuse the recovered rockets as soon as possible, adding that he hoped to launch the Zhuque-3 10 times a year.

Wednesday’s launch was LandSpace’s second attempt to put the Zhuque-3 into orbit and recover its first stage.

During the rocket’s maiden flight in December, the second stage reached orbit but the first stage erupted in a dramatic fireball during its final powered descent towards the landing pad.

After that mission, Zhuque-3 project chief Dai Zheng told state broadcaster CCTV that the recovery had failed because the first stage’s engine had not reignited when it was about 3km above the ground as required.

LandSpace said on Wednesday that, following the first attempt, the rocket was optimised for reusable flight by reducing the number of landing ignition engines, improving the on-board autonomous safety control system, and enhancing thermal protection for re-entry.

Now, the Zhuque-3 is China’s second orbital rocket to demonstrate first-stage recovery. The first was the state-developed Long March-10B, whose first stage was captured by a huge net on an offshore platform after launching from Hainan province in July.

The two rockets have broadly similar payload capacities and are in about the same class as SpaceX’s workhorse, Falcon 9. In expendable configuration, the Long March-10B and Zhuque-3 can carry about 22 and 21 tonnes to low Earth orbit, respectively. With their first stages recovered, the figures fall to about 16 and 18 tonnes.

Unlike the stainless steel design of the Zhuque-3, the Falcon 9 is made using an aluminium-lithium alloy. Dong said that the welding process for stainless steel was easier than for aluminium alloy, adding that the material was also cheap and had good heat resistance.

Recovering the two rockets could prove crucial to the construction of China’s broadband internet megaconstellations. Like SpaceX’s Starlink, Chinese projects such as Guowang and Qianfan envisage eventually placing more than 10,000 satellites in orbit to provide global broadband coverage, creating both a potential global market and infrastructure of strategic military importance.

So far, Starlink has deployed more than 10,000 operational satellites and attracted over 12 million customers worldwide. Its extensive use by Ukrainian forces for battlefield communications has shown the military value of such a network.

By comparison, Beijing’s Guowang constellation and the Shanghai-backed Qianfan network have each deployed only around 200 satellites. Their expansion has been constrained partly by China’s lack of a reusable workhorse comparable to the Falcon 9.

Wednesday’s feat suggests China could translate its engineering talent and manufacturing abilities into cheaper, faster launches, positioning it to compete with the US as both nations accelerate the roll-out of internet satellites.

While US space agency Nasa has left reusable rocket development to commercial partners like SpaceX, China is playing on both fronts, with its state-run space programme building reusable boosters alongside the commercial sector.

The China National Space Administration said on Wednesday that it helped coordinate the Zhuque-3 launch team, adding that it would continue to support the country’s reusable rocket technology.

The next test for China’s reusable rockets will be whether the recovered boosters can be refurbished and flown again, which is necessary to reduce launch costs and support more frequent launches.

LandSpace said the recovery of the Zhuque-3 laid a foundation for subsequent maintenance and reuse flights, and would help China improve launch capabilities to support commercial missions and the deployment of satellite constellations.

item.title: [SCMP] Word on the StrEAT: 6 Hong Kong chefs share pre-service rituals that fuel their kitchens
item.description:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path
item.content:encoded:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path

“We have a fairly small team of four – including [a] dishwasher! We [start the night] by greeting everyone and checking on each other. Show a bit of love to everyone.

“The playlist changes from Cantopop to more casual lofi pop songs like Keshi. Andy Hui is one of Sean’s (our Texan GM’s) favourites. Our team ritual is to sing together. It opens up our voice more before the night starts. ⁠After service begins, we are definitely more locked in to serve our guests.

“We also always stash gummies inside our kitchen to sweeten our service – a bit of a sugar rush also helps!”

Chef Sean Yuen, Jija by Vicky Lau

“Five minutes before service is the ‘calm before the storm’. Everyone is running their final checks, and the air is noticeably tense. I review tonight’s cover count, find out when the peak hour hits, and check for any VIPs or special dietary requirements. Once I have those numbers in mind, the rhythm of the night becomes completely clear.

“Downing a shot of espresso right before service not only wakes me up, but also acts as a mental trigger to switch into battle mode. [We] turn on all the heat lamps at the pass and the moment those lights go on, it means all the prep work is done.

“One hour into service, everyone is fully in the zone – hyper-focused, with the entire kitchen running at a fast yet meticulously organised pace. During peak rush hours, taking a two-second break to grab a sip of water gives me a quick moment to pause, clear my mind, and jump straight back into position.”

Chef Tara Margarita, Bourke’s

“Music is essential for us. Kitchens get hot and high-stress, so the right tunes keep the energy light during prep before the inevitable service rush. Anyone in hospitality knows the absolute pain of listening to the exact same pre-service loop for years on end. We’re lucky to have a diverse team with different cultural backgrounds, so we like to rotate the prep-DJ duties.

“If I’m on the aux, my recent go-to tracks are ‘Summer Romance’ by Incubus, ‘Given Up’ by Linkin Park and ‘Killing in the Name’ by Rage Against the Machine.

“Work is intense, but work isn’t life – it’s important not to lose sight of that. So personally, I always make time to stretch and check in with my team on a human level.

“On fully staffed days, those last five minutes are pure ‘calm before the storm’ and your final chance to double-check line set-ups or fire off last-minute backups. I change into my shift shoes and jacket and pull my hair back in a way that’s guaranteed to hold up for the next 14 hours.

“During service, front of house has made a habit of buying me Kinder Buenos – especially if I’m looking a bit stressed on the pass. I keep a dedicated 1/9 pan in my lowboy [refrigerator] stocked with bite-sized Kinder Buenos to get through the push.”

Chef Ryo Matsui, Torikaze Hong Kong

“Before anything else, I want to see, touch and taste what has arrived that day. It tells me how we need to cook.

“We make sure every station is clean, organised and complete. It may sound simple, but this is important – the state of your station reflects the state of your mind. I need to see the charcoal glowing properly and have my fan beside the grill. The fire is alive, and it changes constantly, so the fan is not only a tool to control the heat; it is how I communicate with it. When the binchotan is ready, the whole station feels ready.

“There is a quiet tension. Everyone is focused on their own station, checking small details one more time. [Then] the kitchen becomes more fluid – less thinking, more instinct. Communication is shorter, movements become more precise, and the team finds its rhythm together.

“When it becomes busy, I return to the next plate. Not the whole service, not the tickets waiting behind it, just the dish in front of me. You cannot control everything at once, but you can always control the quality of the next action.”

Chef Uwe Opocensky, Petrus

“As a junior cook, I was on a station, and being ‘ready’ meant my mise en place was perfect and I was set for whatever came at me during service. These days I run the pass, so readiness looks different. It’s less about my own station and more about checking that everyone else is ready and everything is exactly where it should be.

“The first thing I always do is greet everyone; that sets the tone for the whole day. Then I do a walk-through to see what’s going on: checking the bookings, events and anything that may have changed since the night before. After that, I sit down with my senior chefs and go through notes I’ve written the night before – ideas, things we could do better, things I think we can improve on. It’s important to me that the day starts with the team, not just with the food.

“Consistency is the ritual. I go over the booking sheet one more time. I check that everything is set up and ready – down to the tasting spoons and seat numbers. Then I get a large glass of sparkling water for myself before service starts. By the time I step through the doors of Petrus, I’m focused.

“The one constant through all of it has been a small espresso. It’s less about the caffeine and more about the signal; it’s my way of telling myself I’m ready to go.”

Chef Alex Fargas, La Paloma

“I believe every dish matters, and every person we work with and serve matters. Every day at 5pm we hold a team meeting. We dedicate the first 20 minutes to discussing the previous day’s situations and focusing on customer satisfaction. The next 20 minutes are dedicated to staff training, motivation and development. Finally, the last 10 minutes are spent discussing personal healthy habits, life goals or any important matters anyone has on their mind.

“We take that time to connect, share how we’re feeling, and discuss what we are aiming to achieve on that particular day.

“We set clear objectives for every day and week, assigning both individual and team goals. This keeps everyone connected, aligned with our targets, and fully engaged during our daily meetings.

“We take it one dish and one person at a time, ensuring we give everything the attention it needs to achieve excellence. One step at a time – that’s how we operate at La Paloma.”

item.title: [SCMP] Making tracks through China’s past and present
item.description:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.
item.content:encoded:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.

It took Snow more than two days to cover the 1,000km (621 miles) from Beijing to Xian by rail, but China’s 21st century public transport will make my own pilgrimage to Yanan, with some history-imbued detours along the way, far smoother.

With tickets bought online, I set my sights first on Jinan, the capital of Shandong province, located on the upper reaches of the Yellow River and 400km (249 miles) to the south of Beijing.

At the massive, oval-domed Beijing South station, I board a G-class train that makes light work of the Central Plain, rocketing across an area the size of Paraguay characterised by undulating wheat and rapeseed-flower fields. It takes just over two hours to reach the far side of the mighty Yellow River, a reminder that Beijing was one of the few ancient Chinese cities that were not fed by the “mother river”.

Jinan’s urban district stands to the south of the river. First impressions upon arrival at dusk are of a typical second-tier city composed chiefly of modern high-rises strung together by flyovers. My mood isn’t much improved by the hotel I pre-booked, which is located down a gloomy Shizhong district alley, past street-side barbecue joints populated by drunks, with electrical wires dangling overhead and between adverts for spas and KTV (karaoke television) lounges. The labyrinth of hotel corridors has tobacco-stained carpets and room service comes courtesy of R2-D2-like robots.

Morning illuminates Jinan in a better light.

A short walk leads to Wulongtan (“Five Dragon Pond”), a classical garden comprising several natural springs. It was mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals, the official chronicle of the state of Lu (1042BC-249BC), which existed here before the unification of China under Qin Shi Huang.

Bamboo-lined pathways lead between concave-roofed pavilions and goldfish ponds sprinkled with water lilies. Some park-goers are writing classical verses in calligraphic characters on the ground with giant brushes dipped in water, while a group of aunties practises a traditional sword dance beside a man who, unfazed by their music, drifts through the elegant postures of tai chi.

Wulongtan is one of several public gardens fed by spring water that dominate Jinan and help explain its motto, splashed on numerous billboards: “City of springs, no worries for people”.

To the north, the Jinan Baili Huanghe Scenic Area flanks the south bank of the Yellow River, which, in truth, is more of a coffee colour. Here, elders stretch while courting couples watch the sunset from viewing points along the river’s edges. Farmers still cultivate the muddy riverbanks, using nutrient-rich loess soil that has flowed down from Shaanxi province to feed rows of green vegetables, as they and their ancestors have done since the dawn of Chinese civilisation.

Following the riverfront path eastwards leads to the Luokou Yellow River Railway Bridge. Conventional rolling stock still uses this century-old, German-built viaduct, which was completed in 1912.

Also of German vintage in Jinan are a few villas, a colonial-era post office and the former station house on the Jiaoji Railway – Shandong’s first railway, which connected with the port of Qingdao.

Jiaoji Railway Station, which now houses a museum, was completed in 1915 and built in early European Renaissance Revival style. It is distinguished by a prominent central colonnade beneath a large clock. The line itself has been modernised and no longer leaves from the station-turned-museum, but from Daminghu station, near Daming Lake Park.

Unfortunately, the art nouveau Jinan Railway Station depicted in the museum, and which stood 500 metres (1,640 feet) from Jiaoji station, came to be regarded as “a symbol of colonialism” and was replaced by an unexceptional building in 1992. It’s from here that I depart for Taian, just a 20-minute hop away by high-speed rail.

Taian would be an unremarkable provincial city were it not for a mountain considered so sacred for so many centuries, it has assumed the status of a god.

Mount Tai is the easternmost of China’s nine Daoist peaks, attracting up to a million pilgrims a year, who attempt to follow the emperors’ journey 8km (five miles) up the mountainside, paying homage to Heaven and Earth, at the summit and foot of the mountain, respectively.

I set out early to beat the crowds, but my 6am hotel alarm call is not early enough; everyone else has made the same calculation. It’s not so much a hike, then, as a communal walk along stone steps carved out of the mountainside as far back as Qin times, some two millennia ago.

Amid cypress trees and gushing streams, every rock we pass has been inscribed with poetic verse and it becomes apparent that the passage from the First Heavenly Gate to Jade Emperor Peak owes its glories – the temples and pavilions – to the patronage of the imperial court.

Past the Immortal Bridge, a natural formation of three huge boulders, the ascent to the Nantian Gate, some 1,500 metres (4,920 feet) above sea level, funnels hundreds of walkers between two walls of rock. Almost everyone is grasping the handrails as they haul themselves upwards at this point, cries of “jia you” (“add oil”) ringing out as pilgrims encourage one another to keep going.

There’s more than a sense of achievement to reward those who make it to the top of the mountain, where Tianjie (“Heaven Street”), a tourist strip with plenty of restaurants, awaits hungry hikers.

Unashamedly, I take the cable car back down to Earth, and the following day, I take the morning train to Kaifeng, in Henan province. There’s no fast service between the two cities, so I’m relegated to a second-class bunk in a half-full carriage, a sign that conventional rail might be dying out in the age of high-speed.

My fellow passengers are all tall northerners, their skin cracked by the sun of the high latitudes. Men in leather jackets and tightly fitting shirts walk back and forth along the gangway at 20-minute intervals, to find somewhere to smoke; women fondle their Xiaomi phones. Over seven hours of rail travel, there’s little to do but meditate on China’s heartland passing gently by while sipping tea and dipping into Red Star Over China.

Kaifeng is depicted in one of China’s great masterworks, Along the River During the Qingming Festival, a 12th century scroll painting that hangs in Beijing’s Palace Museum, as the Forbidden City is officially known, and reveals the bustling street markets and classical architecture of the capital of the Northern Song dynasty (960-1127) in its imperial heyday. The view from my taxi suggests the contemporary prefecture-level city is a few centuries past its prime: Soviet-style tenements jockey for space with modern towers, all of which appear to have adopted a colour code inspired by the muddy waters of the Yellow River.

The roads are the domain of e-bikes and e-trikes, which buzz like hornets around a nest within the refurbished city walls that frame the former capital.

In the middle of an anarchic roundabout stands the Drum Tower – three layers of green-tiled roofs atop a grey-brick foundation, the result of a complete 2013 rebuild – looking regal amid the shabby storefronts and chain hotels of downtown Kaifeng. At night, the eaves of the tower are illuminated with LED lights as it becomes the focus of a market. Hundreds of carts are pushed from side streets, to congregate around the tower, and from them issue the hissing and sizzling of cooking oil, with notes of garlic, ginger and pork fat, as diners feast on crispy wheat cakes and mutton noodle soup.

Kaifeng might not ooze the kind of laid-back prosperity I experienced in Jinan, but what it lacks in polish, it makes up for with heritage.

From the Old Town’s central access, Shudianjie (“Bookshop Street”), where some time-honoured book vendors are still in business, it’s easy to walk to some of the chief attractions, including the Shanshangan Guild Hall, a social hub established by northern merchants in the late 18th century.

Flanked by its own mini drum and bell towers, the hall has traditional roofing, the eaves of which have been decorated with lively scenes from the lives of travelling merchants and other wood carvings. One, in the Eastern Hall, depicts a man being dragged along the ground by his horse; others show golden bats, a symbol of luck, beneath animals and birds frolicking among bunches of grapes.

A 10-minute walk away, the Buddhist Daxiangguo Temple is still populated by robed monks 1,500 years after its founding. Watching the faithful prostrate themselves before Arhat statues at the back of the Main Hall, I’m reminded that train travel in China can be as much about time as it is space.

Kaifeng’s principal reminder of its Northern Song heyday is the 1,000-year-old Iron Pagoda, which towers 56 metres (184 feet) over the northeastern corner of the walled city. It is not made of iron but earned its name from the patterned glazed Buddhist tiles on its exterior, which give the tower the russet tones of rusted iron.

Despite Kaifeng’s plethora of historical marvels, it’s the tumble-down backstreets, where the rhythms of life remain unchanged by China’s high-speed dash towards a neon-hued future, that are hardest to bid farewell to when I depart from Kaifeng North station, bound for Xian.

Snow was received by the Kuomintang governor of the city when he visited Xian. I’m met with crowds pushing onto Metro Line 2, eager to get to the walled city centre. Yet, on emerging from Zhonglou station, which lies beneath the Bell Tower, it is impossible not to be impressed with what was, after all, the capital of 13 dynasties. Xian has the panache of somewhere that mattered, and mattered for a very long time – a self-confidence evident in the swagger of its denizens as well as the power architecture: the enormous Soviet-style Bell Tower Hotel, facing the Bell Tower; the “twin Tang towers” to the south of the city – the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and Small Wild Goose Pagoda; the enormous walls and the broad boulevards that stitch it all together. Everything is on a scale that is only really rivalled by Beijing.

Having scarcely encountered another foreigner since leaving the capital, it’s something of a culture shock to witness legions of Western tourists, most of whom are taking advantage of the 30-day visa exemption policy to strike Qin Shi Huang’s Terracotta Army off their bucket list.

There again, Xian was the capital of the cosmopolitan Tang dynasty (618-907) and long served as the eastern gate to the Silk Road. This multicultural history is reflected in the Tang-era Great Mosque, which stands off a narrow, covered alley filled with vendors of tourist tat. One of the largest mosques in China, it was established in 742, although heavily restored during the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), and integrates Arabic features into a familiar Chinese design. Attracting mostly religious tourists from Central and Southeast Asia, the mosque’s tranquillity stands in contrast to the adjoining Muslim Quarter, which gets my vote for the finest street food in East Asia.

After braving the throngs several times for bowls of biang biang noodles, barbecued naan bread and persimmon doughnuts, I feel sufficiently energised to complete my railway quest.

Snow travelled north through fields of opium poppies that “nodded their swollen heads, ready for harvest, along the newly completed motor road” before sleeping “in a filthy hut […] with pigs and donkeys quartered in the next room”. I, on the other hand, cruise across the Loess Plateau at 250km/h (155mph) in an air-conditioned carriage.

The Yan River, a major tributary of the Yellow, bisects Yanan. The waterway and city are best viewed from Pagoda Hill, atop which stands the 44-metre (144 feet) Baota Pagoda, an octagonal brick tower that dates back to Tang times. Most of Yanan’s other tourist sites recall events that took place 90 years ago.

I taxi to the Date Garden, which was the site of the Communist Party Secretariat from October 1943 to March 1947. As well as various war bureaus, the former residences of officials, including Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai, are located in the grounds of this erstwhile warlord’s manor, their humble furnishings still decorating their yaodong (“cave houses”), as earth-sheltered dwellings still common in Shaanxi province are called.

Concluding that to truly appreciate Yanan, I too should sleep in a cave, I consult a taxi driver parked outside the Date Garden, who takes me to Jingjiawan Village, where enterprising locals have converted family cave homes into guest houses.

A bright-eyed, middle-aged man, Xiao Zhang, greets me in the courtyard of the Old Yanan Cave Dwelling Hotel before showing me to my cavern for the night. Snow recounts sharing a kang, a traditional northern bed, with rats. But my kang has an electric blanket, while my cave is equipped with a widescreen television, an en suite bathroom and even voice-activated lights.

After a nap and a shower, I’m told to find an alfresco table on the edge of a cliff overlooking a large valley, a dramatic landscape of windblown yellow soil that has created steep ravines divided by deep gullies. The land here is rich in nutrients and has been cultivated for centuries, a history evident in crumbling terraces that were abandoned in the late 20th century as farmers emigrated to work in east-coast factories.

Lao Zhang, the family patriarch-turned-chef, takes my order and brings me a Wusu beer, with which I toast my journey back in time, from capital to cave.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s growing wealth inequality: will it be an M- or olive-shaped society?
item.description:
An ageing society and a widening income gap threaten Hong Kong’s social fabric. In the last of a five-part series on the city’s five-year plan, we look at what can be done to address these key issues. Read part one here, part two here, part three here and part four here.

At 71, Man Chi-ying is the sole carer for her husband, Fung Yu-hoi, a Parkinson’s disease patient.

Fung, who is also 71, has stiff limbs and, on some days, needs his wife’s help getting dressed. She has to hold his hand to keep him from falling. About two months ago, Fung fell and scratched his face while they were out for a walk.
item.content:encoded:
An ageing society and a widening income gap threaten Hong Kong’s social fabric. In the last of a five-part series on the city’s five-year plan, we look at what can be done to address these key issues. Read part one here, part two here, part three here and part four here.

At 71, Man Chi-ying is the sole carer for her husband, Fung Yu-hoi, a Parkinson’s disease patient.

Fung, who is also 71, has stiff limbs and, on some days, needs his wife’s help getting dressed. She has to hold his hand to keep him from falling. About two months ago, Fung fell and scratched his face while they were out for a walk.

The couple live in a public housing flat in Tsing Yi. They rely on government allowances for the elderly, amounting to a combined HK$8,690 (US$1,108) a month. Their daughter, son-in-law and nine-year-old granddaughter live in Canada.

Man herself is battling multiple health conditions, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol and heart disease, and takes eight types of medication a day.

“I used to believe that I would depend on his care, but it has turned out to be the opposite,” Man said.

“What will happen if something happens to me? Who will look after him?”

Their plight is all too familiar for social workers tending to Hong Kong’s growing low-income elderly community.

As the city draws up its first five-year plan, experts say that a double whammy of a rapidly ageing population and a potential widening of the wealth gap, accelerated by the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), ranks among the most pressing livelihood challenges.

To cope with social challenges presented by demographic changes and worsening disparities, the city needs a comprehensive population policy, they say.

Their calls align with the national 15th five-year plan, which has a chapter dedicated to population policy and identified addressing an ageing society and a dwindling fertility rate as key priorities.

“We need to look at the overall picture of Hong Kong’s demographic changes over the next five years, including both the quantity and quality of the population,” said Nelson Chow Wing-sun, an emeritus professor at the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) department of social work and social administration.

“When planning for healthcare, education, social welfare and housing, it ultimately comes down to population shifts, and the resulting demand for these services.”

Ageing population, demographic shifts and declining birth rate

Significant demographic restructuring has shaped Hong Kong in the past decade.

In 2025, about 1.78 million residents were aged 65 or older, accounting for a quarter of the total population – a 60 per cent increase from around 1.11 million, or 16 per cent, in 2015.

“If any society has over 25 per cent [of the total population] aged 65 or above, it is not going to be sustainable,” said Paul Yip Siu-fai, chair professor of population health at HKU’s department of social work and social administration.

Over the same period, the labour force declined from 3.9 million to 3.81 million. The number of births also fell to a record low of 31,100 last year.

“Our working population is shrinking. But at the same time, our population is still growing,” Yip noted. “It will create a lot of challenges in terms of how we can maintain our population to be developed in a healthy and sustainable manner.”

The trend placed a heavy burden on public finances and healthcare services, while also risking a vacuum in the younger workforce that could slow the momentum of development, Yip said.

Even as residents have left Hong Kong for other places, the city has welcomed newcomers under various talent schemes.

Official statistics showed that authorities approved more than 450,000 applications under a slew of talent admission schemes since 2023, with about 330,000, or 73 per cent, from mainland China.

Among them, around 130,000 applications were approved under the Top Talent Pass Scheme alone. The programme is for high earners or graduates from top universities.

Chow said the continuing arrival of such talent would affect housing demand.

The educated newcomers, together with more mainland students, would also lift the city’s overall educational profile and impact the labour market, especially low-income jobs, he said.

He also highlighted changing family structures, including a rise in single-person households due to an ageing population and more people living alone.

All these shifts would determine the city’s housing, social welfare and healthcare needs, he said, and would require careful planning to address the resulting demands.

While at the upper end, newcomers and residents alike will compete for what they can afford, bidding and outbidding one another, at the lower end, the struggle is vastly different.

Housewife Zeng Meishi is among them. Living in a 200 sq ft flat, the 32-year-old mother of two said it was difficult to make ends meet, with the household relying on her husband’s monthly income of about HK$15,000 from construction work.

The family moved into a transitional housing flat in Cheung Sha Wan last month, paying about HK$5,000 in monthly rent. Before that, they had been crammed into an even smaller subdivided flat.

Apart from rent, utilities and other household expenses, Zeng sets aside about HK$2,000 every month to send to her parents on the mainland.

The family obtains supplies, such as rice and cooking oil, from a food bank, and receives second-hand items such as clothes from relatives.

Zeng travels to Shenzhen to see a doctor when she is ill, even though the journey can make her condition worse.

“As long as we do not go hungry, that is all that matters,” Zeng said.

The family cannot afford to enrol her 10-year-old daughter and six-year-old son in English tuition, which costs about HK$200 per session. They had fallen behind in school and felt disheartened, she said.

“I hope for a better life and that my children can receive a good education to have a more promising future,” she said, as she appealed for more financial subsidies.

Sze Lai-shan, deputy director of the Society for Community Organisation (SoCO), said low-income residents were desperately in need of more cash allowances, jobs and public housing flats, and cheaper medical services, as well as better education prospects for their children.

The NGO called for poverty alleviation efforts to be stepped up in the five-year plan, including identifying more targeted groups such as new arrivals from the mainland and carers.

These groups, SoCO said, should matter as much as the three vulnerable groups already recognised by the city’s welfare safety nets – elderly households, single-parent families and residents of subdivided flats.

It also suggested allocating more resources to families with young children through tailored support programmes to help break the cycle of intergenerational poverty.

AI and the wealth gap

As the national blueprint has tasked Hong Kong with becoming a global innovation and technology hub, the government expects the information and technology (I&T) sector to drive economic growth and create high-quality jobs, thereby improving people’s livelihoods.

However, the rise of AI could pose a deeper long-term challenge – widening income inequality.

Unemployment among younger residents has been climbing. According to the Census and Statistics Department, the jobless rate for people aged 20 to 24 rose from 8.8 per cent in 2023 to 11.2 per cent in 2025, and for those aged 25 to 29, from 4.5 per cent to 5.2 per cent.

The jobless rate in higher-paying sectors is also on the rise.

Unemployment in professional and business services climbed from 2.8 per cent in 2023 to 4 per cent in 2025, while the rate in the information and communications sector rose from 3.6 per cent to 4.2 per cent, both exceeding the overall rate.

Although still below the peak recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic, the figures are approaching levels seen during the 2008 global financial crisis.

While an uncertain economic outlook is partly to blame, academics warn that AI is beginning to displace middle-class, well-paid roles.

“AI can do the co-piloting, can be the research assistants, can do the secretarial job and a lot of the programming job,” Yip said, expressing the fear that AI would change Hong Kong’s income structure from an “olive-shaped” to an “M-shaped” society.

An M-shaped society is one in which the middle class is hollowed out, with two peaks in the high- and low-income distribution reflecting wealth polarisation, while an olive-shaped society has a large middle class and two narrow ends representing the rich and poor.

“If [the middle-class] can learn AI well and adopt well, they will move up. Not learning well, and then they will be pushed down … It is happening. It is just going to get worse, and I am not sure it will get any better,” Yip said.

Cleo Ng, an analyst at a business consultancy firm specialising in digital transformation, is among those hard hit by the rise of AI.

“People in our industry now rely on AI to prepare proposals, but clients themselves can also access AI, so they may no longer need consultants and can already get the same answers,” she said.

“AI has also made it easier for people to enter the profession, but at the same time it has made the job less sought-after than before.”

The 26-year-old observed that demand for manpower in the industry was declining. A project that typically required eight to 10 people in the past now needed only five, with fewer junior positions available.

As consultancy work itself risks being replaced by AI, Ng noted that some clients now preferred to deal directly with technology providers or reduce their budgets, making it harder to secure projects.

“People are frustrated regarding where they should be going,” said Hui Kai-lung, associate provost of academic development and Elman Family Professor of Business at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

“We do not know what options there are for us if we were to change right now. As a result, people want to cling to what they had.”

But he argued that whether AI would widen the wealth gap depended on how people adopted and capitalised on the technology.

While a static snapshot might show a shrinking middle class as some roles gradually disappeared, Hui preferred to look at the dynamic nature of the job market, predicting that new occupations could emerge and fill the gap as innovation advanced.

The national blueprint highlighted the need to address AI’s impact on employment and to create more job opportunities by developing AI and emerging industries.

Hui urged the government to set out a clear 10- to 15-year economic vision and map out how technology could empower key sectors such as finance, tourism, healthcare, and education, alongside a loosely regulated environment that would allow industries to innovate and transform.

HKU’s Yip stressed the need for the government to maintain a balanced approach during the transition, avoiding an excessive tilt towards the I&T sector and manpower misalignment.

He also called for a review of the city’s HK$100 billion annual welfare spending and stronger efforts to retrain residents, particularly underprivileged groups, in AI skills so “no one is left behind”.

Call for a long-term population policy

Beyond such measures, experts urged the authorities to move away from myopic piecemeal schemes and formulate a long-term population policy.

Chow said achieving a demographic composition that supported economic growth and ensuring sufficient services to meet demand were vital.

“The city needs enough manpower and population to support economic growth on one hand, while on the other, it also needs sufficient social services, housing and healthcare to support the demands brought on by these changes,” he said.

The government established the Steering Committee on Population Policy chaired by the chief secretary in 2007, later revamped and expanded it in 2012 to include professionals from various sectors.

The committee published a report in 2015 proposing an array of measures to attract talent, raise the birth rate, and improve care for the elderly, before it was disbanded in 2017.

Former labour and welfare minister Law Chi-kwong acknowledged that the last review of the population policy dated back to 2015. He noted that declining populations were a global trend, citing the mainland, South Korea, Japan and Taiwan.

“Why should Hong Kong be different?” he asked.

According to Law, the city’s strategy should focus on slowing the worsening birth rate, which he believed could not be reversed, and stepping up efforts to attract overseas students by improving housing options.

Population expert Yip, who served on the committee, called for the re-establishment of a high-level, interdepartmental platform to devise a clear population policy, citing the current lack of coordination among bureaus.

“Population policy is a continuous policy … Especially in the last few years, Hong Kong has undergone a lot of demographic changes,” he said. “You do need someone who is overseeing the situation and then monitoring carefully and doing the timely intervention.”

He proposed key indicators, including an annual population growth rate of 1 per cent to ensure sustainable socio-economic growth without exceeding the city’s capacity.

He also called for diversifying talent sources beyond the mainland.

“Once we become too monopolised by single sources, I think that will put ourselves in an unhealthy situation,” Yip said. “Because if there are any changes to these sources, that will affect us.”

He also suggested setting a target for the city’s working-age dependency ratio to avoid overburdening the economically active population.

Yip expected the city’s inaugural five-year blueprint would lay the foundation for a clear population policy.

“Once we know what role we are going to play, then we can plan our manpower provision, our educational system and our population policy, including the migration aspect, so that everything falls into the right place,” he said.

Such a comprehensive policy may help people like Man, if it does not come too late.

She wants to know how there can be support for her ailing husband if she were to fall ill. For now, she feels relief each day they can rely on each other.

“Sometimes when I’m not feeling well, he’ll bring me a glass of water,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Wear now, pay later: the new rules of Southeast Asia’s indulgence economy
item.description:
With its padded leather and gold “CC” lock, Coco Chanel’s instantly recognisable bag is practically part of the uniform for any self-respecting Bangkok property agent – an apt accessory for a city that recently edged into the top 10 anywhere for luxury spending.

But in chastened economic times liquidity and luxury are no longer in lockstep, challenging many of those with expensive tastes to find new ways to keep up appearances while balancing their books.

Jirapun Ngam, 42, works in the fast-paced business of buying and selling the Thai capital’s skyline.
item.content:encoded:
With its padded leather and gold “CC” lock, Coco Chanel’s instantly recognisable bag is practically part of the uniform for any self-respecting Bangkok property agent – an apt accessory for a city that recently edged into the top 10 anywhere for luxury spending.

But in chastened economic times liquidity and luxury are no longer in lockstep, challenging many of those with expensive tastes to find new ways to keep up appearances while balancing their books.

Jirapun Ngam, 42, works in the fast-paced business of buying and selling the Thai capital’s skyline.

She pays for her designer goods on instalments, keeping cash to buy, renovate and flip homes as they hit the market.

“I need cash to invest in my business, but I also want luxury items,” she said. “With instalment plans, I get the product immediately and pay it off monthly with only a small amount of interest.”

Her calculation reflects a growing mindset among Southeast Asia’s aspirant middle class, a cohort unwilling to let their tastes decouple from the super-rich, despite the economic turbulence of the last few years.

Instead, an alternative luxury economy is evolving.

Live-streamed bargains, online resale markets and instalment purchases are bridging the gap between aspiration and affordability.

It is a market tier that is “resilient rather than immune” to economic headwinds, according to Mariella Merlino, a luxury commercial and merchandising executive.

“The higher end of the customer base remains strong, while more aspirational consumption is more exposed to macroeconomic pressure.”

But even in belt-tightening times, setting luxury aside can be hard to do.

Jirapun said the Chanel Classic bag and Rolex watches lent “a polished and distinguished image” to her and her husband.

“Could I afford to buy them without financing? Absolutely. But this makes more sense.”

Similar forces that are squeezing household spending have reshaped how governments plot their economic plans for the coming months as the jarring blows of tariffs, fuel costs and inflationary spikes rip up growth forecasts.

Throughout Southeast Asia, luxury has become a bellwether of confidence – holding firm from Jakarta to Ho Chi Minh City and growing in the region’s bling capital, Singapore.

In Bangkok, a city whose haves flit through a world of glamour and valet-parked supercars, top brands have clustered around the money.

Louis Vuitton and Dior opened concept stores over the last two years – the latter a garish “Gold House” in downtown Chidlom, where ultra-high net worth visitors arrive in Lamborghinis at malls stacked with high-end shops and restaurants.

Thailand’s luxury retail sector is estimated at around US$4.4 billion and expected to grow by 5 per cent each year for the next two to three years, despite the flattening out of demand from China where an economy in the teeth of Washington’s tariffs has lost some of its sheen over the last few years.

The big beasts of Thailand’s luxury property sector certainly have faith in the future.

They are backing the continued spending of the global uber-rich whose record stock gains, tech assets or energy holdings have soared in value while the real economy has been ground down by the US-induced Iran crisis.

On Tuesday, Asset World Corporation – majority-owned by Thai billionaire Charoen Sirivadhanabhakdi, one of the country’s richest people – announced a US$90 million investment in a new ultra-luxury hotel on the city’s Chao Phraya river.

Thailand’s leading mall operators Siam Piwat, Central Group and The Mall Group are also developing hundreds of thousands of square metres of prime Bangkok property for shopping experiences shaped by luxury brands.

“What makes Southeast Asia particularly interesting is that luxury brands are not looking at the region purely as a defensive market. They are investing for future growth,” said Merlino, former regional head of luxury for Singapore-based online fashion giant Zalora.

“The amount of investment going into malls, flagships, hospitality-led concepts and client experiences suggests that both brands and developers see Southeast Asia’s affluent consumer base becoming strategically more important within Asia.”

While those aim at the global super-rich who spend freely as they flit across Asia’s capitals, wealth experts say the thriving second-hand and resale market for luxury points to multiple layers of demand in Southeast Asia.

For Paphon Manaspakorn, CEO of Brandname Money, credit and collateral are proving a lucrative entry point to the luxury market.

He says his company’s balance sheet proves demand for luxury is here to stay, with around 200 million baht (US$6 million) in loans out so far for bags, watches and jewellery – on down payments of 30-50 per cent of the item’s value.

“People are completely open and accustomed to paying in instalments,” he told This Week in Asia, as the embarrassment of buying luxury on finance – or pawning it for quick cash – dissolved.

In fact, the taboo of today’s society may be not having the item, rather than how you got it.

“Your car is on instalments, your house is on instalments. You can see on TikTok that people even do TikTok instalments, or Shopee PayLater,” Paphon said.

Customers pay back at reasonable, legal rates of under 12 per cent a year, he says, insisting there is none of the strong-arming associated with the loan industry in Thailand if clients miss a payment.

“Should luxury only belong to the very wealthy? We wanted to make it accessible – so that you can achieve this kind of success sooner, as long as you are financially disciplined and pay in instalments.”

Instead of a contraction as the global economy bucks under energy price pressures, Paphon forecasts a doubling of the value of loans his firm seeks to provide in coming years.

And the “other side” of the business – pawning luxury items – is also doing a roaring trade.

“As the economy slows, many people come to pawn items to get cash,” he said. “I have a married couple who are customers who pawned two watches worth 11 million baht combined – one a Richard Mille and the other a Patek Philippe.”

Rich getting richer

The world’s super-rich are accumulating so much, so fast that they have in many ways cut ties with the “normal” economy experienced by the majority.

Last year, there were 556,850 ultra high net worth (UHNW) individuals across the world, according to Altrata which maps wealth – a nearly 15 per cent increase on the year, mainly powered by the technology boom.

Altrata’s most recent report, published in June, defines someone with US$30 million or more in assets as UHNW.

The US dominates with about 40 per cent of the world’s UHNW individuals.

But Asia is growing fast, with just over 141,000 people, a quarter of the global number, most of them clustered in China, India, Japan and South Korea.

The Asian super-rich also differ from their American peers, according to Julius Baer, a Swiss wealth management firm.

They are younger – and count many more women among them – and their businesses across manufacturing and tech supply chains have proved adaptive despite the US tariff onslaught on China.

“Luxury demand globally is increasingly concentrated among high net worth and top tier clients, whose spending tends to be less sensitive to short-term economic cycles,” Merlino said. “In Southeast Asia, this is reinforced by continued wealth creation and a growing concentration of affluent consumers across the region.”
