“I think China is probably quite sanguine about all these agreements being signed and looking to use them as an opportunity to push for closer bilateral ties with countries signing the agreements,” he said.

Domestic reality

Besides their geopolitical position, the countries have to manage domestic frustrations, with the public seeing such international manoeuvring as a distraction from pressing needs like health, education and the rising cost of living, according to Smith.

Despite strong post-pandemic economic rebounds as tourism resumed, South Pacific nations remain vulnerable to external shocks, especially energy prices. In May, the World Bank projected that economic growth across 11 Pacific nations would slow to 2.8 per cent in 2026.

Youth unemployment rates are high and rising. Many skilled workers such as teachers and medical professionals are emigrating in search of better wages.

Moreover, the countries’ physical future is in doubt as rising sea levels threaten to submerge swathes of their territory.

In December, the first climate migrants arrived in Australia from Tuvalu, where more than one-third of its 11,000 people have applied for a climate visa to migrate to Australia under a deal struck between the two countries two years ago.

Nasa scientists have projected that half of Tuvalu’s main atoll of Funafuti may be submerged by 2050.

“Small and beautiful”

China funded and constructed major infrastructure in the Solomon Islands after Honiara’s 2019 diplomatic switch.

That included US$119 million for a national sports stadium complex and aquatic centre in Honiara to host the 2023 Pacific Games. Australia, meanwhile, provided a Pacific Games Partnership of about US$11.4 million to support the event.

In November, Beijing signed a framework agreement with five Pacific island nations – Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Vanuatu and Fiji – to upgrade their economic partnership and “boost trade, attract investment, and accelerate industrialisation through flexible trade negotiations”, China’s Ministry of Commerce said at that time.

While China is known for using its trade clout and megaproject expertise to woo developing nations, it is also trying out a more niche strategy to win over locals in the South Pacific.

After Pacific leaders shelved a sweeping regional trade and security deal proposed by China in 2022, Beijing began to deliver “small and beautiful” projects in the Pacific, following President Xi Jinping’s pledges at a Belt and Road Initiative forum in 2023.

A popular buzzword in China’s foreign diplomacy, “small and beautiful” refers to low-budget, small-scale projects that focus on public welfare and communities’ needs.

For instance, China donated and installed hundreds of solar street lights across Nauru and Kiribati, and sent medical teams to remote villages and outlying islands.

In Nauru, a tiny coral reef nation suffering from the devastating environmental impact of decades of mining, Chinese agriculture specialists have introduced soilless cultivation factories, allowing residents who once relied on expensive imports to access locally grown vegetables.

In May, Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown joined Chinese officials in Wuzhou to launch the MV Tuitui Moana, a 43-metre (141-foot) multipurpose vessel built in southern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region to improve transport links and cargo delivery among multiple islands.

Xu of Sun Yat-sen University said delivering tangible local improvements could help secure the public support necessary for sustained engagement.

“These projects are insulated from unpredictable political shifts, such as a government changing hands or a former opposition party coming to power,” he said.

This could also be more cost-effective, Xu said, adding that maintenance costs for large-scale projects – such as highways, ports and shipyards – had been quite high for local governments.

At the same time, such small projects were less likely to trigger caution and pushback from regional powers like Australia and New Zealand, avoiding Western anxieties that Beijing’s infrastructure investments were a form of strategic pre-positioning, he added.

“In this sense, looking at the situation in reverse, China’s future relations and aid programmes with Pacific island nations are likely to have to pivot entirely towards ‘small and beautiful’ initiatives,” Xu said.

Yet, China’s strategic shifts have not gone unanswered.

Australia has reinforced its Pacific ties and ramped up funding following China’s reported attempt to establish a permanent military base in Vanuatu in 2018 and its successful 2022 security agreement with the Solomon Islands.

For the first time since 2021, Canberra overtook Beijing as the dominant lender and infrastructure investor across the Pacific in 2024, providing about 37 per cent of all development spending across the region, according to estimates published by the Lowy Institute on July 28.

China accounted for 6 per cent of the regional development flows, the report said.

item.title: [SCMP] Israel-Turkey tensions rise after Netanyahu orders strikes on Syrian airbase
item.description:
Fears of a military confrontation between Israel and Turkey are growing after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought to assert dominance over Syria by ordering air strikes on a military airfield near the Turkish border.

The eight strikes on the Abu Al-Duhur airbase in northwest Idlib province on Tuesday were characterised by Netanyahu as a warning to Turkey against expanding its military presence in Syria or helping rebuild the Syrian armed forces.

Netanyahu’s office claimed Israel and Syria had agreed to “a status quo in security matters”, which Damascus was “on the verge of breaching” by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at the airbase near Aleppo.
item.content:encoded:
Fears of a military confrontation between Israel and Turkey are growing after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sought to assert dominance over Syria by ordering air strikes on a military airfield near the Turkish border.

The eight strikes on the Abu Al-Duhur airbase in northwest Idlib province on Tuesday were characterised by Netanyahu as a warning to Turkey against expanding its military presence in Syria or helping rebuild the Syrian armed forces.

Netanyahu’s office claimed Israel and Syria had agreed to “a status quo in security matters”, which Damascus was “on the verge of breaching” by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at the airbase near Aleppo.

“Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel’s security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings,” Netanyahu’s office said in a statement issued on Tuesday evening.

The following day, the Israeli leader reframed the strikes as a “message” that he would not tolerate a Turkish military entrenchment in Syria that “advances southward, because it threatens us”.

“We conveyed that message: don’t,” Netanyahu told Israeli Army Radio. “But apparently they didn’t hear it, so we made sure they understood it better”.

His comments followed a rare expression of “deep concern” from Washington at Israel’s “unnecessary escalation”.

Because Israel gave no advance notice, the sudden appearance of its fighter jets on Turkish air-defence radars near the border could easily have triggered a clash.

Tom Barrack, the US special envoy for Syria and Iraq and ambassador to Turkey, said the Turkish military – the second-largest in Nato – “observed the aircraft heading north towards its territory and therefore could have reasonably prepared its own response.”

In 2015, Turkey shot down a Russian fighter jet under similar circumstances after it appeared to threaten an intrusion from Syrian airspace.

Observers echoed Barrack’s assessment in reactions posted on social media.

Turkey and Israel “may have no intention to get into a kinetic confrontation, but they could easily slide into one. Accidentally. Suddenly,” said Asli Aydintasbas, a Middle East fellow at the Brookings Institution. “This is why [Tuesday’s] incident was dangerous.”

Barrack, along with Turkish and Syrian officials, also disputed Israel’s initial claim of a build-up of “Turkish proxies” around Aleppo.

“The [Syrian] government has neither adopted a predatory posture nor maintained proxy forces,” Barrack said in an earlier social media post. “It has, in fact, repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel”.

Spheres of influence

Turkey has operated scores of military facilities across northwest Syria since intervening in the country’s civil war in October 2017.

But after rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa toppled the Assad government in December 2024, Turkish forces have not expanded their geographical footprint, according to observers.

Ankara briefly explored deploying forces to an airbase in central Syria soon after the takeover, but backed down after Israeli strikes hit the facility in March and April 2025, following visits by Turkish military delegations.

This incident established an informal status quo: Israel, which occupied part of southwest Syria soon after Assad’s fall, retained “freedom of action” over the southern half of the country, while the north became Turkey’s sphere of influence.

By striking Abu Al-Duhur on Tuesday, Netanyahu was now “asserting an Israeli security zone that stretches to the Turkish-Syrian border”, said Rich Outzen, a non-resident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council’s Turkey programme, who called the move “not wise”.

Analysts who spoke to This Week In Asia viewed the strikes as an ominous sign of things to come between Israel and Turkey.

Nir T. Boms, a counterterrorism expert and research fellow at Tel Aviv University’s Moshe Dayan Centre, said the incident had raised the risk of confrontation, though he thought “there is a long way to go” before one erupted.

“This is signalling to Damascus which, of course, is related to the growing Turkish role in shaping Syria’s military,” Boms said, adding that Israel was “concerned about this direction”, especially given the “track record of Turkish support for groups that have taken a very brazen line against Israel”.

Shaiel Ben-Ephraim, an Israeli-American geopolitical analyst and outspoken critic of the Netanyahu administration, expressed a similar view – saying that while Tuesday’s air strikes had increased the odds of an inadvertent confrontation with Turkey, “I don’t think that Israel wants a full-out war right now”.

He saw Netanyahu’s decision to escalate tensions partly as a political manoeuvre meant to rally right-wing support ahead of October’s general election.

“The typical use of security is to frighten voters into voting for the right,” said Ben-Ephraim, who is a senior analyst with strategic advisory firm Atlas Global Strategies.

Still, he warned of a “genuine risk” that miscalculation could trigger a wider confrontation, because “there are no clear borders for Turkish or Israeli influence in Syria and for Turkey this seems to be a primary interest”.

Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of the Washington-based risk consultancy Gulf State Analytics, said tensions between Turkey and Israel had been rising for years, “particularly since Ankara began filling a major vacuum in Syria” after Assad’s ousting in late 2024.

The latest strikes, within 45 miles (72km) of the Turkish border, “constitute a troubling development” because they showed that Israel “does not want to see Syria, under any leadership, rebuild itself militarily”, he said.

Such a scenario risked undermining Israel’s “vision for total dominance over the region”, Cafiero added, pushing the Netanyahu government to do “anything within its means to prevent any actor in the neighbourhood from challenging Israeli hegemony”.

So far, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has responded with relative restraint, rejecting Netanyahu’s claims of a military build-up as “untenable” on Wednesday, saying they “stem from Netanyahu’s intent to pursue expansionist and destabilising policies in the region ahead of the elections in Israel”.

But with Netanyahu’s leading rivals sharing his concerns about Turkey, analysts doubt a change of Israeli leadership would soften Israel’s approach towards Ankara.

“Most importantly”, the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) were “hard-wired to solve every problem with military force and there is no counter, no diplomatic approach, to rein them in”, Ben-Ephraim said.

The Israeli foreign ministry had long ceased to counterbalance the IDF in any meaningful way and the concept of deterrence had “completely given way to pre-emption”, he said.

Ben-Ephraim expects “a long, tense confrontation between Turkey and Israel as Turkish ambitions increase while US power wanes” in the Middle East, Israel “grows more isolated” and Iran rebuilds.

Boms, by contrast hopes “a real change” in the Israeli government could “open a new slate” for different relationships across the region, Turkey included.

“But it takes two to tango and it does not seem that Erdogan is in a dancing mood,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Has Philippines’ Marcos missed his chance to stop the Dutertes?
item.description:
Less than two years before the Philippines chooses its next president, Ferdinand Marcos Jnr still has no candidate to carry his banner.

Sara Duterte-Carpio, his estranged vice-president and fiercest political rival, has already declared her intention to run and remains the early front runner, despite an impeachment trial that could bar her from politics.

Marcos said on August 14 that he would “certainly endorse a candidate” in 2028 but added: “Who that is I cannot tell you because even I don’t know.”
item.content:encoded:
Less than two years before the Philippines chooses its next president, Ferdinand Marcos Jnr still has no candidate to carry his banner.

Sara Duterte-Carpio, his estranged vice-president and fiercest political rival, has already declared her intention to run and remains the early front runner, despite an impeachment trial that could bar her from politics.

Marcos said on August 14 that he would “certainly endorse a candidate” in 2028 but added: “Who that is I cannot tell you because even I don’t know.”

The one candidate he almost certainly will not support is Duterte-Carpio, daughter of former president Rodrigo Duterte. Their 2022 alliance helped unite two of the Philippines’ most powerful political dynasties before collapsing into open war.

By launching her 2028 presidential bid earlier this year, the vice-president set up a succession battle that could decide not only who controls the Malacanang presidential palace after Marcos’ single, constitutionally limited six-year term, but also whether the country swings back towards Duterte-style strongman politics and a more China-friendly foreign policy.

On paper, Marcos’ former allies have rarely looked more vulnerable.

Rodrigo Duterte is in The Hague awaiting trial at the International Criminal Court on charges of crimes against humanity, while key allies of the family have been arrested on plunder charges.

At home, the Marcos administration has also allowed the machinery of government to move against Duterte-Carpio, who faces impeachment on allegations of corruption and betrayal of public trust.

A conviction on just one charge would be enough to remove her from office and bar her from future elections.

Yet Duterte-Carpio is still standing, and gaining ground. A June poll by WR Numero Uno showed her satisfaction rating rising to 55 per cent, from 33 per cent in March, while Marcos stood at 36 per cent.

Recent surveys by Pulse Asia Research Organisation, OCTA Research, WR Numero Research and Momentum Research have also shown her leading the early 2028 presidential field.

Analysts are now questioning whether Marcos moved too late to prevent the Dutertes from regrouping before the next election.

Ronnie Holmes, Pulse Asia president and a professor of political science and development studies at De La Salle University in Manila, called it “the central political puzzle” of Philippine politics.

Marcos had opportunities to contain the Dutertes earlier, Holmes said – including during the first impeachment initiative against Duterte-Carpio last year – but “chose accommodation over confrontation”.

“That decision may have allowed the Duterte camp time to regroup and rebuild its political base,” Holmes told This Week in Asia.

The rivalry is all the more combustible because Marcos and Duterte-Carpio rode to power together in 2022, uniting two dynasties with deep emotional claims on Philippine politics.

Marcos, the son and namesake of the late dictator ousted in the 1986 People Power Revolution, returned his family to Malacanang.

Duterte-Carpio brought with her the political machine her father built first in Davao City and then nationally as president, a machine powered by Mindanao’s resentment towards Manila, anti-elite politics and the strongman image Duterte cultivated through his deadly war on drugs.

Their alliance collapsed into a fight neither side has yet been able to finish.

The Marcos administration’s main weapon is the ongoing Senate impeachment trial, in which prosecutors are seeking to prove allegations of corruption, unexplained wealth and betrayal of public trust.

Senior officials in the executive branch have testified in support of the case, including allegations that Duterte-Carpio plotted to assassinate the president.

On August 11, the justice department filed a “grave threats” charge against the vice-president over a 2024 video in which she claimed to have hired an assassin to kill Marcos, his wife and his cousin.

Duterte-Carpio has denied any wrongdoing and says the cases against her are politically motivated.

The Duterte camp’s counter-attacks have produced weaker results. Supporters tried to evoke the spirit of 1986 by gathering at the EDSA Shrine in Quezon City in November 2024 and calling for Marcos’ resignation, but the protests failed to draw either mass public support or backing from the military.

Duterte endurance

The failed protests did not end the feud, they merely brought home the stalemate. Marcos has wounded the Dutertes but not yet neutralised them, lending weight to their supporters’ taunts that the president is “weak”.

Dr Jean Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines, said Marcos’ strategy had produced “hits and misses”, which had made that perception seem “warranted”.

Holmes said Marcos was “only recently” doing enough to prevent a Duterte comeback – “and arguably too late”.

Part of the problem, analysts say, is that the Duterte brand has proved sturdier than the legal cases against the family.

“Their enduring strength lies in the image projected by the former president, a brand that is purportedly anti-elite and decisive,” Holmes said.

Vic Rodriguez, a Duterte ally, put it down to “the Duterte charisma”. He credited Duterte-Carpio with an ability to “effortlessly connects especially with the masses. Without a doubt her father’s daughter”.

“Marcos relies on brute force, Dutertes [rely] on near-cultic popularity”, Rodriguez said.

Rodrigo Duterte was the first Philippine president to come from Mindanao, a southern region long resentful of what many there see as the dominance of “imperial Manila”.

The family’s pride in being Mindanaoan “makes many people in Luzon uncomfortable”, Rodriguez said.

Holmes agreed, saying: “Their brand as political actors from the periphery resonates, particularly in Central Visayas [Region] and Mindanao, which together account for roughly a third of the electorate.”

Franco said the Dutertes had tapped into the “imperialist Manila discourse” while also reviving the appeal of strongman rule.

“The father was able to surface the strongman appeal that Filipinos think is the answer to the perception that Filipinos need to be disciplined to improve law and order,” she said.

The family still has a large core of self-styled “Duterte Diehard Supporters”, or DDS, a badge of loyalty that has survived years of criticism over the drug war.

For many supporters, the Dutertes’ coarse language and threats are not liabilities but proof of toughness.

Dr Nuelle Duterte, a cousin of Duterte-Carpio and niece of Rodrigo, put it plainly: “Their brutality appeals to people. Matapang sila [they’re fierce], vs Marcos, who is weak.”

Racing towards 2028

That contrast could matter even more as the 2028 race approaches. Analysts say a victory for Duterte-Carpio could alter both the Philippines’ foreign policy and its style of governance.

Her father sought closer ties with Beijing during his presidency, playing down the South China Sea dispute and cooling security ties with Washington – an approach Marcos has largely reversed.

A Duterte-Carpio win could therefore trigger “a significant foreign-policy recalibration towards China” and raise concerns about “institutional accountability” and democratic governance, Holmes said.

Rodriguez rejected this view, however. “Nothing is farther from the truth. It is classic Marcos disinformation that is unfounded,” he said. “A Sara Duterte [presidency] will be similar to her Davao legacy of professionalism, efficiency and the Duterte brand of peace and order.”

For now, the race is still up for grabs. A survey released last week by Momentum Research showed Duterte-Carpio leading the list of possible presidential candidates, picked by 44.2 per cent of respondents.

Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo, who ran for president in 2022 and has said she is not interested in running again, came second with 23.8 per cent.

One option Marcos may still consider is persuading Robredo to run after all, paired with Senator Raffy Tulfo as her running mate.

Two surveys, by Octa Research in July and Tangere in May, suggested that hypothetical ticket could beat a Duterte-Carpio pairing with Senator Imee Marcos.

Val Villanueva, a former election strategist and now a finance columnist and analyst for Rappler, said current research data pointed to the Robredo-Tulfo tandem as “probably the most electorally competitive pairing against Sara Duterte”.

item.title: [SCMP] India joins China and South Korea in push for Arctic shipping routes
item.description:
Climate change and conflict are conspiring to open up the Arctic to Asian commercial shipping, with China, South Korea and India all eyeing the icy short cut to Europe.

Last Saturday, Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launched the first scheduled weekly container service across the top of the world, marking the realisation of Beijing’s long-held ambition to build a “Polar Silk Road”.

It will not sail alone for long, however. This Sunday, South Korea’s PanStar Group plans to send its own pilot vessel from Busan through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) towards ports in the UK, the Netherlands and Poland.
item.content:encoded:
Climate change and conflict are conspiring to open up the Arctic to Asian commercial shipping, with China, South Korea and India all eyeing the icy short cut to Europe.

Last Saturday, Chinese shipping company Sea Legend launched the first scheduled weekly container service across the top of the world, marking the realisation of Beijing’s long-held ambition to build a “Polar Silk Road”.

It will not sail alone for long, however. This Sunday, South Korea’s PanStar Group plans to send its own pilot vessel from Busan through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) towards ports in the UK, the Netherlands and Poland.

India is also preparing to dispatch its first cargo ship along the same corridor next year.

“In 2027, we are planning to have the first pilot vessel running through the Northern Sea Route. We are seeing huge possibilities,” S. Venkatesapathy, a joint secretary in India’s shipping ministry, reportedly told the Arctic-Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk, Russia, on August 13.

Two crises are pushing Asian shippers north. The first is climate change: warming sea temperatures mean that the Arctic ice pack is no longer impassable in summer, opening a navigable window running roughly from July to October.

The second is geopolitics. Threats to shipping in the Red Sea, layered atop the near-total closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, have forced many shippers to divert around southern Africa, adding mounting costs and up to two weeks to journeys that once ran through the Suez Canal without incident.

The NSR promises to slash transit times between Asia and northern Europe by roughly two weeks compared to the Suez run, shortening shipping distances by up to 40 per cent.

Sea Legend says it can make the journey from Ningbo, China, to Felixstowe in the UK in around 20 days vs about 40 days via Suez.

“The NSR and the related Northeast Passage have great potential to connect Asia and Europe faster and more easily, and this potential is gradually starting to be realised,” said Ivan Lidarev, an Asian security expert at the Institute of South Asian Studies in Singapore.

“Significantly, it will also help transit more Russian energy resources to Asia.”

A route European explorers searched for and failed to conquer from the 1500s onwards is now the subject of serious commercial planning.

More than a short cut

For China, whose two-way goods trade with Europe reached €759 billion (US$887 billion) last year, according to European Union statistics, the advantages are obvious.

“China will be the main beneficiary,” Lidarev said. “The route will greatly facilitate its trade with Europe, a crucial trading partner amid tensions with Washington, and avoid US-controlled sea lanes and chokepoints.”

India’s interest in the NSR was as much about signalling as logistics, according to Cedomir Nestorovic, a geopolitics professor at ESSEC Business School who said using the route would advertise New Delhi’s “strategic autonomy” to Washington while also opening up a new channel to access Russian oil, gas and minerals.

Not only could the route shave weeks off India’s shipping times to Europe, Lidarev said it also offered Delhi leverage in talks on a long-awaited free-trade agreement with the United States.

Equally important was the enhanced connectivity to Russia’s far east that using the NSR could offer, said Uday Chandra, a political-science professor at India’s Ashoka University, pointing to Delhi’s parallel push to increase links between Vladivostok and Indian port cities such as Chennai, Visakhapatnam and Paradip.

China’s head start dated back to 2013, Chandra noted, when the first commercial transit of an Arctic shipping route by a Chinese merchant ship took place, five years before Beijing formalised its Polar Silk Road ambitions in a 2018 policy paper.

South Korea, meanwhile, plans to use Sunday’s trial voyage to test the commercial viability of the NSR, with its vice-minister of oceans and fisheries Nam Jae-hon recently proclaiming that the Arctic passage was “bound to become an alternative to Middle Eastern routes”.

The government-funded Korea Institute for Economic Policy think tank has estimated that travelling through the Arctic could cut journey times to Europe by about 10 days, shaving some 7,000km off the distance travelled.

In addition to South Korea, Lidarev said Japan had also shown an interest in the route, with Southeast Asian states such as Singapore set to follow, should the geopolitics align.

“Over the long term, if climate trends further extend the navigable window, East Asian economies will inevitably utilise the corridor to optimise seasonal trade,” Nestorovic said.

No Hormuz replacement

Despite the growing interest, traffic through the NSR remains modest. Last year, Norwegian non-profit research foundation the Centre for High North Logistics tracked 88 vessels making 103 transits, up from 97 in 2024 and just 43 in 2022.

Tanker shipments carrying Russian crude oil and petroleum products accounted for the bulk of the traffic last year, according to an analysis by the Eurasian Rail Alliance Index, alongside dry bulk carriers likely transporting coal eastward.

The route has its limits, however, offering no relief for energy flows restricted by chokepoints in the Middle East, which historically accounts for roughly half of China and India’s oil imports.

“The NSR cannot replace the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca for Asia’s energy security,” Nestorovic said.

“The Arctic route connects northern Europe and Russian energy fields to East Asia, but it is geographically irrelevant for Middle Eastern energy flows.”

The NSR cannot replace the Strait of Hormuz or the Strait of Malacca for Asia’s energy security

Cedomir Nestorovic, geopolitics professor

Then there are the practical challenges. Navigable without icebreaker support for only three to four months a year, the NSR is also unpredictable due to the shifting Arctic ice floes and shallow waters that prevent the passage of mega-ships, according to Nestorovic.

Add to that sparse search-and-rescue coverage, steep insurance costs and environmental rules limiting commercial scale, and he said the route should be considered a supplementary seasonal corridor rather than a wholesale replacement for existing maritime arteries.

Environmental groups see other trade-offs. The non-profit Clean Arctic Alliance and Norwegian Bellona Foundation NGO have warned that the soot emitted by ships’ exhausts settles on Arctic snow and ice, increasing heat absorption and speeding up the melting of polar ice caps that opened up the route in the first place, exacerbating the effects of climate change.

Those trade-offs do not appear to be slowing Asia down, however, and a sea passage explorers gave up on centuries ago is now, for a brief window each summer, open for business.

Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

item.title: [SCMP] China banned ivory, but Vietnamese gangs keep the trade alive
item.description:
Three months after leaving an inland port far up the Congo River, a consignment of timber arrived in Vietnam this summer concealing a secret it would take customs officials three weeks to uncover: nearly 1.2 tonnes of elephant ivory, smuggled halfway across the world.

Tracking data reviewed by This Week in Asia shows the shipment travelled some 9,000 nautical miles (16,700km) – with stops in Sri Lanka and Singapore – before reaching Quy Nhon, a port on Vietnam’s central coast.

Custom officers were tipped off to the contraband, sealed inside hidden compartments with wax, by port scanners that flagged hollow cavities in the timber.
item.content:encoded:
Three months after leaving an inland port far up the Congo River, a consignment of timber arrived in Vietnam this summer concealing a secret it would take customs officials three weeks to uncover: nearly 1.2 tonnes of elephant ivory, smuggled halfway across the world.

Tracking data reviewed by This Week in Asia shows the shipment travelled some 9,000 nautical miles (16,700km) – with stops in Sri Lanka and Singapore – before reaching Quy Nhon, a port on Vietnam’s central coast.

Custom officers were tipped off to the contraband, sealed inside hidden compartments with wax, by port scanners that flagged hollow cavities in the timber.

On August 6, they drilled into the hollowed-out logs and found 221 pieces of sawn tusk, most likely destined for China and potentially worth millions of US dollars.

Port authorities called it the largest seizure on record for Quy Nhon, yet it was far from the first time smuggled ivory was uncovered at a Vietnamese port.

Between 2009 and 2018 alone, some 56 tonnes of ivory were seized in Vietnam, according to international NGO the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), with a further 20 tonnes linked to the country seized elsewhere.

CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, bans the trade in elephant ivory, requiring permits for the sale and transport of old artefacts.

After decades of being decimated by poaching, some of Africa’s elephant populations are now stabilising, largely thanks to China’s ban on elephant ivory sales. Imposed at the end of 2017, the ban slashed demand in what was the world’s largest market.

China’s domestic ivory ban, which leaves a loophole for people to keep possession of registered tusks highly prized in ornate carvings, followed its ban on the domestic rhino horn trade in 1993.

Prices for both ivory and rhino horn have tumbled since, and Africa’s elephants, decimated by poaching that cut numbers from around 1.3 million in 1979 to roughly 415,000 by 2015, have begun a tentative recovery, with conservationists now putting the total population at 450,000-490,000.

Compared to a decade ago, when “we had industrial-scale poaching and smuggling, we have made significant inroads”, said John Scanlon, CEO of the Elephant Protection Initiative, a pan-African alliance aimed at ending the ivory trade.

He credits a coordinated push by source, transit and destination countries, and praises China for crushing ivory stockpiles rather than merely banning their sale. But he is careful not to declare victory yet.

“That doesn’t mean to say [poaching] has stopped, or it cannot, in some unpredictable way increase again,” he told This Week in Asia. “You can’t rest on your laurels.”

The Hydra network

Demand for ivory has fallen in China since the ban, but black-market smugglers still carry out their illegal trade through Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, where the newly wealthy prize elephant tusks as a marker of status.

Vietnamese syndicates now sit among the main players in a trade estimated to be worth hundreds of millions of US dollars a year.

In 2023, Nigerian courts jailed three Vietnamese nationals – Phan Viet Chi, Phan Hong Quan and Duong Van Thang – for six years apiece after convicting them of running the African end of a smuggling network nicknamed “Hydra”.

Hydra was not new to law enforcement. Five years earlier, Thai police had already moved against the Bach brothers, dual Vietnamese-Thai nationals linked to the network, arresting a suspected kingpin and even a wildlife-crime inspector at a Bangkok airport.

One of the brothers, Boonchai Bach, was detained in 2018 for allegedly smuggling 14 rhino horns worth around US$1 million from Africa to Thailand, but the case against him collapsed after a witness recanted.

An NGO later lamented that “one of the biggest wildlife crooks ever caught in history” had been let go. The Thai Supreme Court did sentence Bach to five years in prison in 2022, but he remains a fugitive.

At the market’s peak, a kilogram of rhino horn fetched around US$60,000 to US$65,000 – more than the price of cocaine and roughly on par with gold.

Impunity, still

This month’s seizure in Quy Nhon showed that “many of the other faces behind it [the ivory trade] still operate with impunity”, said Linh Nguyen, a senior wildlife campaigner with the EIA.

“Vietnamese and Chinese-led networks are still working across Africa and there is a sense that they are moving between southern Africa to Kenya, Tanzania and west,” she said, following the herds – and gaps in enforcement – wherever they lead.

Vietnam has made strides to shake off its unwanted reputation as a smuggling hub. Sentences for wildlife crime now run as high as 15 years behind bars and the EIA reports that both arrest and imprisonment rates have climbed.

“Vietnam has made a lot of efforts, but it can’t solve this problem alone,” Linh said, citing the circuitous route smugglers take as evidence of a global supply chain. “The government needs to engage with countries throughout the chain.”

The pressure has not let up elsewhere in the region, either. On August 16, authorities in Laos’ Bolikhamsai province, bordering Vietnam, seized 1.75 tonnes of tusks tied to a trafficking network and arrested 11 foreign nationals, the Laotian Times reported. Their nationalities were not disclosed.

CSI Savannah

Scientific advances have made it harder for wildlife traffickers to prosper. Forensic testing and DNA analysis can now trace a seized tusk back to the region that it came from, while intelligence sharing between customs agencies helps investigators zero-in on the syndicates working specific ports or smuggling corridors.

Interpol, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and a clutch of investigative NGOs now stand ready to assist almost any customs post in the world.

The Elephant Trade Information System, a global seizure database maintained by the WWF’s animal-trade monitoring arm Traffic, shows that more than 12 tonnes of ivory were seized in Vietnam at the trade’s peak in 2018.

“We can now find out very easily from forensic samples whether seized ivory comes from recent poaching, long-standing stockpiles or natural mortality of an elephant,’’ Scanlon said.

But conservationists know they face a formidable adversary, with deep pockets.

“A lot of this larger-scale smuggling is facilitated by corruption … transnational and organised by corrupting officials across boundaries,” Scanlon said.

In the illicit ivory trade, money still opens borders just as effortlessly as it unlocks commercial markets.

“Vigilance is key,” Scanlon added. “We don’t want to see this illegal market explode again.’’

item.title: [SCMP] China’s drone production capacity can only meet 60% of war demand: study
item.description:
Even when fully mobilised, China’s industrial system would only be able to meet 60 per cent of the country’s military demand for drones in a conflict, according to a rare study looking into the expected effects of a sudden war.

The estimates were produced by an artificial intelligence model that covered a multilevel supply chain linking drone assembly plants with subsystem and component suppliers. The study also accounted for inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets and civilian factory conversion.

The paper was published online in the Journal of System Simulation on July 24. It was led by Professor Zhang Jihai, director of the National Defence Mobilisation Research Centre, and his team from the Beijing Institute of Technology.
item.content:encoded:
Even when fully mobilised, China’s industrial system would only be able to meet 60 per cent of the country’s military demand for drones in a conflict, according to a rare study looking into the expected effects of a sudden war.

The estimates were produced by an artificial intelligence model that covered a multilevel supply chain linking drone assembly plants with subsystem and component suppliers. The study also accounted for inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets and civilian factory conversion.

The paper was published online in the Journal of System Simulation on July 24. It was led by Professor Zhang Jihai, director of the National Defence Mobilisation Research Centre, and his team from the Beijing Institute of Technology.

The university has a strong military research background and is among the few Chinese universities subject to US sanctions.

“Modern warfare competition is no longer merely about the performance of weapon systems, but more fundamentally about industrial capacity – especially the comprehensive capability of production mobilisation for military equipment,” the researchers wrote.

The study found that capacity expansion could not quickly close the gap because new production lines took time to build.

Recent conflicts have shown how quickly modern wars can consume precision weapons, with Reuters reporting on August 4 that the US Army had used “virtually all” of its army tactical missile systems and precision strike missiles during its five-month war with Iran.

The war in Ukraine gives an even clearer example for drones, with a Pentagon official saying on July 27 that Ukraine was expected to produce 6 million to 7 million small first-person view attack drones in 2026 – about 500,000 a month – while US production remained a fraction of that level.

“Under high-intensity demand shocks, the supply chain, although possessing certain mobilisation and recovery capabilities, still faces a significant supply-demand gap,” the researchers wrote.

But the simulation also raises a bigger question about the scale of mobilisation, as the result would look very different if a major war brought companies that did not normally produce military equipment into the defence supply chain.

“Modern warfare, like wars in the past, is ultimately about supply chains,” said a Chinese weapons and equipment expert, who declined to give his name because of the sensitive nature of his work.

He warned that the ability to rapidly expand production could matter as much as the weapons already available. The expert holds a doctorate in weapons and equipment engineering and works in a field involving classified facilities.

“The rapid production capability can fully meet the demand, but the supply of core components is not that simple,” he said.

What would happen in China during a period of war would likely be similar to what happened “during the Three Major Campaigns”, the weapons specialist said.

The rapid production capability can fully meet the demand, but the supply of core components is not that simple

Chinese weapons specialist

He was referring to the three decisive strategic battles between the People’s Liberation Army and Kuomintang forces during the Chinese civil war. “It is a classic example [when] ordinary people were all mobilised to supply materials,” he said.

Such mobilisation could produce a very different outcome from a model that counted only existing military and civilian weapons manufacturers, according to the expert.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, for example, Chinese companies outside the medical sector rapidly switched production to masks and other protective equipment when demand surged.

In a major war, manufacturers that do not normally produce weapons could similarly become part of the military supply chain. These could include companies producing electronics, batteries, vehicles, machinery and consumer technology.

The distinction matters because a factory that does not make drones today may still have machinery, electronics expertise, battery technology, supply networks or manufacturing capacity that could be adapted for military production.

Zhang’s simulation therefore describes only one version of wartime capacity. A nationwide industrial mobilisation involving large civilian manufacturers could produce a very different result.

China already dominates large parts of the global drone supply chain and holds a huge share of the consumer drone market. Chinese-made consumer drones account for roughly 90 per cent of the US consumer market.

But industrial dominance in peacetime does not necessarily mean that production can be rapidly converted into military output during a major war.

The study used an unmanned aerial vehicle supply chain to simulate a sudden wartime surge in demand. The model linked military demand with a multilevel supply chain covering equipment and component suppliers, subsystems and a final assembly plant.

It also included inventories, production capacity, order backlogs, budgets, production safety and the ability of civilian manufacturers to switch to military production.

Civilian factories could not be converted instantly because of limits on capacity, technical adaptation and conversion efficiency.

“Capacity expansion and conversion are not activated continuously, but rather exhibit phased triggering and discontinuous implementation,” the researchers wrote.

In one simulation, demand rose to three times its normal level after the war began.

The system responded by releasing inventories, increasing overtime production, building new production lines and converting civilian capacity. Yet cumulative wartime order fulfilment reached only 63.4 per cent.

The unnamed expert said the study should therefore be treated mainly as an “argumentative study” rather than a prediction of what would happen in an actual war.

Zhang’s team compared no mobilisation, rule-based mobilisation and an AI-based strategy across 30 simulations. Median wartime order fulfilment rates were about 34 per cent, 51 per cent and 58 per cent respectively.

The AI strategy’s average fulfilment rate was 8.4 per cent higher than the rule-based approach. It was also 24.3 per cent higher than no mobilisation.

“The large language model-based [AI] mobilisation strategy achieves superior delivery performance and a higher wartime order fulfilment rate compared with no-mobilisation and rule-based mobilisation strategies,” the researchers wrote.

The AI model assessed inventory, production capacity, order pressure and budgets before selecting suppliers for expansion and civilian firms for conversion.

The model also found that increasing available mobilisation funding from 60 per cent to 140 per cent of the baseline raised wartime order fulfilment from 54.9 per cent to 62.3 per cent. Further spending produced smaller gains.

Factory construction times, conversion capacity and other physical constraints limited how quickly additional funding could create usable production capacity.

“There is a clear trade-off constraint between equipment supply assurance and production safety,” the researchers wrote.

item.title: [SCMP] Licence to savour: Hong Kong craft brewers push for on-site beer permits
item.description:
When a 100-strong South Korean tour group approached a Hong Kong craft beer manufacturer for a tour and tasting session, the operator declined their request.

The refusal was not down to a lack of confidence in the product or a staff shortage. It was regulatory: the brewery simply lacked a licence to serve its beer on the premises.

“It is not easy doing manufacturing in Hong Kong,” said Luke Yardley, founder of local craft beer brewery Yardley Brothers.
item.content:encoded:
When a 100-strong South Korean tour group approached a Hong Kong craft beer manufacturer for a tour and tasting session, the operator declined their request.

The refusal was not down to a lack of confidence in the product or a staff shortage. It was regulatory: the brewery simply lacked a licence to serve its beer on the premises.

“It is not easy doing manufacturing in Hong Kong,” said Luke Yardley, founder of local craft beer brewery Yardley Brothers.

“It is just a missed opportunity when in every other country – if you are in London, New York, Dublin – customers can go for a day out and visit the brewery. They get to have a nice experience where they can consume alcohol on site. And the key thing is they can buy alcohol on site,” he added.

Yardley is not alone. Many of Hong Kong’s craft beer manufacturers operate in industrial buildings under food factory licences to house their giant equipment and save costs, which makes applying for liquor licences difficult.

The situation has prompted calls for a review of the licensing regime governed by the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) to allow them to offer some samples for customers to taste on-site, which industry leaders and a lawmaker have said may help drive the city’s tourism economy.

Hong Kong has around 15 home-grown craft breweries producing more than 30 distinct local beer brands, with some being exported for international consumption.

In Hong Kong, catering operators have to obtain liquor licences from the Liquor Licensing Board to serve alcohol, which are usually granted to licensed restaurants and clubhouses with compliance certificates issued by the home affairs minister.

For premises without such documentation, their applications for liquor licences have to undergo extra scrutiny from other government arms, including the Planning Department, Fire Services Department and buildings authorities, leading to lengthier approval times.

Yardley has been running his brewery for 10 years, and the factory in Kwai Chung now produces around 15,000 litres of beer per month.

He said Hong Kong was home to a few top beer makers in Asia, but the regulatory hurdles made it difficult for producers to promote themselves “confidently”.

He called for a review on the current licensing regime, and urged authorities to explore the feasibility of introducing a dedicated liquor licence for breweries, allowing them to offer tasting samples to visitors, which he said might also attract more tourists to Hong Kong.

“A concern [could be] having it out of control where you have nightclubs in industrial buildings and that is not what we are proposing,” he said.

Also expressing similar frustration was Christopher Wong See-wai, head brewer and a co-founder of Heroes Beer in Yau Tong, who said it was a pity that all household beer brands in Hong Kong come from overseas.

“The reason why microbreweries in other countries could win support from their neighbourhood community, expanding their influence to a broader area, was through residents’ visits to learn what they were doing,” said Wong, who is also the co-founder of a few other local breweries.

“The biggest problem in Hong Kong is that people do not even know we exist.”

For a niche brand such as Heroes, which specialises in “experimental beer” and produces around 40,000 litres of beer per year, building a reputation to rival established names like Blue Girl, San Miguel and Carlsberg is difficult without local community engagement, according to Wong.

“There are many luxury homes in Yau Tong. If I have a licence, people can come to my brewery, sit down, have a cup of beer after work, and join a tour to learn more about us,” he said.

Also a restaurant operator himself, Wong said many breweries were able to meet the conditions for obtaining liquor licences. He questioned the government’s reluctance to expand the licensing regime to them, when there were already many retail and even gym operators in industrial buildings.

Lawmaker Adrian Pedro Ho King-hong said breweries in Hong Kong were facing “massive challenges” in running tasting tours because of the licensing regime as well as land-use restrictions.

He agreed that authorities should explore introducing a dedicated “taproom licence” with certain restrictive conditions such as their size and capacity to avoid turning factories into entertainment venues, under which licensees could lead visitors to tour the production premises and distribute small samples.

“Introducing a taproom licence regime can on the one hand enhance the international publicity of Hong Kong brands, and on the other hand, it is good for the tourism industry as many visitors would like to tour our local breweries,” he said.

During a recent public consultation session for Hong Kong’s first home-grown five-year plan, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu acknowledged that the city needed globally recognised local brands and pledged to provide policy support.

Ho said he would meet authorities to discuss the matter after collecting information and opinions from the industry, but cautioned that progress required cross-departmental collaboration.

Even if the FEHD approved serving alcohol on-site at breweries, there could be further restrictions on land use stipulated by authorities and the Deeds of Mutual Covenant governed by the buildings’ incorporated owners, he added.

“It takes time and I think we need a starting point in promoting industrial building revitalisation,” he said.

In response to the South China Morning Post’s inquiry, the FEHD stressed that operations of commercial or retail activities in industrial buildings should also comply with other statutory requirements, such as zoning plans, government lease conditions and building and fire safety legislation.

“The FEHD will continue to work closely with relevant policy bureaus and departments to examine feasible options that support local food trade while upholding regulatory standards and community interests,” it said.

The Development Bureau said catering services were permissible in wholesale converted industrial buildings under its revitalisation scheme.

It added that it was reviewing the scheme and would explore the possibility of widening non-industrial uses in non-wholesale converted industrial buildings, taking into account emerging market needs and interdepartmental feedback.

item.title: [SCMP] Why China’s reusable rocket breakthrough matters for the PLA’s ‘kill chain’
item.description:
A pair of landmark rocket recoveries in recent weeks has brought China a step closer to mastering reusable launch technology – a breakthrough analysts said could give the People’s Liberation Army an advantage in combat by increasing the resilience of its satellite-supported “kill chain”, the process of identifying, tracking and engaging a target.

In a first for China, commercial rocket company LandSpace recovered a stainless-steel booster using deployable legs after an orbital flight earlier this week. This followed a successful launch last month by state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which achieved the world’s first recovery of an orbital-class booster at sea using a net-capture system.

Defence experts said the technology would dramatically lower the cost of putting satellites into space and increase the frequency of launches. Mastering reusability will improve the PLA’s space capabilities – including communication, navigation and surveillance – much like how SpaceX supports the US military.
item.content:encoded:
A pair of landmark rocket recoveries in recent weeks has brought China a step closer to mastering reusable launch technology – a breakthrough analysts said could give the People’s Liberation Army an advantage in combat by increasing the resilience of its satellite-supported “kill chain”, the process of identifying, tracking and engaging a target.

In a first for China, commercial rocket company LandSpace recovered a stainless-steel booster using deployable legs after an orbital flight earlier this week. This followed a successful launch last month by state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), which achieved the world’s first recovery of an orbital-class booster at sea using a net-capture system.

Defence experts said the technology would dramatically lower the cost of putting satellites into space and increase the frequency of launches. Mastering reusability will improve the PLA’s space capabilities – including communication, navigation and surveillance – much like how SpaceX supports the US military.

Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst with the Canberra-based Australian Strategic Policy Institute’s defence strategy programme, said space was the most crucial operational domain in modern warfare.

He said modern militaries relied heavily on space for everything from communications and battlespace awareness to positioning, navigation and timing using systems such as GPS.

Without those abilities, militaries could be left “effectively deaf, dumb and blind”, severely degrading their ability to communicate, understand what is happening on the battlefield and conduct operations, Davis added.

SpaceX has become a core enabler of US military space power. It provides rockets and relatively low-cost access to orbit to deploy and replenish large military satellite constellations through US Space Force projects, such as the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture.

LandSpace and CASC have yet to demonstrate the ability to reuse the recovered first-stage booster, but experts said reusability itself was the bottleneck.

Timothy Heath, director of the Virginia-based research firm Perceptum, said the principal advantage for the People’s Liberation Army would be the ability to replace or increase space capabilities during a conflict.

“In a conflict, the reusable rocket launch capability would allow the PLA to quickly recover from losses of space platforms or to expand space capabilities quickly,” he said.

“This could enable the PLA to maintain situational awareness, navigation and communications even as it loses satellites to adversary attacks.”

Namrata Goswami, a professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies, said these reusable launch systems would become part of an integrated national infrastructure supporting commercial mega-constellations, military satellites, logistics and ultimately greater freedom of action in space.

She said reusable rockets, combined with replacement satellites and rapid launch operations, would be particularly important in a Taiwan contingency because the PLA increasingly relied on satellites for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) as well as communications, BeiDou navigation and targeting across the Indo-Pacific.

“China is moving towards near-real time situational awareness that can support the tracking and targeting of mobile US and allied forces,” Goswami said.

“If damaged ISR or communications nodes can be replenished rapidly by China, disrupting the space layer may produce only temporary degradation rather than breaking the kill chain.”

Lieutenant General Douglas Schiess, the incoming US chief of space operations, said during his July nomination hearing that “the threat China poses is real”. He urged the US Space Force to strengthen its ability in the region to counter threats such as the PLA’s rapidly expanding space operations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific.

“They are using their intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance efforts to target our forces much farther than they ever have in the past. They’ve built a kill chain to be able to see our carrier strike groups, our bombers at much farther pace, speed and distances,” Schiess said.

In July 2023, China deployed swarms of satellites to monitor the Talisman Sabre joint military exercise between the US, Australia and other partners, ABC News reported at the time.

According to the Australian news service, 300 Chinese satellites conducted more than 3,000 overflights to survey ground-based activities.

China in 2024 established the PLA Aerospace Force, placing it directly under the Central Military Commission.

“I think the US will probably recognise that they have to live with the fact that the Chinese will be able to put satellites into orbit very quickly in the same way the Americans can,” Davis said.

“And I think that where the contest happens is not so much on Earth in terms of the US destroying Chinese launch systems or China destroying US launch systems. The contest happens in space where you have to fight in space on orbit.”

Space has become a key area of US-China competition. While China is still a few years behind the US, which has now moved to tackle full reusability with the Starship programme, experts said LandSpace’s achievements would help narrow the gap and erode the American advantage in space.

“Dropping the cost to launch will open up China’s space sector and encourage a lot of innovation and new space technologies that could have benefits for its national security,” said Victoria Samson, chief director of the space security and stability programme at the Washington-based Secure World Foundation.

“This might allow China to catch up to the United States in terms of space launch.”

Analysts said that the ability to produce satellites was also critical. Goswami said reusable rockets could become consequential when combined with China’s development of mass-produced satellites and large constellations.

As of April, China had 55 satellite manufacturing facilities with a combined annual production capacity expected to reach 7,360 satellites by 2030, according to Beijing-based research firm Hello Space.

SpaceX said in a regulatory filing earlier this year that it was able to produce an average of about 70 Starlink satellites per week between December and April, equivalent to roughly 3,640 satellites a year.

“We have seen Ukraine’s ability to use SpaceX’s Starlink satellites to fight Russia has become an important source of advantage. If China can launch many military satellites quickly and cheaply, this could provide a critical edge in battle,” Heath said.

item.title: [SCMP] The Mistral paradox: Europe’s push for tech sovereignty relies on China’s Z.ai
item.description:
On August 11, a tiny line buried in a lengthy press release from French company Mistral AI spoke volumes about the strategic and technological dilemmas facing the European Union, as the bloc prepares to navigate an autumn period full of geopolitical and trade upheaval.

In a bid to roll out “European infrastructure for sovereign AI”, Mistral – Europe’s great hope in the global artificial intelligence race – said it would begin offering other companies’ models, while keeping the service itself under European control.

Mistral’s model of choice is GLM-5.2, an open-weight large language model developed by Zhipu, also known as Z.ai, one of China’s six “AI tiger” companies, included since 2025 on the US’ entity list because of national security concerns regarding military modernisation.
item.content:encoded:
On August 11, a tiny line buried in a lengthy press release from French company Mistral AI spoke volumes about the strategic and technological dilemmas facing the European Union, as the bloc prepares to navigate an autumn period full of geopolitical and trade upheaval.

In a bid to roll out “European infrastructure for sovereign AI”, Mistral – Europe’s great hope in the global artificial intelligence race – said it would begin offering other companies’ models, while keeping the service itself under European control.

Mistral’s model of choice is GLM-5.2, an open-weight large language model developed by Zhipu, also known as Z.ai, one of China’s six “AI tiger” companies, included since 2025 on the US’ entity list because of national security concerns regarding military modernisation.

The decision to plug a Chinese AI brain into what would effectively be a European shell has raised eyebrows given the shoddy state of EU-China relations, but on practical terms it makes some sense.

Despite a deluge of political chatter about creating a sovereign European AI offering, the bloc has lagged both the US and China in investment and innovation.

Geoeconomics expert Shahin Vallee from the German Council on Foreign Relations said that a pivot to “AI adoption rather than innovation” therefore represented “the right strategy for Mistral and for Europe”.

Europe “cannot compete or win on frontier models and raw computing power” and with US companies generally favouring closed models, “GLM-5.2 was simply the strongest option on the table”, he wrote in a note.

However, Mistral’s choice was also a demonstration of how Europe’s political and commercial incentives frequently pull the company in different directions.

While the EU is engaged in a bitter trade dispute with China and desperately trying to wind down its reliance on Beijing, European companies are finding themselves enticed by cheap and advanced Chinese technological offerings.

As well as Mistral, a series of European carmakers including Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Stellantis, have partnered with Chinese outfits to tap what is seen as their superior electric vehicle technology.

Mistral’s was “a geopolitical move with profound ramifications that the US demanding more ideological alignment from its allies is unlikely to reverse and might in fact accelerate”, Vallee wrote.

It is a dynamic that places Brussels more firmly in the crossfire of a US-China tech rivalry that has already taken some unexpected twists.

While Europe’s governments have shown willingness to follow American tech initiatives – the European Commission and several member states signed up for the US-led Pax Silica initiative in June – there is some suggestion that US policies are pushing its companies into Beijing’s arms.

“When I was in Brussels in June, I was surprised that the mood towards America was more negative than towards China,” said Joerg Wuttke, a Washington-based partner at consultancy Albright Stone Group.

“Because the Chinese are predictable, practical, and you can do stuff with them, and they stick to it normally,” said Wuttke, who spent decades as the top European business lobbyist in China.

“Turnberry and all that happened afterwards has basically eroded any trust in the US administration, it’s just never ending.”

On August 14, three days after Mistral’s announcement, Reuters reported that the US planned to force Pax Silica signatories towards exclusive technological alignment – a move that could eventually make European use of Chinese models politically difficult or incompatible with the initiative’s direction.

On the same day, Bloomberg reported that Washington had sent letters to Nato allies suggesting the deployment of US military assets would be predicated on how supportive they were of Trump’s foreign policies, including his war on Iran.

A day earlier, a White House report named the EU among a “tier 1” group of trading partners facilitating the “illegal transshipment” of Chinese goods to dodge US tariffs.

The week before, the European Central Bank was said to have been “blindsided” by Washington’s dramatic sale of euros to prop up the ailing Japanese yen.

“There’s a squeeze on Europe from various fronts to extract more wealth out of it,” said Davide Oneglia, a London-based macroeconomist at research firm TS Lombard. “Europe is seen as still rich enough to pay for stuff, while not strong enough to defend itself industrially, technologically or militarily.”

At the same time, Beijing has been aggressively pushing an alternative to the US model of closed, proprietary AI platforms, presenting its own models as open, global goods.

Kyle Chan, an expert in China’s industrial policy, wrote in his High Capacity newsletter that “China’s main message to the world is: ‘We’re Android, and the US is Apple’”.

“The US offers a closed system where power and profits flow back to Washington and American corporations. China offers an open system where everyone, including the Global South, can participate and benefit.”

The ultimate goal of China’s policies is to dilute American influence in frontier technologies globally, according to Chan.

“Beijing casts China as the open partner and the US as the hegemonic gatekeeper willing to restrict access to technology for its own national interest,” he said.

“That argument likely resonates because many countries already worry about over-dependence on American technology platforms, a concern sharpened by recent US restrictions.”

According to Vallee, the extra wrinkle of AI could have “profound ramifications” ahead of an autumn in which the EU-China trade dispute is expected to come to a head.

“To me the combination of US aggression and China’s openness is pushing Europe into tighter cooperation with China,” he said in an interview.

“My sense is that the opinion in Europe, rightly or wrongly, over the last few years has evolved towards considering that the risk with the US is a similar, if not greater to the risk from China.”

However, deepened corporate exposure on Chinese technology could undermine Brussels’ efforts to take Beijing to task on trade, Vallee said. “I find it hard to imagine that the EU actively engaged in the highest level of technology integration with China through AI will attempt a very hardball strategy on trade.”

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, an Asia-focused economist focused at the Brussels-based Bruegel think tank, warned that using Chinese models just because of US export controls could be a dangerous strategy for European firms. “The idea that they’re open weight doesn’t mean that they’re free.”

Eventually, companies will be commercially required to charge for these models if they are to survive, according to Garcia-Herrero. “This is an additional dependence,” she said. “We also shouldn’t go there because that would give China an additional leeway on us.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s wealthy used grey zones to avoid taxes. Have new rules painted them into a corner?
item.description:
For Sarah Wang, a Shanghai-based tax lawyer who specialises in structuring offshore trusts, most of her high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth clients have hit pause on their arrangements.

“Some clients were midway through establishing offshore trusts, but now they have put their plans on hold following the new regulatory developments,” she said. “Others weighing up similar structures are also shelving their plans for the time being.”

The “new developments” in question were rules unveiled by the Ministry of Finance on July 24, which for the first time set out clear provisions governing individual income tax levies on offshore trusts.
item.content:encoded:
For Sarah Wang, a Shanghai-based tax lawyer who specialises in structuring offshore trusts, most of her high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth clients have hit pause on their arrangements.

“Some clients were midway through establishing offshore trusts, but now they have put their plans on hold following the new regulatory developments,” she said. “Others weighing up similar structures are also shelving their plans for the time being.”

The “new developments” in question were rules unveiled by the Ministry of Finance on July 24, which for the first time set out clear provisions governing individual income tax levies on offshore trusts.

With China’s wealthiest individuals increasingly targeted in the country’s tax enforcement drive, tightening scrutiny of offshore trusts comes as another sign of Beijing’s long-term institutional resolve rather than a means of generating short-term liquidity.

“Mounting fiscal pressure makes it necessary for the central government to broaden the tax base,” said Ge Yuyu, a professor at the Shanghai National Accounting Institute. “Targeting HNW individuals also aligns with the country’s goal of common prosperity.”

The enactment of the new rules follows months of intensified tax enforcement actions, mainly targeting tax avoidance among the ultra-rich – including undeclared offshore revenue – as well as top online influencers.

For the wealthy, the new policy means that there is even less room for grey-zone tax avoidance. It imposes a uniform 20 per cent rate across every stage of a trust’s life cycle: the transfer of assets into the trust, annual gains stemming from asset appreciation and its eventual wind-up.

And as long as most of their income is generated within the mainland, even those who have changed their nationality remain subject to the regulations.

“Previously, the law merely required that anyone who has offshore trusts should pay tax, but it lacked detailed implementing provisions. This update fills the regulatory void,” Ge said.

I don’t expect to see any new offshore trust formations over the coming months

Sarah Wang, Shanghai tax lawyer

Are offshore trusts still trustworthy?

The three primary offshore hubs traditionally favoured by Chinese investors are the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda, according to an article written in 2023 by He Yingxin, an official at the Sichuan branch of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (Safe).

“That’s because those jurisdictions enjoy strong international recognition, boast a well-established legal framework and offer innovative iterations of traditional trust structures – all of which greatly facilitate offshore trust formation,” He said.

There are no official statistics tracking the total volume of offshore trusts set up by Chinese investors. However, multiple lawyers and financial industry practitioners said that setting up offshore trusts has remained popular among wealthy individuals over the past two years for three reasons: asset protection, wealth succession and – last but not least – tax planning.

An inheritance dispute within the family of the late Zong Qinghou, the billionaire founder of Chinese soft-drink giant Wahaha Group who died in 2024, shed light on the amount of wealth tycoons were able to transfer to overseas accounts. In the court case, Zong’s three children born out of wedlock sought to freeze an offshore trust worth US$1.8 billion set up in Hong Kong.

According to Hong Kong court filings, Zong Qinghou signed a letter of entrustment dated February 2, 2024, appointing his daughter Kelly Zong Fuli to act as settlor to establish three offshore family trusts for the children.

If a court ultimately validates the existence of the trusts, the finance ministry’s new rules stipulate individual income tax liabilities when transferring assets into them – with the potential bill reaching US$360 million, according to estimates from Wang, the tax lawyer. Where the trust holds financial assets, annual gains generated by such assets will also carry a 20 per cent levy.

“The regulations are stringent, perhaps too stringent,” Wang said, adding the ministry’s announcement has delivered a heavy blow to the industry, with offshore trusts losing their appeal as a vehicle for tax planning. Many of the overseas trustees she has spoken with are now taking a wait-and-see stance, she said.

“Some trustees are now considering rolling out stricter Know-Your-Client procedures for Chinese clients, especially on source of funds. It is expected that establishing offshore trusts will become more complicated for mainland individuals, with substantially more paperwork required,” Wang said. “I don’t expect to see any new offshore trust formations over the coming months.”

The central government also appears to be encouraging affluent individuals to settle their tax liabilities voluntarily.

Under the new rules, individuals who transferred assets into offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025 will receive a 90-day window to make the relevant declarations to the tax authorities and settle any outstanding liabilities without incurring late-payment penalties.

Why personal income tax?

The finance ministry’s announcement came as a jolt to players in the trust sector. But to those versed in China’s tax system, the move was widely anticipated. A common sentiment among analysts: First tighter rules for cross-border stock trading, and now this.

Since last year, authorities have called on mainland citizens to self-declare their overseas capital income dating back to 2022. Offshore earnings from stocks are subject to a 20 per cent tax on capital gains and dividends, alongside potential late fees. Official data shows taxpayers reporting overseas income settled roughly 13 billion yuan (US$1.93 billion) in additional taxes during the first five months of 2026.

The Common Reporting Standard (CRS) – an information-sharing agreement among countries’ tax authorities designed to prevent tax evasion – also facilitated the exchange of data not only on stock trading but also offshore trusts, Ge said. China committed to adopting the CRS in 2014 and began its first round of CRS exchanges in September 2018.

“In recent years, a growing number of affluent individuals have set up offshore trusts, with tax reduction being one of the prime drivers. Considering the strained fiscal situation, the policy moves by the government were inevitable,” he added.

In fact, targeting the wealthy may long have been on Beijing’s radar. He Yingxin of Safe wrote that “domestic entrepreneurs accumulate wealth with the backing of national resources – including banking loans, preferential policies from local authorities and domestic market demand. If they ‘cash out’ on the mainland and then move their wealth offshore to avoid tax obligations, it will trigger severe losses of domestic capital.”

He also singled out the Haidilao hotpot brand. Though the globally popular chain restaurant was founded in southwest China’s Sichuan province in 1994, it has essentially become Singaporean on paper.

“Even though 87.6 per cent of Haidilao’s revenue [in 2022] came from the mainland, the company’s owner and his wife are already Singaporean nationals and their assets have already been moved offshore … The company’s owner has evaded substantial personal income tax liabilities.”

Oversight has continued to intensify and expand over the past year. Jason Zhao, an insurance agent at Shanghai-based Manulife-Sinochem Life Insurance, said that several of his clients have received calls from tax authorities asking them to declare dividends from overseas insurance policies.

“Tax officials didn’t ask my clients to pay back taxes – it was just a declaration requirement for now,” Zhao added.

One professor with close ties to the State Taxation Administration (STA), who requested anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said that prioritising individual income tax was a natural policy choice for the central government.

“There are essentially no other levers left for Beijing to raise additional tax revenue,” the professor said.

“The sluggish economy has ruled out bigger increases in the value-added tax (VAT), while soft auto demand is weighing on consumption tax receipts. And amid the prolonged property market slump, expanding property tax pilot programmes to more cities is off the table – that leaves only individual income tax.”

Compared with developed economies, Chinese authorities are heavily reliant on indirect methods of taxation – such as VAT – for revenue rather than direct ones such as income taxes. The country’s personal income tax, meanwhile, has a narrower taxpayer base and a lower collection compliance rate, while also imposing a heavy tax burden on income from labour and a much lighter one on capital.

But thanks to Beijing’s recent policy push, individual income tax has reclaimed its position as China’s third-largest tax category out of a total of 18 after four years, overtaking consumption tax. In the first half of 2026, personal income tax revenues topped 898 billion yuan, marking an increase of 13.1 per cent year on year.

At a press briefing on July 28, Wang Shiyu, an official at the STA, attributed this shift to three factors: a buyout capital market, fast-growing sectors such as technology, and stepped-up tax oversight targeting high-income individuals.

“We have continued to strengthen tax compliance and set up supervision,” Wang said. “For taxpayers who need to settle outstanding tax liabilities, we provide full-cycle follow-up and guidance. At the same time, we are also standardising the tax oversight of offshore gains.”

Tax administration data shows that since 2024, the top 10 per cent of earners by annual income contributed just over 90 per cent of all personal income tax declared and paid.

If your wealth fails to contribute to the domestic economy, then the government expects you to pay tax

Jason Zhao, Shanghai

How stringent is too stringent?

Nevertheless, questions remain about whether policymakers can refine the rules and make them more equitable.

For instance, suppose an individual transfers stocks worth 100 million yuan into an offshore trust. One year later, the value of those stocks doubles. But even if no action is taken with respect to the shares, the trust owner would still be liable for personal income tax on gains that exist only on paper.

“Under China’s Individual Income Tax Law, taxation on income from asset transfers hinges on two conditions: transfer of asset ownership and realisation of proceeds,” Li Xin, a lawyer at Shenzhen-based DeHeng Law Offices, wrote in a report released in late July. “Yet the new finance ministry regulations mandate levying tax on paper gains … This clearly exceeds the scope of its legal mandate.”

Currently on the mainland, both on-paper and actual capital gains from freely tradeable shares are exempt from taxation. Only the profits from selling lock-up shares and dividend income are subject to tax. For cross-border trading, however, investment gains are subject to annual tax levies.
