“Onshore and offshore investments are subject to differential tax treatment. I don’t think that’s fair,” said Wang, the Shanghai-based tax lawyer.

“It appears clear that the central government aims to keep capital within the country, either to shore up the capital market or bolster consumption,” said Zhao, the insurance agent. “If your wealth fails to contribute to the domestic economy, then the government expects you to pay tax. I believe that is the underlying logic at play here.”

Lawyers and finance practitioners said HNW individuals have yet to settle on alternatives to offshore trusts and are employing a cautious approach for now.

Meanwhile, their stance on tax avoidance appears to have shifted amid the widening crackdown that has closed an increasing number of regulatory loopholes.

Wang Shiyu of the STA revealed that 99.95 per cent of taxpayers ordered to settle outstanding tax liabilities have filed their declarations, adding that “taxpayers have shown markedly stronger awareness of tax compliance.”

“There is no legitimate tax avoidance. Any tax avoidance constitutes tax evasion,” said Ge of the Shanghai National Accounting Institute.

His views were shared by a domestic entrepreneur who wished not to be identified, and whose firm is awaiting its listing on the tech-focused ChiNext board.

“There appears to be little room for tax avoidance. Any attempt may lead to retroactive tax collection later. I want to stay out of the headlines, so law-abiding tax payment makes the most sense for me,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
item.description:
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.

In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?

Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.
item.content:encoded:
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.

In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?

Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.

Young Chinese affectionately call him “Grandpa Cute” or “Dumbledore”, after the beloved Harry Potter character, while his gentle, jargon-free reflections on education, purpose, anxiety, relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) and cultural understanding resonate deeply in a fast-paced, high-pressure society.

Through an intimate Q&A format, Macfarlane has amassed more than 2.4 million followers in roughly one year since launching on the Chinese social media platform RedNote in 2025, with videos often gaining millions of views.

His channels on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – and Bilibili, another major video-sharing platform, have also attracted about 170,000 and 540,000 followers, respectively.

Beyond answering personal questions, Macfarlane addresses timely topics, ranging from discussions about football during the World Cup to rituals around China’s tomb-sweeping day.

Macfarlane, who originally started sharing his ideas on YouTube, expanded his online outreach to China, which he has visited 20 times and where he taught as a visiting professor, at the suggestion of his editor at Cam Rivers Publishing.

Driven by his long-standing vision to bridge academia and the public, Macfarlane launched his social media presence in China with the aim of communicating with the Chinese public and learning more about the country.

According to Macfarlane, his deep familiarity with China, built through these connections alongside his extensive research on the country, has been a cornerstone of his rapid social media growth, enabling him to relate his answers to his Chinese audience.

“I can speak to them as people whose culture and history I know something about, and I think that makes them feel that I’m not a stranger,” Macfarlane said in an interview.

For instance, when addressing questions about China’s national higher education entrance examination, or gaokao, he drew on his knowledge of Chinese educational history, Macfarlane said.

Understanding the exam’s role as a critical ladder for social advancement allowed him to empathise with the intense pressure students faced from parents and teachers, helping them to navigate their anxieties with genuine insights.

Macfarlane’s anthropological and historical perspectives offer comfort to China’s young generation by framing their personal struggles within a broader historical and spatial context.

Many of his audience said they found relief in realising that their private worries were shared by peers across different times and cultures, allowing them to learn from how others navigated similar challenges.

Yang Zhongcheng, a 20-year-old student at Beijing University of Technology, has rarely missed an update since he started following Macfarlane on RedNote in 2025. “This helped me jump out of the well and view myself from a broader, more compassionate perspective,” he said.

Surrounded by peers locked in fierce academic competition and facing the rapid advance of AI, Yang felt disoriented by the overwhelming pace of society but had learned to let go of his perfectionism and focus on the present through Macfarlane’s content.

Yang added that he particularly appreciated Macfarlane’s non-patronising approach. “[He] makes me feel we are totally equal, and that he’s keeping us company rather than lecturing us.”

Echoing this sentiment, Macfarlane observed that a lot of Chinese education and family life was hierarchical. While young people were accustomed to being told what was right or wrong, they often harboured a quiet resistance to top-down lecturing, he said.

Macfarlane also attributed his appeal to his Cambridge background and distinct delivery characterised by a refined accent, clear language and a measured pace.

According to Macfarlane, the questions he receives cover themes spanning jobs to relationships and technology changes, yet nearly all boil down to how to cope with a rapidly shifting world.

“Is there really no future for humanities majors?” one user wrote in the comments section of Macfarlane’s RedNote channel. “How can an ordinary person lead a fulfilling life?” another asked, while a third wondered, “Why do humans never seem to learn from historical lessons?”

Macfarlane said the questions were not surprising “because China has gone through the biggest economic, social, political and ideological change of any civilisation in history in the fastest time”.

He noted that such a swift and dramatic transformation had a profound impact on people’s psychology, attitudes and feelings, with the younger generation of Chinese bearing the brunt.

Unable to draw on the experiences of their elders, who grew up in an entirely different era, young Chinese were left to question almost everything. Into this void stepped Macfarlane, offering an empathetic listening ear and a broader perspective.

Beyond personal solace, the channel has also fostered cross-cultural understanding. Instead of traditional top-down lectures, these digital interactions encourage young viewers to ask questions and discuss ideas openly in the comments.

Li Lin, a 19-year-old student whose desire to explore Western culture was sparked by the videos, said Macfarlane’s content “inspires young people to grasp the differences between East and West, while actively exploring diverse cultures and the depth of civilisations”.

Driven by the professor’s insights, fellow viewer Yang was even inspired to spend a few weeks visiting Cambridge.

While Macfarlane clearly knows China well, some of his audience feel that his advice occasionally misses the mark because of the inherent limits of viewing the country through a Western lens.

For Li, Macfarlane’s different viewpoint is a benefit. “Eastern and Western thoughts are neither right nor wrong; they are simply distinct perspectives shaped by different historical and social backgrounds,” she said.

“And this very difference is precisely the bridge for us to learn from and understand one another.”

Cultural exchange is largely one-way

Macfarlane acknowledged that the cultural exchange generated by his videos remained largely one-way, with Chinese audiences making far more effort to understand the West than vice versa.

Yet he noted that the reach of his videos extended beyond China, drawing in “TikTok refugees” who migrated to RedNote when a ban of the platform in the United States seemed imminent last January.

Against this backdrop, Macfarlane said he hoped his channel would serve as a bridge to the wider world, sparking curiosity about China among non-Chinese audiences and gradually dispelling deeply rooted mistrust.

He also aimed to foster a deeper realisation of China as one of the world’s “greatest, most ancient, and most sophisticated civilisations” – one with immense wisdom to share, especially after having made such great efforts to absorb the best of the West, he added.

However, Macfarlane stressed that such mutual dialogue remained hindered by prejudice in the West, even as language barriers had gradually faded with AI translation technologies.

Western perceptions of China were often decades out of date and compounded by geopolitical anxiety, he argued. China’s rise challenged long-held assumptions in the West about its superiority in political governance, free-market capitalism, innovation and religious faith.

“Our economies have stalled and inequality is growing hugely in the West. And then we look at China – China is still growing reasonably and it has, to a considerable extent, made that wealth available across [society],” Macfarlane said.

He also pointed to a subconscious Western fear of retaliation stemming from a history of imperialist aggression against China, which has fuelled political and media distrust.

Despite these geopolitical headwinds, Macfarlane remains convinced that the solution lies in sustained, grass roots engagement.

“The deep answer is more exchange – more Chinese coming here, more of our Western people going to China, working with and becoming friends with Chinese,” he said. “And then we might have a chance of living in a more peaceful world.”

item.title: [SCMP] Philippine flood-control scandal resurfaces after latest monsoon deluge
item.description:
The latest floods to hit Metro Manila and parts of the Philippines’ main island of Luzon have turned a familiar seasonal disaster into a renewed test of political accountability for President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, as anger over allegedly corrupt flood-control projects returns to the centre of public debate.

Analysts said the deluge had sharpened scrutiny of the slow-moving investigation into allegedly substandard and non-existent flood-control works, exposing the gap between Marcos’ anti-corruption message and the lack of visible results in communities that continue to bear the brunt of extreme weather.

Metro Manila was inundated on Monday with 201.7mm of rain in just five hours, leaving residents wading through floodwaters, vehicles stranded and some areas not usually considered flood-prone submerged.
item.content:encoded:
The latest floods to hit Metro Manila and parts of the Philippines’ main island of Luzon have turned a familiar seasonal disaster into a renewed test of political accountability for President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, as anger over allegedly corrupt flood-control projects returns to the centre of public debate.

Analysts said the deluge had sharpened scrutiny of the slow-moving investigation into allegedly substandard and non-existent flood-control works, exposing the gap between Marcos’ anti-corruption message and the lack of visible results in communities that continue to bear the brunt of extreme weather.

Metro Manila was inundated on Monday with 201.7mm of rain in just five hours, leaving residents wading through floodwaters, vehicles stranded and some areas not usually considered flood-prone submerged.

Outside the capital, villages across parts of Luzon were also swamped after weeks of southwest monsoon rains, forcing thousands of families from their homes and reviving a familiar question: why does the country keep flooding despite huge sums spent to prevent it?

That frustration was reflected by Senator Panfilo Lacson, who questioned why communities continued to be submerged year after year, despite nearly 2 trillion pesos (US$32.4 billion) being poured into flood-control projects since 2011.

“1.939 trillion pesos funded the DPWH [Department of Public Works and Highways] flood control management programme under three presidents from 2011 to 2025, and the result is uncontrolled floods,” he said in a statement on Tuesday.

In the town of Macabebe in Pampanga, a store owner barricaded the front of his shop with sacks of rice to stop water from seeping in, an image some local media outlets and content creators portrayed as a sign of creativity and resilience.

But other Filipinos pushed back online, with several posts rejecting the familiar celebration of resilience gaining traction.

“Can we pressure our government to come up with better solutions instead of romanticising Filipino resilience?” one widely shared post said. “Our fellowmen shouldn’t be suffering through this in the first place … as if we don’t pay taxes and we don’t have billions of funds for flood control projects.”

Another post, which drew more than 7,000 reactions, captured the frustration more bluntly: “Rain is natural. Heavy flooding isn’t. Until now, no one has been held accountable for the billions’ worth of corruption in flood control projects. Until now, the government remains reliant on aid.”

Scandal back in focus

The latest floods have returned attention to the country’s investigation into allegedly corrupt flood-control projects, while intensifying criticism of the government’s failure to protect communities from a disaster that returns with each rainy season.

During his state of the nation address in late July, Marcos announced that errant high-ranking officials of the DPWH, contractors and lawmakers had been detained and charged over their involvement in the scheme, a year after investigations began.

In his address the previous year, Marcos said 545 billion pesos had been spent on flood-control works since 2022 across nearly 10,000 projects, but most had been found to be substandard or “ghost” projects, implicating a number of lawmakers, government officials and contractors who allegedly colluded in the scheme.

Last month, the Department of Justice said 841 million pesos had been recovered from those implicated in the scandal and deposited in the national treasury.

As of late July, 45 individuals and two contracting firms had been charged in 26 flood control-related cases in court.

But observers echoed a public sentiment that has grown louder with each flood: progress in holding people accountable and getting answers from the scandal has been too slow relative to its scale.

“More than a year since the issue was raised, there were only a few people who were charged in courts. At this stage, most of the alleged perpetrators should have been facing the judicial process,” said Nathaniel Candelaria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman.

Arjan Aguirre, an assistant professor in Ateneo de Manila University’s political science department, said the investigations had moved too slowly given the scale of the allegations and the amount of public money involved.

“At this point, we should already be seeing clearer findings, stronger accountability and concrete action against those responsible,” he said.

Aguirre said the slow pace of the investigations raised concerns they might not be fully independent or could become politicised, especially if people felt they were being used to target political opponents or pressure lawmakers.

“Ultimately, the credibility of the probe will depend on whether it can demonstrate that accountability is being pursued consistently, regardless of political affiliation,” he added.

Political risk

Observers said the sluggish pace of inquiry would only sow further distrust in the Marcos administration, as the president grappled with modest ratings.

Marcos’ trust rating dropped to 34 per cent in June from 35 per cent in March, while his rival, Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio, polled at 57 per cent, according to local pollster Social Weather Stations.

“This year’s flooding could further deepen public anger and distrust towards the government,” Aguirre said.

Every time communities were submerged, Aguirre said people were reminded not only of the billions supposedly spent on flood control, but also that the same vulnerabilities persisted.

Despite the Marcos administration touting its accomplishments in the anti-corruption investigation and Marcos himself promoting a stronger anti-corruption message, analysts said actual shortcomings would continue to overshadow any progress.

“While some people were already facing cases, I do not think the administration is successful in this issue … the people need to know the truth about the flood control scandal and those who were involved, regardless of political affiliations, must face justice,” Candelaria said.

Aguirre said the Marcos administration appeared to be putting considerable effort into improving its image and promoting an anti-corruption message, but this had not been matched by the same urgency in addressing the flood-control scandal and institutionalising reforms.

Marcos risked having his anti-corruption agenda viewed as “political messaging rather than meaningful reform” if people continued to experience flooding while seeing little concrete progress in the scandal, Aguirre said.

With flooding still a constant threat for many Filipinos, the issue looks set to haunt the administration right up to the 2028 national elections, when Duterte-Carpio has indicated she will run for the presidency.

“The Duterte camp has been using the flood control scandal against Marcos from the beginning and I expect them to continue doing so in the 2028 campaign. They have been effective in framing the issue as evidence that Marcos is politicising the investigation and protecting his allies,” Aguirre said.

“The delays we are seeing now only give greater credence to that narrative. If the government fails to produce clear findings, prosecutions, and reforms, the Duterte camp can easily turn the scandal into a broader argument that the Marcos administration talks about anti-corruption but is unwilling to hold its own allies accountable.”

item.title: [SCMP] US designates academic Min Zin as ‘wrongfully detained’ in China
item.description:
The US State Department said on Thursday that it had determined after a detailed investigation that Min Zin, an American political analyst of Chinese descent detained by Beijing last month, was being improperly held.

That formal designation shifts the case from a State Department consular issue to one handled by its presidential office dealing with hostage affairs.

Thursday’s terse statement, which said the decision was made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, adds another irritant to the fraught bilateral relationship just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to hold a summit in Washington.
item.content:encoded:
The US State Department said on Thursday that it had determined after a detailed investigation that Min Zin, an American political analyst of Chinese descent detained by Beijing last month, was being improperly held.

That formal designation shifts the case from a State Department consular issue to one handled by its presidential office dealing with hostage affairs.

Thursday’s terse statement, which said the decision was made by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, adds another irritant to the fraught bilateral relationship just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to hold a summit in Washington.

“Secretary Rubio has determined that US citizen Min Zin is wrongfully detained in China,” the agency said in a release attributed to Assistant State Secretary Dylan Johnson. “This follows an extensive review of the circumstances surrounding his June 3 detention in Yunnan, China, where Mr Zin had travelled to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government.”

The US agency further noted that this is the second wrongful detention designation involving China, following the case of Youlin Chen, a seismologist arrested in November 2024 at Beijing International Airport as he prepared to fly home to Boston.

“The safety and security of US citizens is the State Department’s top priority,” the State Department added. “We will continue to advocate for Mr Zin and call for the release of all US citizens who are arbitrarily detained or exit banned in China.”

The Chinese embassy in Washington said China is a country governed by the rule of law. “Its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law, and there is no such thing as so-called wrongful detention,” said embassy spokesman Liu Chang.

In the past, however, Beijing has maintained that any imprisonment and travel restrictions imposed on Americans are legitimate and in keeping with Chinese law.

In June, a week after the arrest, Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian announced at a regular press conference that Zin had been detained on suspicion of “engaging in espionage and endangering China’s national security” without elaborating.

Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer with Global Reach, a nonprofit group that works with families to return Americans wrongfully detained abroad, said in an interview on Thursday that he received assurances from the National Security Council [NSC] that the Trump administration will raise these cases with Xi next month if they are not resolved.

“President Trump has been really consistent since taking office in his second term that bringing home Americans is a personal priority for him,” Lebson said. “He hasn’t just told his people to do it. He has personally involved himself in the efforts.”

Global Reach has worked closely with the Chen family and advised Zin’s family informally, he said, adding that Trump’s efforts have seen some 110 Americans returned.

Zin, also known as U Min Zin, was a student activist during Myanmar’s 1988 pro-democracy uprising. After hiding for several years in Myanmar, he fled to Thailand before applying for and receiving asylum in the US.

He received a master’s degrees in Asian studies in 2010 and political science in 2011 from the University of California, Berkeley, and advanced to a doctoral degree program in political science at UC Berkeley. He is not currently enrolled.

In 2016, Zin founded the Institute for Strategy and Policy – Myanmar (ISP-Myanmar) and has written extensively in Foreign Policy and other journals about the Southeast Asian nation’s post-coup politics and economy. He has also written about Beijing’s influence in Myanmar’s border regions, including its ties to both the military government and ethnic armed groups.

The institute, originally based in Yangon, relocated to Thailand after the 2021 military coup that ousted Aung San Suu Kyi’s democratically elected government and plunged Myanmar into civil war.

In a statement on Thursday, ISP-Myanmar said it welcomed the State Department designation and urged the agency to make Zin’s release a top priority ahead of next month’s summit.

China is Myanmar’s largest trading partner and a key investor, particularly through Belt and Road Initiative projects such as the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor, oil and gas pipelines, ports and mining operations. China has publicly backed the junta and maintained engagement despite the ongoing conflict and criticism of the political transition.

Chen’s case, meanwhile, remained largely under the radar until last month when his relatives went public about his detention nearly two years after the arrest, also on espionage charges.

Their disclosure came shortly after Trump brought up Chen’s case with Xi during their May summit in Beijing, Lebson said, and Global Reach was hearing from NSC and State Department officials that there was little indication of movement from Beijing.

China formally charged Chen on May 1, 2025, with espionage, leading to his wrongful detention designation in March of this year. Chen’s speciality involves using public seismological data to measure underground nuclear tests, notably studying North Korea’s past test blasts.

The Biden administration secured the release of three Americans from China in November 2024. An equal number of Chinese were released at the same time. The rare exchange saw the US ease its travel warning on visiting China and drop a “D” designation indicating a nation that wrongly detains visitors.

Lebson said the two cases and Thursday’s statement could see tougher travel warnings reimposed, adding that there seemed to be a disconnect between Beijing’s desire for more people-to-people exchanges and the potential chill these cases may have on tourists, academics and corporate executives.

Under the 2020 Levinson Act, a wrongful detainment designation is determined based on a set of criteria that may include innocence, whether the detention is designed to increase leverage on the US, how it relates to human rights activity and whether the legal proceedings violate due process standards.

A wrongful detention label moves the case from the State Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs – which handles routine traveller help – to the Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs, which has more tools and clout.

These may include drawing on dedicated negotiators who are authorised to work with high-ranking US and foreign officials, intelligence agencies and third parties to secure the detainees’ release; the use of public and political pressure, as seen with Trump’s May request; and the potential for financial sanctions, travel bans or diplomatic penalties.

Zack Cooper, an analyst with the conservative American Enterprise Institute and a former NSC official, said Thursday’s relatively short statement and its attribution to an assistant secretary may be an effort to balance their desire for a successful summit with a bid to gain the release of Americans.

In July, shortly after Trump made his appeal to Xi in May, China agreed to release Beijing Zion Church founder Pastor Ezra Jin Mingri after 266 days in detention.

“The administration might hope that they can use this moment ahead of the Xi visit to make progress on wrongfully detained American citizens, just as they did with Pastor Jin earlier this summer,” Cooper added.

These cases add to a long list of differences between the two nations involving strategic technology and rare earths restrictions, export bans, military chest thumping, tariffs and trade.

item.title: [SCMP] Why North Korea is ‘keeping the door open for dialogue’ with Trump
item.description:
At first glance, Kim Yo-jong’s latest message to Washington looked like a rebuff to US President Donald Trump’s insistence that he would meet her brother Kim Jong-un later this year.

But analysts said the North Korean leader’s powerful sister stopped well short of shutting down Trump’s outreach, using a carefully worded statement to leave room for renewed summit diplomacy while making clear that Pyongyang intended to set the terms for any return to dialogue.

In her statement, released by North Korean state media late on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong dismissed Trump’s decision to scale back joint US-South Korea military exercises as meaningless, demanded a complete halt to the drills and warned again against what Pyongyang calls Washington’s “hostile” policy.
item.content:encoded:
At first glance, Kim Yo-jong’s latest message to Washington looked like a rebuff to US President Donald Trump’s insistence that he would meet her brother Kim Jong-un later this year.

But analysts said the North Korean leader’s powerful sister stopped well short of shutting down Trump’s outreach, using a carefully worded statement to leave room for renewed summit diplomacy while making clear that Pyongyang intended to set the terms for any return to dialogue.

In her statement, released by North Korean state media late on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong dismissed Trump’s decision to scale back joint US-South Korea military exercises as meaningless, demanded a complete halt to the drills and warned again against what Pyongyang calls Washington’s “hostile” policy.

Yet the statement also contained openings that appeared calibrated for Trump.

Kim Yo-jong neither confirmed nor denied Trump’s claim that the North Korean leader had responded positively to his latest overture, saying only that it was “perhaps” the one foreign policy matter involving the country’s “supreme leadership” about which she was not informed.

She also emphasised that Pyongyang had repeatedly said Kim Jong-un held “personally good memories and feelings” towards Trump.

The ambiguity allowed North Korea to avoid embarrassing Trump while reaffirming the “excellent” personal relationship between the two leaders, analysts said, suggesting Pyongyang aimed to keep the door open to talks, but only if Washington accepted a much higher entry price.

That could include US acceptance of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, the exclusion of denuclearisation from the immediate agenda and a negotiating framework shaped by Pyongyang rather than Washington, they said.

Trump, meanwhile, appeared to hint that North Korea’s denuclearisation could be put on the back burner during the initial stage of any renewed negotiations.

Shortly after the statement was released, Trump said he would meet Kim Jong-un later this year, noting that North Korea had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons.

His remarks came amid reports that he was pushing for a meeting during his next trip to Asia, likely to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit scheduled to take place in Shenzhen, China, in November.

“Yeah, I will be,” Trump told reporters when asked whether he expected to meet Kim Jong-un later this year.

On whether he was exchanging written letters with Kim Jong-un, Trump said, “I can’t tell you that.”

Trump held three ultimately fruitless bilateral meetings with Kim Jong-un during his first term: in Singapore in June 2018, Hanoi in February 2019 and the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019.

Observers say Trump’s renewed attention on North Korea could reflect his eagerness to score a major foreign policy coup, potentially helping divert attention from the protracted war against Iran, which has tarnished his image as a peacemaker and contributed to inflation ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

But it remains to be seen whether Kim Jong-un will respond to Trump’s overtures, given North Korea’s growing ties with Russia and China, which have reduced Pyongyang’s need for help from the United States, analysts say.

“By publicly reaffirming the ‘excellent relationship’ between Kim and Trump, Pyongyang is keeping the door open to dialogue,” said Hong Min, a senior analyst at the Korea Institute for National Unification.

Even if Trump exaggerated Kim Jong-un’s alleged positive response to a meeting, Pyongyang’s statement showed how it was avoiding embarrassing the US leader, Hong added. “Taken more positively, the message could be interpreted as: ‘We have received no message, so if you are serious, then send a genuine one.’”

Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said Pyongyang was raising all the security issues it considered relevant to its interests, thereby increasing the threshold for dialogue.

The statement also widened the security agenda beyond Washington, including Japan’s recent military moves and South Korea’s development of nuclear-powered submarines.

Kim Yo-jong on Wednesday issued a direct threat against Japan, warning that if it “attempts to make the wrong choice, it will now face an immediate and unsurvivable, annihilating strike”.

The key takeaway from her message, Yang noted, was not whether communication had taken place regarding a possible resumption of Trump-Kim summit diplomacy, but rather North Korea’s emphasis on the preconditions for restarting dialogue.

“Pyongyang is arguing that merely scaling back US-South Korea joint military exercises is not enough and that Washington must fundamentally abandon its hostile policy towards North Korea,” Yang said.

“By rejecting reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, while also raising concerns over Japan’s recent military moves and South Korea’s development of nuclear-powered submarines, North Korea appears to be seeking to raise the threshold for resuming US-North Korea dialogue.”

The timing of the statement, coinciding with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul, also appeared intended to demonstrate Pyongyang’s determination to maintain the initiative on Korean peninsula issues and signal to both China and Russia that North Korea would not recklessly rush into dialogue with the US, Yang noted.

For Yu Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, the statement suggests Pyongyang continues to see value in the personal rapport between Kim Jong-un and Trump even as it dismisses the significance of scaling back military exercises.

“This could be an attempt by Pyongyang to separate Trump from broader US policy towards North Korea, keeping open the possibility of resuming their summit diplomacy,” Yu said.

Professor Lim Eul-chul of the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University said Pyongyang was well aware that Trump was in urgent need of a fresh diplomatic coup ahead of the November midterm elections.

“Kim Jong-un also understands that even if another summit with Trump does take place, the talks could be derailed at any time due to opposition in Washington or Trump’s own whims,” Lim said.

“Nevertheless, from North Korea’s perspective, the uncertainty created by Trump represents not only a threat but also a strategic opportunity.”

That could allow Kim to maximise his leverage until Trump came forward with sufficiently dramatic concessions, potentially including a permanent end to US-South Korea military exercises and explicit public recognition of North Korea as a nuclear-armed state, Lim said.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University, agreed that Pyongyang was unlikely to agree to talks any time soon.

With North Korea benefiting financially from helping Russia in the Ukraine war and receiving Moscow’s blessing for its de facto nuclear status, Easley said all these gave Kim Jong-un “leverage to demand greater support from Beijing”.

While the North Korean leader might seek “further economic and reputational benefits” from Washington, Easley predicted this would occur after the US midterm elections when Trump “is expected to be in a weaker domestic political position and in search of headline-grabbing foreign policies”.

item.title: [SCMP] How Vietnam’s ‘streamlining revolution’ may lead to uneven success
item.description:
Third plenums are ordinarily the quiet part of Vietnam’s political calendar. Between its five-yearly congresses, the Communist Party of Vietnam governs through numbered plenums of its Central Committee (CC): the first two settle personnel decisions, and the third, six months on, usually does no more than ratify the term’s work programme.

This time, the third plenum of the 14th CC, held from July 20 to 24, did more. It set out the next phase of the country’s most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades: the move from streamlining the apparatus to building the capacity to govern.

An unusually crowded agenda of 13 major items includes issues such as the development model, the land law and national security. These were organised around General Secretary To Lam’s “four strategic shifts”: improving the party’s leadership capacity and the state’s operating quality; unifying the governance of development space and national resources; shifting growth towards productivity, technology and human capital; and moving from reactive crisis management towards prevention and resilience.
item.content:encoded:
Third plenums are ordinarily the quiet part of Vietnam’s political calendar. Between its five-yearly congresses, the Communist Party of Vietnam governs through numbered plenums of its Central Committee (CC): the first two settle personnel decisions, and the third, six months on, usually does no more than ratify the term’s work programme.

This time, the third plenum of the 14th CC, held from July 20 to 24, did more. It set out the next phase of the country’s most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades: the move from streamlining the apparatus to building the capacity to govern.

An unusually crowded agenda of 13 major items includes issues such as the development model, the land law and national security. These were organised around General Secretary To Lam’s “four strategic shifts”: improving the party’s leadership capacity and the state’s operating quality; unifying the governance of development space and national resources; shifting growth towards productivity, technology and human capital; and moving from reactive crisis management towards prevention and resilience.

The four shifts together describe the developmental state To Lam wants to build: one that steers growth through deliberate coordination rather than leaving it to markets alone. But the first shift – improving the party’s leadership – is the hinge on which the others turn. The second, a unified development space, requires local institutions capable of executing plans drawn up in Hanoi. The third, productivity-led growth, requires predictable regulation and quick approvals. The fourth, prevention over reaction, depends on the ability to detect problems early and respond coherently.

This is what makes the plenum a turning point in the “streamlining revolution” to cut the size of the state bureaucracy. In the past 12 months, the reform concentrated on structure: for example, reducing the number of provinces and centrally governed cities from 63 to 34, abolishing the district tier of government and consolidating commune-level units. It also removed people: nearly 210,000 civil servants and public employees took early retirement or severance under the restructuring. That was the first test, and the leadership passed it. The plenum entailed a second, and perhaps harder test: whether the machinery emerging from upheaval would be effective.

Vietnam now has two tiers of local government, provinces and communes. The communes, the lower of the two, absorbed most of what the missing district tier used to do. This constitutes more than 1,000 tasks, including issuing land-use certificates, granting construction permits and administering welfare. But the communes inherited the workload of the districts without inheriting its specialists. When the district tier was abolished, its staff had various options: move up to the provincial level, shift down to the commune level or leave the service altogether. Only a third of the commune’s 150,000 staff arrived that way. The rest had always worked at the commune level and had little experience in handling land titling or construction permits.

Nor did staffing keep pace with size. The average commune now has more than twice as many staff as before but three times as many residents, on top of the district’s old caseload. That leaves one official for roughly 700 people, against 490 before the mergers. This is why communes are so easily overwhelmed by their new tasks. In one documented case, a commune has 49 staff serving more than 66,000 residents, a ratio of one official for 1,350 people.

The strain is measurable. The Ministry of Home Affairs admits that only 30 per cent of commune staff fully meet the requirements of their new duties. This is already visible in service delivery. A nationwide survey found that only 71.1 per cent of land-certificate applicants received results on time, more than a quarter of applicants had to deal with multiple offices, and 12 per cent resorted to informal intermediaries. The figures do not suggest universal failure, but they reveal functional overload and uneven competence at the tier on which the new system depends.

The Central Committee’s Conclusion 76, issued days after the plenum, recognised the problem. It identified factors such as incomplete institutions, unclear decentralisation, mismatched staffing, thin resources and weak digital integration as obstacles to effective government. The committee also sought to shift the reform’s emphasis from organisational streamlining to operating quality. The centre is to set the framework, the provinces will coordinate, and the communes implement.

The remedies match the diagnosis. Devolved responsibilities are to come with the resources to discharge them, staffing is to follow workload rather than adhere to a strict quota, and specialists are to be steered towards communes. Cadres will be judged by results and public satisfaction, and those who innovate in the public interest are promised greater protection. The Politburo’s Plan 06 turns this into a timetable, assigning institutions to revise laws and clarify authority this year, with integrated databases, commune-level digital systems and a new evaluation framework due in 2027. By naming the responsible bodies, it makes delays easier to track.

That improves the reform’s prospects. Success, though, is likely to be partial and uneven.

The first problem is sequencing. Communes have already carried expanded responsibilities for a year, while the legal, staffing and digital fixes run into 2027. Re-training commune staff will not be completed until 2031. The burden of transition, therefore, falls on communes before the tools needed to manage it are in place.

The second is that specialist capacity cannot be created by decree. The rotation of specialists from higher tiers and training can ease shortages, but land, planning, finance and technology require experience that many rural and remote communes cannot quickly acquire. Flexible staffing works only if local authorities have access to capital, recruitment powers and qualified personnel.

The third concerns discretion. Output-based evaluation and digitalisation improve accountability, but they also create new reporting burdens. Poor databases cannot produce reliable indicators, and artificial intelligence cannot reconcile unclear laws or contradictory instructions. Conclusion 76’s governing principle is that accountability and supervision extend as far as the authority granted. That is sound design. Yet the main constraint on officials is not too little supervision. Rather, it is uncertainty over which decisions are his to make, and whether he will be protected when a reasonable one goes wrong.

Vietnam’s streamlining revolution has produced a smaller state, and the plenum has correctly diagnosed why this is not enough to deliver the “strategic shifts” that To Lam wants. Whether the new state becomes more capable will depend less on what Hanoi can measure, but more on whether the appropriate resources, expertise and authority reach the communes.

Nguyen Khac Giang is Visiting Fellow at the Vietnam Studies Programme of ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He was previously Research Fellow at the Vietnam Centre for Economic and Strategic Studies. This article was first published by ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s Bali financial hub ‘a matter of survival’: economic tsar
item.description:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.
item.content:encoded:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.

Indonesia, safely removed from the Iran war’s turmoil, was the obvious choice, he said.

“They said ‘We’d like to move our assets, we’d love very much to stay away from here and live in Bali, because it’s so peaceful in Bali’,” he recalled. “The Middle East conflict is not going to end next month or next year, I don’t believe that.”

Speaking to This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Nusa Dua Forum in Bali on July 17, the 78-year-old chairman of Indonesia’s National Economic Council was a study in moustachioed calm – a far cry from the crisis of confidence that has roiled Southeast Asia’s largest economy this year.

For us … it’s a matter of survival

Luhut Pandjaitan, National Economic Council chairman

Investors, spooked by scepticism over Prabowo’s populist policies and rattled further by a global energy crisis that sent fuel prices soaring, have pulled billions out of Indonesia in recent months.

Acknowledging the market rout and concerns over money laundering, Luhut pledged greater transparency and to stamp out corruption.

“Without this, it’s very hard to gain trust and credibility,” he said, going on to describe the financial hub in existential terms. “For us … it’s a matter of survival.”

On Tuesday, Indonesia’s parliament passed legislation paving the way for the new financial centre just 20 days after talks on it had first begun.

Its precise location and the full range of associated incentives are still under wraps, but Luhut says the legislative speed should come as no surprise – he first floated the idea two years ago.

The centre could be up and running as soon as next month, he said, hinting that Prabowo might time an official announcement to coincide with the country’s independence day on August 17.

Instead of Indonesia’s civil code, the centre will operate under international commercial law, according to Luhut, who drew a parallel with Hong Kong.

“It’s like one country, two systems,” he said. “Which is not the ideal … But the purpose is to improve the credibility and trust of Indonesia.”

Sceptical of the notion that only Singapore, Hong Kong or the United Arab Emirates could host such hubs, Luhut said he had consulted a range of investors – from American hedge fund manager Ray Dalio to the Porsche family – and found them in agreement.

“They said they love the aura of Bali,” he quipped.

Separately, at the forum – co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara – Indonesia’s former coordinating minister of maritime and investment repeated his pitch to a room filled with officials, investors and family office principals.

“We’re going to be very transparent. We’re going to be more efficient, there’s going to be less corruption,” he declared. “I’m pretty confident about that.”

Unshaken optimism

Luhut’s optimism does not end at the new international financial centre. He is convinced Indonesia’s digitalisation push and its young, skilled workforce can deliver Prabowo’s target of lifting economic growth from 5 to 8 per cent by 2029.

“I think 8 per cent – with digital infrastructure support, artificial intelligence and also with the family offices – I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he said, brushing off economists’ scepticism.

Technological progress over the past few years had been nothing short of “beautiful”, Luhut said, outlining how data collected from eight government ministries and major institutions now fed into an AI-supported system to drive efficiency gains.

“Indonesia will be different within two years,” he vowed, referring to a local “brain and talent factory” he founded where students are selected based on IQ scores and put through a curated curriculum.

Addressing the prevailing gloom surrounding coverage of Indonesia’s economy and policies, Luhut blamed a failure of messaging and argued that there was an information disconnect between the government and the public.

Earlier this year, global index provider MSCI warned it could downgrade Indonesia from emerging to frontier market status amid concerns over transparency and stock market manipulation. A May deadline it set to see signs of progress has since been pushed back to November.

A brighter spot came earlier this month, when S&P reaffirmed Jakarta’s sovereign credit rating, forecasting that recent financial strains would ease thanks to higher commodity prices and spending cuts.

The government projects its budget shortfall to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, just shy of the 3 per cent statutory ceiling. Prabowo’s flagship free meals programme – a cornerstone of his populist economic agenda – has drawn much of the flak for exacting a heavy toll on state finances since its launch in January 2025.

On Tuesday, the programme’s budget was slashed again – now reduced by more than 100 trillion rupiah (US$5.6 billion) from its original allocation – and the agency chief charged with overseeing it resigned a day later, citing health reasons.

Luhut defended the scheme as essential to inclusive growth and insisted the administration had committed to making it more “targeted” by focusing on remote areas.

“You have to adjust, because every province faces a different situation,” he said.

Indonesia’s troubleshooter

Luhut’s current role is just the latest chapter in a political and business career spanning four decades.

A former four-star army general, he first entered politics as Indonesia started its transition to democracy in the late 1990s, before stepping away several years later to build a business empire in energy, minerals and coal.

He returned in 2014 after helping finance Joko Widodo’s successful presidential campaign that year, becoming his chief of staff – a newly created position – and trusted troubleshooter, later spearheading both Indonesia’s downstreaming strategy and its pandemic response.

Also Widodo’s point man on China, Luhut called Jakarta-Beijing relations “very good”, revealing plans for an impending meeting between Prabowo and around 20 Chinese firms invested in Indonesia.

In May, Chinese businesses had raised concerns about Jakarta’s rising levies and stricter enforcement, with several Indonesian ministers pushing back, insisting the country must prioritise sovereignty over its natural resources.

To avoid misunderstandings, Luhut said Prabowo’s relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping had to become “much closer”.

“I said to the president, the biggest investor in this country is still China, whether you like it or not,” he said, noting that Beijing was “very willing” to share its technology and research capabilities.

Prabowo’s stricter demands of tycoons – including a plan to funnel proceeds from palm oil exports and other key resources through sovereign wealth fund Danantara to curb under-invoicing – has further unnerved investors, but Luhut shrugs off the unease.

“This country, with a 300 million population, it’s not easy to govern,” he said. “But we explain to them that the best time to invest in Indonesia is today.”

During the 2024 presidential election, when Luhut backed Prabowo’s campaign, he declined any ministerial post, opting instead to remain an adviser, according to state news agency Antara.

Asked about Widodo’s surprise return to the political stage this year – touring the country to support his son Kaesang Pangarep’s Solidarity Party – Luhut was philosophical,

“Jokowi is still active because, of course, he has to survive,” he said, referring to the former president by his popular nickname. “Otherwise, if you retire fully, it’s easy to get very old.”

Luhut described urging both presidents to maintain a harmonious relationship for the country’s sake, which Widodo did in 2019 when he made former electoral rival Prabowo his defence minister.

“He was my deputy, and now he’s my boss,” Luhut said of the current president. “If it’s just the two of us, we talk in a very relaxed way. But I still respect him, because this is an institution. And we have to respect that.”

For a man widely seen as one of Indonesia’s most influential unelected figures, Luhut professes being content with his position just beneath the summit of power.

“I’m happy with what I am. That’s my destiny,” he said. “Everything under this sky, whatever it is, I try to contribute as much as I can because I love this country.”

Fittingly, he closed his pitch to investors at the Nusa Dua summit not with numbers, but a feeling. “You’ll never get bored in Bali,” Luhut said. “Whenever I land in Bali I can feel friendliness, harmony and hope.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore jails and canes man for abusing boy, 6
item.description:
A man was sentenced to nine years and 10 months’ jail, and eight strokes of the cane on Friday for abusing multiple young boys who were under his care.

The man beat his youngest victim – a six-year-old boy – with a hanger more than 600 times, forced him to hold a push-up position for hours, and made him sleep in the toilet and drink his own urine.

The boy suffered severe injuries as a result, including to his ribs, lungs and kidneys, and was hospitalised for 46 days.
item.content:encoded:
A man was sentenced to nine years and 10 months’ jail, and eight strokes of the cane on Friday for abusing multiple young boys who were under his care.

The man beat his youngest victim – a six-year-old boy – with a hanger more than 600 times, forced him to hold a push-up position for hours, and made him sleep in the toilet and drink his own urine.

The boy suffered severe injuries as a result, including to his ribs, lungs and kidneys, and was hospitalised for 46 days.

The 31-year-old Singaporean man took care of young foreign students who lived in accommodation provided by the company where he worked, which his aunt owned. The man, who cannot be named to protect the identities of his victims, also abused two other boys, aged 10 and 11.

He had also pleaded guilty in July to making a false declaration related to hiring a foreign domestic worker to perform housekeeping duties for the accommodation.

District Judge John Ng said the sentence sent out the community’s collective message – that the ill treatment and abuse of young vulnerable victims cannot be tolerated and that any cruelty against them is “wholly to be condemned”.

He noted that the most serious of the man’s offences were committed against his youngest victim.

The facts “speak for themselves” on the brutality the man inflicted, said the judge, reiterating in detail what happened to the boy.

The judge noted that the man’s mitigation plea referenced the physical abuse he allegedly suffered at the hands of his alcoholic father and gangster older brother.

Judge Ng said he trusted that the man’s personal background was cited not to excuse his cruel acts on his victims, especially the six-year-old boy.

“But I have to say, on the other hand, being a young boy who had suffered at the hand of abusers, the offender should have been in a better position not to repeat such terrible treatment of vulnerable victims who had trusted him to care for them and even to protect them,” he added, as the man bowed his head in the dock.

“It was noted specifically by the psychiatrist that even if these allegations were true … it did not exculpate his physical abuse of the children under his care,” said the judge, citing a report by a doctor with the Institute of Mental Health.

When the man pleaded guilty in July, Deputy Public Prosecutors Timotheus Koh and Cheronne Lim asked for between nine years and six weeks to 10 years and eight weeks’ jail for the man, on top of six strokes of the cane.

Most of the man’s actions were captured on CCTV, and the videos “really show the extent of the depravity” of his actions and the cruelty he inflicted on his young victims, Koh said at the time, adding that the videos are very difficult to watch.

Defence lawyer Sarbrinder Singh of Sanders Law, had argued for seven years and two weeks’ prison and caning for his client instead.

In mitigation, the defence claimed that the man suffers from sleepless nights and that he was very remorseful for his actions.

The man requested to delay his sentence by one week to carry out prayers next week. The judge denied his request.

The man was responsible for managing the accommodation and teaching the primary school students mathematics and English, despite having no teaching or childcare qualifications.

In one incident, after noticing that the 10-year-old boy did not do his homework, the man demanded an explanation. Upon failing to get one, he punched and slapped the boy in the face at least five times.

He punched the boy in the face multiple times again when he could not answer one of the questions while doing his homework.

The next day, the boy’s teachers observed the bruise on his cheek and the school counsellor lodged a police report.

The man also made the two older boys hold a push-up position and hit them with a hanger multiple times.

His youngest victim – the six-year-old boy – moved into the accommodation under the man’s care in January 2023. The 31-year-old would punish the boy frequently, the court heard.

Other than forcing the boy to hold a push-up position, he also made him sleep in the toilet and fed him bread and water instead of proper meals.

In the incident that led to the 46-day hospitalisation period, the man abused the boy for about 18 hours – hitting him with a hanger at least 620 times, stomping on him at least 45 times and kicking him in the ribs at least once.

When his aunt, who was also his employer, arrived at the unit, she saw the state the boy was in and told the man to stop physically punishing the boy, but the man continued to hit and kick him.

He only stopped after his aunt carried the boy out of the toilet and away from him.

His aunt wanted to send the boy to the hospital immediately, but the man dissuaded her because he was scared and worried that he would be arrested, the court heard.

Days later, the woman called the boy’s parents. She brought him to the hospital early the next day, when the boy complained of breathing difficulties and was coughing badly.

Upon arriving at the hospital, he was immediately transferred to the resuscitation room and then the children’s intensive care unit, where he stayed for 15 days.

He suffered from lung injuries caused by blunt force and kidney failure, requiring kidney dialysis for nine days. The kidney failure also resulted in severe hypertension, or high blood pressure, the court heard.

The six-year-old boy also suffered from rhabdomyolysis – a muscle injury where muscles break down – and multiple rib fractures.

An individual who is convicted of voluntarily causing grievous hurt to a person may be punished with a jail term of up to 10 years, a fine and caning. If the victim is below 14 years old, they could face up to twice the maximum punishment.

For ill-treating a child or young person, the man could have been sentenced to up to eight years’ jail, a fine of up to S$8,000 (US$6,200), or both.

For making a false statement in a work pass application, he could have faced up to 12 months’ jail, a fine of S$15,000, or both.

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing calls US tariff report ‘false narrative’ as named hub Mexico plans new China curbs
item.description:
China rejected a White House report on Thursday that accused its exporters of routing goods through Mexico and other countries to avoid US tariffs, hours after word emerged that Mexico was preparing to restrict Chinese products further.

He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, told a regular press briefing in Beijing that the report “ignored facts and distorted reality by treating normal international trade and investment as fraud”.

He called it a “typical exercise in unilateralism and protectionism” intended to “suppress and block Chinese products”, and accused Washington of “blaming external factors for its own economic problems”.
item.content:encoded:
China rejected a White House report on Thursday that accused its exporters of routing goods through Mexico and other countries to avoid US tariffs, hours after word emerged that Mexico was preparing to restrict Chinese products further.

He Yadong, a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce, told a regular press briefing in Beijing that the report “ignored facts and distorted reality by treating normal international trade and investment as fraud”.

He called it a “typical exercise in unilateralism and protectionism” intended to “suppress and block Chinese products”, and accused Washington of “blaming external factors for its own economic problems”.

“The high differentiated tariffs imposed by the United States are the real cause threatening the security of global supply chains,” He said.

The spokesman demanded an immediate end to what he called irresponsible accusations and said China would keep developing commercial cooperation with all parties on the basis of equality and mutual benefit.

The report puts the annual value of the trade anywhere between US$40 billion and US$303 billion.

Its estimates of 450,000 American jobs and up to US$150 billion in lost output are presented as model-based illustrations, although the text concedes that the shift in US import sourcing after 2018 does not prove all displaced Chinese trade was illegally diverted.

Beijing’s protest comes as the country the report names as the biggest conduit has said nothing in its own defence, while the largest foreign investors in Mexico press the government to act on the accusation rather than dispute it.

The Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, the White House unit run by trade adviser Peter Navarro, released the 25-page document a week ago under the title “The Great Transshipment Scam”.

It named more than 40 countries it said carried elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Mexico sits in the top tier of risk, alongside Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, a group where the report says the risk is embedded within broad and otherwise legitimate trade flows.

Chinese exporters conceal the true origin of their goods by carrying out sewing, labelling, packaging or inspection work in third countries, the document alleges, naming Mexico, Canada and several in Southeast Asia among the places used to benefit from more favourable terms with the US.

Mexico is ranked among three leading hubs worldwide, along with India and Vietnam, through which the US Commerce Department traced a combined US$67 billion in Chinese goods into the American market last year.

The publication added to friction over semiconductors, artificial intelligence and rare earths ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned state visit to Washington on September 24.

The trip will be the first meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump on American soil since Trump returned to office.

Mexico under pressure to widen tariffs on Chinese goods

Meanwhile, Mexico plans to restrict selected Chinese goods and raise duties already in place, Bloomberg reported on Thursday.

Mexican officials have discussed the idea with Washington and have yet to settle on how far to go, two people familiar with the talks told the South China Morning Post, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.

Neither knew whether the measure would come by decree or through Congress.

Steelmakers, textile and apparel producers and heavy vehicle manufacturers have pushed for the measures, arguing that dumping is damaging domestic output and employment.

Washington has asked Mexico City to adopt tariffs mirroring those it applies to Chinese steel and aluminium under Section 232, with the aim of building a common tariff policy for North America.

The request comes as the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) is under way, after Washington declined an automatic extension.

Mexico already taxes many of those goods under a package Congress approved in December.

The measure took effect on January 1 and applies duties of between 5 and 50 per cent to 1,463 products from countries without trade agreements with Mexico, among them China, India, South Korea, Indonesia, Brazil and Turkey.

Seventeen sectors are covered, including textiles, footwear, steel, aluminium, plastics, cars, auto parts and household appliances.

Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard said at the time that the package was designed to protect 350,000 Mexican jobs and would add about 0.2 per cent to inflation.

President Claudia Sheinbaum framed the measure as country-neutral when it was approved. The duties applied to states with which Mexico had no trade agreement and are not aimed at restricting trade between nations, she said. Ebrard said Mexico was not taxing goods because of where they were made.

A Section 232 mirror would name China in the text of the measure and set the US rate as its reference point, ending that neutrality.

Beijing responded to the December package by urging Mexico to correct what it called “erroneous practices of unilateralism and protectionism” as soon as possible, and said an investigation it opened in September 2025 into trade and investment barriers in Mexico remained under way with no conclusion announced.

American businesses operating in Mexico have urged the government to move first rather than contest the accusation.

The American Society of Mexico, a group representing US companies and citizens in the country whose honorary president is the US ambassador, said on Wednesday that Mexico should raise traceability and demonstrate with data where value is actually created.

Larry Rubin, who leads the organisation, said the main risk was not individual cases of triangulation but the absence of verification mechanisms robust enough to stop suspicion spreading to entire manufacturing sectors.

“Mexico has to reach the USMCA review with clean hands and open data,” Rubin said.

Traceability, information-sharing and origin verification mechanisms for sensitive sectors should be built with the US and Canada, the group said, without turning them into obstacles for legitimate supply chains.

It also argued that Mexican export growth could not be explained by an equivalent rise in goods arriving from China.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry and the Chinese embassy in Mexico City did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: [SCMP] Live-streamed Philippine school shooting raises alarm over ‘memetic violence’
item.description:
A deadly school attack in the southern Philippines is drawing scrutiny as part of an apparent regional pattern of youth violence that echoes the staging, symbolism and online spectacle of mass shootings overseas.

Authorities are investigating whether the incident in Zamboanga, in which a student reportedly broadcast parts of the attack online, was influenced by exposure to digital media, while analysts said the case underscored the risk of “memetic violence” – in which past atrocities are glorified online and recast as scripts for imitation.

The attack took place on Tuesday morning at the junior high school campus of the privately run Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City, where police said a student brought weapons onto campus, opened fire inside a classroom and killed a fellow student. Investigators are still examining the sequence of events and the student’s motive.
item.content:encoded:
A deadly school attack in the southern Philippines is drawing scrutiny as part of an apparent regional pattern of youth violence that echoes the staging, symbolism and online spectacle of mass shootings overseas.

Authorities are investigating whether the incident in Zamboanga, in which a student reportedly broadcast parts of the attack online, was influenced by exposure to digital media, while analysts said the case underscored the risk of “memetic violence” – in which past atrocities are glorified online and recast as scripts for imitation.

The attack took place on Tuesday morning at the junior high school campus of the privately run Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City, where police said a student brought weapons onto campus, opened fire inside a classroom and killed a fellow student. Investigators are still examining the sequence of events and the student’s motive.

Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso said in a radio interview on DZBB that the student had live-streamed the attack through a body-worn camera. Olaso also said that the gunman shot at a teacher and a Grade 10 student before taking his own life.

The shooter’s father, a customs police officer, was relieved of his duties after the attack as investigators looked into reports that the firearms used belonged to him.

The attack occurred a little over a week after a 14-year-old in Thailand killed seven people in a rampage that began at home and continued at a public school on the outskirts of Bangkok.

It also came less than two months after two students opened fire at a public high school in Tacloban City in the central Philippines in June, killing at least three students and injuring 20 others.

School shootings remain rare in the Philippines, where gun ownership is regulated, although illegal firearms remain in wide circulation.

For analysts, the recent attacks are troubling less because they point to a single ideology than because they suggest a shared grammar of violence in which young perpetrators appear conscious of how their actions will be seen, shared and remembered.

These incidents shared characteristics such as “meticulous premeditation, a deliberate attention to aesthetics and presentation and a drive for notoriety through mass violence,” said Saddiq Basha, a senior analyst at the International Centre for Political Violence and Terrorism Research at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

The pattern had been emerging “since at least last year, probably earlier,” said Munira Mustaffa, a Kuala Lumpur-based security analyst who heads Chasseur Group and previously worked in counterterrorism roles in Malaysia’s government and military sectors.

Mustaffa said what had changed was that the last three attacks in the Philippines and Thailand were completed instead of being disrupted, “which is what has finally made it visible”.

“Authorities and observers have been slow to connect them because the modality differs each time, and that is complicated by the perpetrators’ very young age,” she added.

Beyond blaming games

The Zamboanga attack has brought renewed focus to whether children in the Philippines are being drawn into harmful online subcultures through gaming platforms or adjacent chat spaces after similar concerns were raised following the Tacloban school shooting.

Officials have been examining whether such cases bear the imprint of nihilistic violent extremism (NVE) – a loose term for online subcultures that glorify destruction, cruelty, mass violence or self-harm – but experts said the label should not be applied to the Zamboanga case without stronger evidence.

In a television interview with ANC, Olaso characterised the shooter as a “very bright student” but noted that he was a “Roblox fanatic”, referring to the popular online gaming platform that has faced scrutiny over concerns involving child safety, grooming and extremist content in connected online spaces.

Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that although authorities had yet to conduct a forensic examination on the shooter’s electronic devices, they had a “great degree of confidence” that Roblox had influenced the shooter’s actions.

“Roblox in itself is not a dangerous game. It is the chat group that is beside it, that is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place,” he said at a briefing on Wednesday.

Authorities had previously looked into online games as a potential pathway for radicalisation during the Tacloban attack in June, while officials also examined suspicions that the Tacloban shooters were influenced by 764, a nihilistic violent extremist network accused of targeting vulnerable children online.

At a congressional hearing, Senator Risa Hontiveros also cited a photo of one Tacloban suspect wearing a KMFDM shirt – a reference associated with the 1999 Columbine High School shooting in the US – as among the signs investigators were examining.

“It is very difficult to accept that our country must face another school shooting,” Hontiveros said in a statement on Tuesday.

“For now, we cannot say whether this incident is connected to nihilistic violent extremism or other similar online communities that we have started to investigate following the Tacloban shooting,” she added.

Observers said social media could play a role in shaping such incidents but could not by itself explain why a young person would choose to attack a school.

“Social media does play a role, in the sense that it can expose individuals to the aesthetics and call-to-action of Western perpetrators of mass violence, especially amplified within the online echo-chambers of like-minded individuals,” Basha said.

“Yet, online exposure alone is insufficient to account for such acts, and we have to consider factors such as the grievances formed offline.”

The fact that the Zamboanga incident was live-streamed has drawn comparisons with earlier attacks designed to reach an online audience, such as the 2019 Christchurch mosque attack, though experts said the available evidence did not establish a direct ideological or subcultural link.

“Until we know what exactly he was exposed to online, consumed or inspired by, it is difficult to make conclusive statements,” Mustaffa said, adding that the shooter’s body camera indicated “the attack was built to be watched and the attacker intended to have an audience.”

“Aside from the premeditated act of live-streaming … there are currently no concrete indications that the perpetrator of the Zamboanga mass shooting was influenced by any specific violent online subculture, though I would not be surprised if he was,” Basha said, adding that any attempt to tie him to one at this point would be speculative.

Mustaffa said gaming platforms such as Roblox were more accurately understood as possible venues for radicalisation, not causes.

“The games aren’t what radicalising them, it’s the socialising or bonding that took place during the co-op, and there’s always a risk of grooming during those interactive sessions. The Zamboanga attack was likely animated by the attacker’s own grievance, and personal grievance is the one persistent element across the attacks in the region so far,” she said.

Basha said that while authorities might look for adult groomers influencing young perpetrators, as in the Tacloban case, they should not overlook the possibility of “peer-to-peer, horizontal grooming between youths within these online communities”.

As authorities in the Philippines, Thailand and across the region adapt to the recent cluster of attacks, Mustaffa warned against reaching for “simple explanations like blaming games, or building a narrative around the perpetrator’s bullying or personal struggles. Those things may well be part of the picture, but they don’t explain the decision to attack, and treating them as an explanation makes the next case more likely.”

“Turning schools into fortresses won’t help, and it isn’t practical … What’s needed is a networked effort across parents, schools, law enforcement, and platforms, and the first task is working out what that looks like in practice,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia fears military ‘miscalculation’ near Sabah amid US-China rivalry
item.description:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.

“When you have more military assets operating within a relatively confined geographical space, the possibility of miscalculation, misunderstanding or even a small incident escalating into something more serious naturally increases,” he said.

“Geographic proximity is therefore an important consideration for us,” Khaled added. “Even if an incident does not directly involve Malaysia, any escalation in areas close to us could have wider implications for our security and for stability in the South China Sea.”
