Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.

Observers said such moves threatened to damage alliance coordination, causing disquiet among regional partners and handing China a strategic opening to dilute America’s network of regional partnerships.

Trump posted on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to scale back what he termed “inappropriate and hostile” military drills with South Korea – exercises traditionally aimed at deterring North Korea, a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful” during his time in office.

He added that he had ordered the US defence secretary to “substantially reduce” the drills, citing Seoul’s reluctance to support America’s efforts towards the “denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

As Seoul and other US partners navigate the latest shocks, Wang will begin a two-day trip to Seoul on Wednesday, his first bilateral exchange trip in five years.

Trump’s call for reduced commitment came just hours before Washington and Seoul launched the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield drills, one of the two major annual exercises.

Lee Dong-gyu, a senior research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said Trump’s statements revealed his willingness to trade alliance security for political gains, such as re-engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a calculation Lee said would increase Seoul’s trust deficit in its alliance with Washington.

William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said the statement matched Trump’s usual playbook of signalling frustration towards allies he viewed as failing to respond to US demands for support.

“While the order may be a tactical move from the US, it could undermine long-standing trust between the two countries and prompt Seoul to put more resources into hedging between Beijing and Washington,” he said.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, said that curtailing joint manoeuvres risked undermining operational coordination and weakening deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia.

Experts noted that the latest remarks would unnerve regional partners such as the Philippines and Japan, saying their frictions with China left them particularly exposed.

Trump has regularly criticised US allies during his second term, intensifying concerns over the reliability of Washington’s commitments and pushing partners towards self-reliance and strategic hedging.

However, in a sign of reassurance, the US undersecretary of defence for policy, Elbridge Colby, used his first Southeast Asia tour last week to stress that Washington was not disengaging from Asia but “digging in” to maintain a favourable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific.

But he added that Washington was prioritising burden-sharing as it realised its allies “can and are prepared to do more”.

According to Yang, Washington’s allies will bear in mind the more transactional foreign policy outlook that Trump subscribes to and try to respond to demands from Washington.

Meanwhile, Lee noted that Beijing was likely to exploit the scaled-back exercises as a tool, seeking to constrain Seoul’s participation in the US alliance network and diminish America’s military footprint in the region.

“At the same time, leveraging its friendly ties with Pyongyang, China is likely to intensify both its appeasement and pressure on South Korea under the pretext of fostering a favourable environment for US-North Korea dialogue,” Lee said.

Trump’s directive has sparked anticipation of his renewed engagement with Kim, although it remains uncertain whether the North Korean leader will reciprocate – particularly as Pyongyang appears to hold more cards than at the last summits with Trump in 2018 and 2019.

Following his summit with Kim in Singapore in June 2018, Trump abruptly suspended major joint military exercises with South Korea, calling them provocative, inappropriate and too expensive.

But since the collapse of high-level diplomacy in 2019, Pyongyang has aggressively expanded its missile tests and gained more battlefield experience by sending its soldiers to take part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Lee Choong-koo, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, said Trump’s directive was part of a broader US diplomatic charm offensive towards North Korea – one that might require China’s cooperation.

Seoul has long expected Beijing to play a role in bringing Pyongyang back to the negotiation table, as Pyongyang neglects Seoul’s repeated calls to improve inter-Korean relations.

“His move may encourage greater diplomatic engagement between the US and China on North Korea,” Lee Choong-koo said, adding that Beijing might welcome Trump’s announcement.

“With Foreign Minister Wang Yi expected to visit Seoul this week, China may emphasise that its support is essential to advancing South Korea’s diplomatic initiative to launch multilateral peace talks.”

On Monday, Trump told reporters that Kim had responded to his recent overtures and described the current state of communication as “very positive”. Kim has not yet commented publicly.

Easley, however, offered a more sceptical assessment. He argued that Pyongyang was not interested in talking because it was profiting from Russia’s war on Ukraine while modernising its own military.

“The Trump administration’s ongoing difficulties negotiating with Iran do not enhance its credibility with the Kim regime.”

Meanwhile, some observers pointed out that Trump’s announcement could further weaken US-led deterrence against China – a development that might work in Beijing’s favour.

The mismatch between US strategic documents on defending the first island chain and Trump’s decision on joint drills with South Korea would strengthen regional countries’ belief that they needed to adopt risk-reduction measures against the US, Yang said.

“This trend will benefit China, as it creates an opportunity for Beijing to drive a wedge between the US and its regional allies.”

The first island chain consists of several strategic arcs – stretching from Japan and Taiwan through the Philippines to Borneo – that underpin a US-aligned security architecture to check Beijing.

Although traditionally not viewed as part of the chain, South Korea, now hosting some 28,500 US troops under a decades-old alliance, is increasingly seen as the northern anchor of the chain’s defence network.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s universities race to embrace AI as job demands transform
item.description:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.
item.content:encoded:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.

The platform would be piloted in selected courses during the initial phase and be progressively made available for other courses where AI “adds educational value and augments learning objectives”, the university said in a statement.

Other universities are also expanding the use of the technology, with many mandating AI literacy courses.

Starting this month, students at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) were given full access to a suite of Google AI tools, including Gemini Enterprise, as part of what the institution coined an “ambitious effort to transform its undergraduate education with AI”.

The university aimed to embed AI into 40 per cent of its courses by 2030, to reach its goal of producing students who could create and work with AI agents, it said.

“So much is happening so quickly with AI, and universities are playing catch up,” said Reuben Ng, an associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

There was a huge skills gap in the employment market, with many job notices requiring AI skills left unfilled, he said. “One of the key purposes of Singapore’s universities is to funnel people towards the job market, so they need to create students that have these skill sets.”

Vijayakumar Tangarasan, International Workplace Group’s country head for Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei, said most local employers were willing to “pay a premium” for AI literacy, and academic qualifications alone were no longer the focus.

“Singapore’s modern workforce demands a symbiotic combination of technological literacy and irreplaceable human qualities,” he said, highlighting the importance of technological and human skills.

“As AI becomes increasingly embedded in our daily workflows, the traditional checklist for talent is being rewritten.”

AI paradox

While critics in the education field have long worried that generative technology is eroding critical thinking, Singapore’s universities seem to have a change of heart on AI.

Aaron Thean, NUS’s deputy president of academic affairs and provost, said the institution aimed to use the tools not as replacements, but as “powerful amplifiers of human intellect, creativity and judgement”.

While the goals set out are achievable, whether AI proves a boon or bane largely depends on how it is used, according to educational experts.

If a student were to accept the first output from the prompt, the tool would become a substitute for thinking, said Ina Conradi Chavez, an associate professor at NTU’s School of Art, Design and Media. But if students were to reject, re-prompt and critique, the technology would help refine thinking, she added.

Still, Conradi highlighted several risks, such as the inability to discern AI-generated content from authorship and the acceptance of visually plausible but incorrect output.

Mutlu Cukurova, the 18th CJ Koh professor at NTU’s National Institute of Education, acknowledged that current evidence showed the technology posed more harm, potentially leading to stagnant and declining competency levels. Recent research also found that it reduced persistence, with students instinctively turning to AI to solve difficult problems, he added.

But Cukurova said AI could have a positive impact if the system were built to ask, rather than answer or solve. “Intellect, creativity and critical thinking are not by-products of access to capable tools, but outcomes of deliberate design.”

Conradi urged institutions to teach students to use AI to examine bias and train data, rather than primarily for generative or interpretive purposes. “Students who only use AI generatively will be replaced by the next generation of tools and those who learn to interrogate AI critically will not.”

She highlighted that not all AI-assisted works should be put in the same box, noting the difference in user effort between continuously refining prompts and accepting the first output.

“Public conversation collapses everything into a single category called ‘AI art’ or ‘AI use’. That framing does real damage,” she said. “The paradox is real, but often framed the wrong way.”

Evolving assessments

With chatbots producing polished essays and high-definition visuals within seconds, concerns about plagiarism and integrity have also surged.

Last year, three NTU students were penalised for academic misconduct and given zero marks for an assignment after they were found to have used generative AI tools. Their assignments had contained non-existent academic references and statistics or broken web links.

Surveillance and detection were a “losing battle”, said Curukova, who is also a professor of learning and AI at University College London.

He urged institutions to design tasks that would require students to interact with and evaluate AI and its output. “A graduate who can prompt well but cannot judge when the output is wrong, or when the task should not have been delegated at all, is not AI-competent,” he said.

NTU will be moving away from automated surveillance to assessment designs that evaluate student learning, according to local media, citing an email from the institution to its faculty last Thursday.

Recognising that the detection tools used currently were “fundamentally unreliable”, the university said it would stop using them next year.

Conradi has already shifted her assessment focus. She now evaluates her students based on documentation and oral explanations, rather than the final product alone. Her students are asked to present their works on screens or at exhibitions, and she studies how they adapt conversations about their submissions to different audiences.

She also requires students to detail their use of AI, including exact prompts, rejections and reasoning behind each input.

“Assessment built around the finished artefact alone is increasingly meaningless,” she said. “The principle is now to assess the practice, not just the product.”

Ng noted that AI had sparked a return to the pen-and-paper format in physical settings, a method which he had adopted with his students.

“There needs to be a space where people do deep thinking and work, such as journaling with a pen and paper, debating or reflecting,” he said. “We need protected time for these things which cannot be replaced by technology.”

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s decision to scale back South Korea drills unsettles Asian allies: ‘makes no sense’
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”

Trump’s decision to side with North Korea, which strongly objects to the annual joint military exercises, was “firmly in the ‘hard-to see-how-it-could-be-worse’ category”, said Danny Russel, former assistant secretary of state for East Asia and the Pacific in Barack Obama’s administration.

Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary

Danny Russel, a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute

“It is tragically upside-down. Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary,” said Russel, now a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “He is protecting Kim Jong-un’s sensitive feelings from an unfriendly signal at the expense of US-South Korean security.”

Trump on Sunday ordered the US military to downsize the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which began on Monday as scheduled. It is not known which parts of the training are being scaled back.

His announcement baffled many in South Korea, which has been closely allied with the US for decades and where national security is a top priority due to threats from nuclear-armed North Korea.

It also drew instant criticism from many Democrats in Congress. “Treating one of America’s closest allies like an adversary weakens our alliances and benefits China and North Korea,” Representative Greg Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tuesday Tokyo strongly supported joint security cooperation with key defence backer Washington and neighbour Seoul.

“As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region,” Koizumi said during a visit to Australia.

His Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, said Canberra was “very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear programme as well as its missile programme, and we have consistently made that point”.

South Korean officials have said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks. Seoul’s presidential office said on Tuesday the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean peninsula”.

Its unification ministry – responsible for relations with the North – said it could not confirm whether communications between Kim and Trump had taken place. “While communication channels between the two sides exist, we cannot verify the specific content of the exchanges,” it said.

‘Great respect’

Trump on Monday doubled down, posting a photo of North Korea’s leader speaking on a phone. The caption read: “Hey Donald … We cool, right?”

Asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Monday if Kim had replied to entreaties for talks, Trump said “he has”, without elaborating. The president called the development “very positive”. The White House declined to provide further details.

“Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” Trump said. “I understand him; he understands me.”

Retired US Ambassador Robert Wood, who served under Republican and Democratic presidents, said the joint military exercises were critical to deterring North Korea, which has shunned any talks with the US over its nuclear programme and has accelerated weapons testing.

“We also don’t want South Korea to draw the conclusion that a nuclear weapons capability is the only guarantee it has to ensure its security,” Wood said.

Matthew Kroenig, who previously served in defence and intelligence positions in Republican and Democratic administrations, said polls show that South Koreans had increasingly supported the idea of pursuing their own nuclear weapons.

“The United States has been working really hard to try to persuade South Korea that they are protected,” said Kroenig, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank. Scaling back the exercises “potentially undermines that message”.

Trump’s turnabout came even after the South Koreans worked to flatter the American president, eager to gain favour on critical issues such as trade and defence.

As soon as he sat down for his meeting with Trump last year, new President Lee Jae Myung praised the Oval Office’s elaborate decor. Laying it on thick, Lee affirmed Trump’s assertion that Kim would not have pursued his nuclear ambitions had Trump won a second consecutive term in 2020, while dangling the prospect of an eventual Trump Tower in North Korea.

Trump just hours earlier had appeared to show sympathy for Lee’s predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol, who had been ousted from office after imposing martial law in December 2024.

On Tuesday, Lee’s office said the Ulchi exercise was defensive and not intended to attack the North or raise tensions.

Removing umbrella

Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Trump’s scaling back of the exercises might prompt long-time allies to think more about their own security without US help.

“They are hoping that the American umbrella is there for the future,” said Kupchan, who worked on the National Security Council under Democratic presidents Bill Clinton and Obama, “but they have to at least contemplate the idea that Uncle Sam won’t be there for them”.

Kupchan said Trump was not mistaken in wanting to have South Korea, as well as the Europeans, contribute more to their defence. But, he said, the president’s unpredictable approach cut through the solidarity that undergirded those alliances “because he ends up insulting allies”.

Fried said Trump seemed unwilling to “take a win” after browbeating Nato members and Asian allies into increasing their defence spending.

“Nato is building up, South Korea is building up, Japan is building up. Trump has a problem with taking the win,” said Fried, who is currently at the Atlantic Council. “It’s like he wants to burn it all down.”

John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under president George W. Bush, said the Korea decision showed how inconsistent the Trump administration could be in its policy pronouncements. But in general, he said, the US had maintained long-term alliances.

“If these things grow in frequency and in importance, obviously we will be in the process of taking apart the alliance system, which has served us so well since the end of World War II,” said Herbst, who also is with the Atlantic Council. “But despite some statements which seem to head in that direction, we have not headed there in a consistent, strong way.”

Kupchan agreed. While the president’s language could be taken as “we’re done with you”, he said, “the reality is that, at least as of today, Trump has left intact America’s forward bases and its core alliance relationships”.

Whether Trump’s message to South Korea will amount to a meaningful policy change or a fleeting social media post is up in the air.

“He’s an unpredictable president,” Kroenig said. “If we move on and the exercises go as planned and we never hear anything about this again, I wouldn’t be surprised.”

Additional reporting by Bloomberg, Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] Can Indonesia build on rising EV demand to become a production powerhouse?
item.description:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.

The event launched what Prabowo and the government described as a “national electric-motorcycle ecosystem”, with a government release saying the initiative would include lower instalment rates and zero down payments.

Prabowo also said Indonesia aimed to begin mass production of home-grown electric cars no later than 2028.

The bigger test will come with a separate EV stimulus package, which officials have said will be announced shortly and is expected to set the rules for which vehicles, battery types and local producers receive support.

In his 2027 budget address on Friday, Prabowo linked those consumer incentives to industrial policy, promising support for domestic electric-motorcycle production and outlining plans for a wider supply chain covering batteries, components, software and after-sales services.

“Electric motorcycle subsidies and probably later electric cars will create markets for the national industry,” Prabowo said.

The key question is how far the eligibility rules will support local factories, component suppliers, battery production, technology transfer and jobs, rather than only reducing the cost of vehicles already on the market.

Earlier this month, officials said the stimulus would cover about 500,000 electric motorbikes and focus on products creating high value in Indonesia, but domestic-content (TKDN) requirements were still being finalised.

Purchasing incentives

The incentives being considered include a full exemption from the luxury goods sales tax and a government-borne value added tax incentive of 40 per cent for eligible models.

The relief would apply strictly to battery EVs, excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrid types. Battery composition was also confirmed as a criterion, with officials weighing whether to favour nickel-based batteries over other chemistries.

The Association of Indonesia Automotive Industries (Gaikindo) recorded sales of 69,739 battery EV units in the first half of 2026, an 80.8 per cent year-on-year increase for the category.

A July 15 report by Detikoto, an Indonesian car news portal, based on Gaikindo sales data, showed the top five brands dominating the national EV market were BYD at 30.73 per cent, followed by Jaecoo at 24.36 per cent, then Geely, Wuling and GAC Aion.

These figures indicate a rapidly expanding market where consumer incentives could play a decisive role.

In May, the Indonesian Business Council said electric motorcycle sales exceeded 100,000 units in 2024 for the first time but fell to 55,059 the next year after the previous subsidy programme – at 7 million rupiah (US$393) per unit – ended.

“This shows that public interest is growing, but affordability remains a key factor in consumer decisions,” the council said.

Missing segments

For analysts, the bigger question is whether fresh incentives can draw more production into Indonesia, rather than simply accelerate sales in a market still led by foreign brands.

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, said Indonesia had developed nickel processing at one end of the chain and vehicle assembly at the other without building enough of the stages between them.

“There is a hollow in the middle of the whole nickel supply chain,” Bhima said.

The entry of Chinese carmakers expanded the Indonesian market but had not yet been sufficiently connected to other parts of the country’s industrial ecosystem, he added. “We are just the market. We are not the producers that gain more value-added from this EV penetration.”

Bhima said much of the new vehicle investment concentrated in assembly, while EV and battery investment was capital-intensive and had a lower employment multiplier than Indonesia’s established automotive industry and its network of component makers and service businesses.

Indonesia does have vehicle and battery manufacturing projects in the works, including Hyundai and Wuling electric-car plants in Cikarang, HLI Green Power’s battery-cell facility in Karawang and planned ventures involving Indonesia Battery Corporation, CATL, Antam and a Chinese group led by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt.

But analysts said the existence of large projects did not show whether Indonesia was creating enough local suppliers, skilled jobs or technology transfer across the middle of the supply chain.

There is also a battery-chemistry question.

Bhima said many Chinese EVs entering Indonesia used lithium iron phosphate batteries and other chemistries, rather than nickel-based ones, meaning the technology did not match Indonesia’s nickel-based strategy.

Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said earlier this month the government was considering differentiated incentives for nickel-based compositions, such as nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries.

Siwage Dharma Negara, a senior fellow and co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said the proposed stimulus should be understood in two stages.

“The short-term objective is basically to reduce fuel-subsidy consumption. To promote the industry, it is going to take some time,” Siwage said.

Large investment figures, he said, did not by themselves show how many jobs or domestic suppliers would be created because mineral-processing and battery projects were capital-intensive and did not need such a large workforce.

That puts more weight on TKDN regulations, which are meant to push carmakers towards local sourcing.

Currently, locally produced electric cars must reach a minimum of 40 per cent TKDN through 2026, 60 per cent from 2027 to 2029 and 80 per cent from 2030 onwards, according to a Gaikindo summary of the regulations.

Siwage said enforcement could end up being “more flexible” if companies failed to meet commitments and the government worried about losing investment, tax revenue or employment. “The goalposts keep moving. They try to make it more flexible, and of course that makes it less credible.”

Indonesia’s approach contrasts with Thailand’s EV3.5 plan, which uses escalating production obligations requiring manufacturers to build two domestic units for every imported EV in 2026 and three in 2027.

“Thailand has greater bargaining power because it offers an established supplier network, supporting infrastructure and a mature automotive cluster. Thailand has also become a production hub for hybrid vehicles,” Siwage said.

Bhima also pointed to Vietnam, which offered workforce capability, greater policy certainty and simpler bureaucracy.

“Without a more integrated industrial policy,” he said, “Indonesia risks remaining a large consumer market, or a supplier of raw or processed materials, rather than developing the middle of the EV supply chain.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Siberia’s warming landscape could shatter Trump’s Arctic ambitions
item.description:
As the United States, Russia and China race to turn a melting Arctic into the world’s next major economic gateway, their strategic ambitions face a hidden threat: thawing permafrost.

Since returning to office last year, US President Donald Trump has pushed to expand America’s Arctic footprint. This includes investing in icebreakers to counter Russian and Chinese shipping ambitions, unlocking natural resources in Alaska and renewing efforts to buy or annex Greenland.

Yet, as the three powers vie for control of Arctic sea lanes and minerals, rapidly thawing permafrost in Russia’s Siberia could derail their plans. According to a new international study led by Chinese scientists, the massive cost of collapsing ground threatens to overshadow the region’s economic potential.
item.content:encoded:
As the United States, Russia and China race to turn a melting Arctic into the world’s next major economic gateway, their strategic ambitions face a hidden threat: thawing permafrost.

Since returning to office last year, US President Donald Trump has pushed to expand America’s Arctic footprint. This includes investing in icebreakers to counter Russian and Chinese shipping ambitions, unlocking natural resources in Alaska and renewing efforts to buy or annex Greenland.

Yet, as the three powers vie for control of Arctic sea lanes and minerals, rapidly thawing permafrost in Russia’s Siberia could derail their plans. According to a new international study led by Chinese scientists, the massive cost of collapsing ground threatens to overshadow the region’s economic potential.

Warming in the Arctic is occurring almost four times faster than the global average. This phenomenon, known as Arctic amplification, has triggered a rapid thaw of the permafrost that covers most of the region.

Permafrost refers to the ground in cold regions that has stayed at a temperature below 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) for at least two consecutive years, and its melting could release a huge amount of greenhouse gas that pushes temperatures even higher.

Around 46 per cent of the northern hemisphere’s permafrost is in Siberia.

By 2050, higher methane emissions as a result of permafrost thaw and increasing wildfires in Siberia could offset 20 per cent of the global methane reduction required to meet our climate targets, according to the study led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on August 6.

Methane is the second most abundant human-made greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide, but it is more than 28 times more potent at trapping heat in the atmosphere, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

Increasing methane emissions from thawing permafrost could result in a “climate-carbon feedback” loop – a cycle where permafrost degradation releases greenhouse gases that in turn further amplify climate change.

“Global targets to keep global mean temperatures below even 2 degrees Celsius of preindustrial values will be compromised, even if only a fraction of the carbon presently stored in permafrost thaws and is released to the atmosphere,” the team said.

On the ground across the Arctic, the consequences of losing permafrost are already unfolding. This includes land subsidence, landslides, soil volume loss, coastal erosion, and shifting of land from terrestrial to aquatic, because much of the region’s land is bound together by ice.

Thawing permafrost not only alters the natural landscape, but also poses a major threat to human infrastructure, according to a study published in the peer-reviewed journal Polar Science in June last year. Buildings, roads, railways, airports, pipelines, oilfields, and mines are already being affected by the current state of thaw.

By the middle of the century, about 69 per cent of fundamental circumpolar infrastructure, including industrial facilities, is at risk of damage, according to the researchers from Paris-Saclay University, the Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research, and research centre Nordregio.

They found that thawing across the entire Arctic circumpolar permafrost region – across Russia, Canada, Alaska, Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Finland, Sweden and Iceland – could result in tens of billions of dollars in economic losses by mid-century.

Russia, which has both the largest permafrost area and the most infrastructure built on its permafrost, is the most at risk of economic loss. This includes its mining, oil and gas operations, a critical corner of the country’s economy.

Alaska is another region that could face major losses, with permafrost present on about 80 per cent of its land surface.

The Polar Science study said there were advantages to a de-iced Arctic, including reduced heating costs, diminishing sea ice allowing for more marine and coastal development, the expansion of agricultural land and the potential to exploit more local resources.

Russia highlighted some potential positive consequences in a 2020 national action plan for climate change adaptation, including “improved conditions for transporting cargo in the Arctic seas” and greater access to the country’s extended continental shelf.

The icy Northern Sea Route – the shortest passage between the Asia-Pacific and Western Eurasia – is becoming navigable for longer periods each year because of global warming.

As the world witnesses multiple shipping crises, from the Suez Canal to the Strait of Hormuz, the promise of an alternative Arctic sea lane emerging from under the ice has drawn intense interest from Russia, China and the US.

Trump says he wants to acquire Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, for “national security” reasons.

However, some believe his interest in Greenland and the wider Arctic is driven by lucrative, untapped natural resources below the ice, which will become easier to exploit as the region warms.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Greenland is not immune to permafrost thaw, which threatens infrastructure as the ground grows unstable and prone to collapse. Hotter conditions could also create more vegetation and peat fuel for wildfires.

For any mining ambitions in the Arctic, the Red Dog mine in Alaska – one of the largest zinc mines in the world and a major local employer – serves as a cautionary tale.

Thawing permafrost has increased particulate levels in the creek where the mine pumps its treated waste water. As a result, downstream levels have surged above regulatory limits despite no change in the mine’s actual discharge, according to a report by the Alaska Beacon in December.

To resolve the issue, operator Teck Resources may need to spend hundreds of millions of dollars and up to a decade to develop a solution, such as a waste-water pipeline to the ocean.

Last week, Trump withdrew federal support for the Arctic Report Card – an annual report on issues such as changing sea ice and thawing permafrost that NOAA has published for two decades, according to the Alaska Beacon on August 12.

In Russia, fossil fuel producers have spent years adapting to thawing permafrost – taking steps such as driving foundation piles deeper into the ground and investing in technology to keep the ground frozen to avoid disrupting operations.

Thawing permafrost also poses a risk to human health. It can mobilise environmental contaminants like the heavy metal mercury and pathogens such as emerging infectious diseases that would otherwise have remained trapped in ice, according to the Polar Science paper.

In 2016, an anthrax outbreak in northwestern Siberia’s Yamal district that killed more than 2,300 reindeer and resulted in the death of a young boy was linked to the thawing of the bacteria from permafrost, according to Russian news agency Tass.

Another Polar Science paper published in June last year noted that the Russian invasion of Ukraine had made permafrost thaw mitigation more challenging, with Russian-Western joint research suspended and Western scientists denied access to vital Russian monitoring stations.

Data collection is crucial for properly monitoring the permafrost carbon feedback mechanism and anticipating climate tipping points, but this break in collaboration is a “serious blind spot” for the Western scientific community, according to the researchers from UiT The Arctic University of Norway and France’s School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences.

Moscow’s most recent national action plan for climate adaptation, approved in June, targets key challenges including permafrost degradation and infrastructure resilience in thawing regions.

According to the Norway-France team, Russia is supporting the development of a state-run permafrost monitoring system and increasing monitoring infrastructure to measure emissions.

While localised measures such as rewilding and adaptive infrastructure can delay thawing, the consensus among scientists is that curbing global warming is the only viable long-term defence against widespread permafrost thaw.

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji, China’s chief engineer of economic reform and former premier, dies aged 97
item.description:
Former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, who helped engineer one of the greatest economic reforms in human history, died of an illness on Wednesday in Beijing. He was 97.

Zhu, who served as China’s premier from 1998 to 2003, is remembered for shaking up the centrally planned economy, overhauling the state-owned enterprise (SOE) sector and tackling corruption.

He was the mastermind behind negotiations for China’s World Trade Organization (WTO) entry in 2001, which opened China up to the international market and ushered in major changes in the Chinese economy.
item.content:encoded:
Former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, who helped engineer one of the greatest economic reforms in human history, died of an illness on Wednesday in Beijing. He was 97.

Zhu, who served as China’s premier from 1998 to 2003, is remembered for shaking up the centrally planned economy, overhauling the state-owned enterprise (SOE) sector and tackling corruption.

He was the mastermind behind negotiations for China’s World Trade Organization (WTO) entry in 2001, which opened China up to the international market and ushered in major changes in the Chinese economy.

Working under former Communist Party leader Jiang Zemin, Zhu led the modernisation of China’s taxation and financial systems, which were fundamental to economic reform.

Zhu also played a key role in ensuring the smooth handover of Hong Kong in 1997, and led Beijing’s handling of the Asian financial crisis in 1997 and 1998.

In a statement on Wednesday, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu thanked Zhu for his support to the city, while expressing his deepest condolences on his passing.

He said Zhu “had supported Hong Kong in staying united and striving to leverage its strengths amid such challenges as the Asian financial crisis, resolutely upholding the prosperity and stability of Hong Kong as an international financial centre”.

“I am sincerely grateful for his care and support for Hong Kong’s economic and social development over the years,” Lee said.

“He had visited Hong Kong on multiple occasions in his different positions, reaching out to Hong Kong people from all walks of life.”

Economist Lawrence Lau Juen-yee, former vice-chancellor and president of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said Zhu had realised the devaluation of the Chinese currency “would not only not improve the situation for China but would make things worse for everyone else”.

“He therefore decided to hold the renminbi exchange rate steady and engage in other expansionary measures such as a full refund of value-added taxes upon exporting of Chinese goods. It worked.”

“He was also committed to help Hong Kong through the crisis and had contingency plans in place. Fortunately, the collapse of Long-Term Capital Management and the drying up of credits for hedge funds targeting Hong Kong made the contingency plans unnecessary,” he said.

Zhu’s last public appearance was in October 2018 in Beijing, when he met members of the Advisory Board of the School of Economics and Management at Tsinghua University.

The meeting was attended by former US Treasury secretary Henry Paulson, Apple CEO Tim Cook and Ginni Rometty, CEO of IBM at the time.

The official obituary released by state news agency Xinhua on Wednesday described Zhu as “an outstanding member of the Communist Party, a long-tested and loyal Communist fighter, an outstanding proletarian revolutionary and statesman, and an exceptional leader of the party and the state”.

It credits him with helping the country navigate through the immense impact of the Asian financial crisis and “resolutely safeguard the prosperity and stability of Hong Kong as an international financial centre”.

It also noted that he had shifted to proactive fiscal and monetary policies to maintain stable and rapid economic growth.

The official obituary highlighted Zhu’s role in advancing economic system reform, pointing to his overhaul of state-owned enterprises, where he prioritised clearer property rights and the separation of government functions from business operations.

The statement also shed light on his instrumental work in leading the “arduous negotiations” that secured China’s entry into the WTO, a move that reshaped the country’s integration into the global economy.

Paul Triolo, partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, recalled meeting Zhu while working at the US embassy in Beijing from 1995 to 1997.

“Zhu was a unique Chinese government figure at the time – articulate, urbane, able to discuss complex economic issues with ease with Western officials and businessmen,” Triolo said.

He said Zhu’s interactions with figures such as economists Joseph Stiglitz and Alan Greenspan marked a rare period when a senior Chinese leader was able to have a “real give and take” with Western leaders on topics of global importance.

Denis Simon, former vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, said Zhu “used Western pressures to achieve deeper reforms that would have been hard to accomplish without a major external push”. Simon, who teaches at Tsinghua University’s Schwarzman College, met Zhu in New York in 1990.

He said these achievements had paved the way for China’s economic surge, though at a serious social cost, including tens of millions of displaced state-sector workers across old industrial hubs.

“China today may need Zhu’s candour, technical competence and willingness to confront vested interests, but it cannot simply reproduce his late-1990s strategy,” he said.

“The current challenge requires not only reducing excess capacity, but also strengthening household demand, rebuilding the social safety net and changing the incentives that currently encourage local governments and firms continually to overinvest.”

Pascal Lamy, director general of the WTO from 2005 to 2013, said, “I have always kept an immense consideration and respect for Premier Zhu Rongji, who will remain in history on the podium of China’s modernisers.”

“The way he handled China’s accession to the WTO was a masterful lesson in geopolitics and geoeconomics,” he said.

Following his retirement from the premiership in March 2003, Zhu continued to support central authorities under the leadership of Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, according to the obituary.

“He remained concerned about the great cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics and firmly supported the building of party conduct and integrity and the fight against corruption,” it said.

It added that Zhu had “deep affection for the public, stressing that government workers must act as public servants, dare to speak the truth, not be afraid of offending people, not seek special privileges, take on heavy responsibilities and tackle tough issues responsibly and deliver practical results”.

When Zhu became premier in 1998, he set up and led the National Science, Technology and Education Leading Group to promote the close integration of science, education and the economy to boost national prosperity, according to a 2013 story published by Economic Information Daily.

In the 1990s, when China’s high inflation, mounting debt and SOE losses threatened financial stability, Zhu targeted the risks by centralising fiscal policy, cutting red tape and closing or privatising failing enterprises.

Zhu was “the true founder of China’s socialist market economy”, said Wang Dan, China director at Eurasia Group.

“Subsequent reforms of similar depth have been absent from China; subsequent policies have essentially been reinforcements of the reforms he spearheaded in the 1990s,” she said.

Wednesday’s official obituary praised him for promoting the re-employment of laid-off and unemployed workers and strengthening the social security system.

Born in 1928 in Changsha, the capital of the central province of Hunan, Zhu graduated from Tsinghua University in 1951 with a degree in electrical engineering and joined the civil service, working on regional and national economic policy.

He served as vice-premier in charge of China’s economy between 1991 and 1998 before taking on the role of premier.

Additional reporting by Dannie Peng, Ji Siqi and Xiaofei Xu

item.title: [SCMP] Wok with Yan’s return: Hong Kong-Canadian TV chef Stephen Yan resurfaces decades after disappearing
item.description:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.
item.content:encoded:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.

“When [Polo] went back to Italy, he learned how to make it all right,” says Yan to the camera, in his Cantonese-inflected English, “but he changed the name chow mein to spaghetti and changed wonton to ravioli. Wok the heck, I’m going to make one thing perfectly clear: I want to make this thing right and correct. I don’t want to make it the wrong way. I want to make it the Yan way.”

Once Yan had plated a dish, he’d invite someone from the audience to dine with him, and, this being Canada in the 1980s, they would not all be proficient with chopsticks. Yan would open a fortune cookie, translate the Chinese message inside and then, as the credits rolled, the rest of the studio audience would make sure no food went to waste.

With the coast-to-coast-to-coast reach of the CBC, Yan became a national figure and arguably the first Asian celebrity television chef in the West.

“I watched [Yan] with my grandparents because, back then, your house had one TV,” says Karon Liu, who was only a few months old when his family moved to Toronto in 1987, one of more than 355,600 Hongkongers who moved to Canada in the late 80s, according to the Canadian International Council. “So, what they watched, you had to watch,” says Liu, who is now a food reporter with the Toronto Star newspaper. He remembers his grandmother hollowing out a cucumber and filling it with stir-fried beef, making it look like a boat, because that’s what Stephen Yan did in one episode.

“He was the Chinese Julia Child. He wasn’t some snooty Michelin French chef; he cooked the way my grandmother would cook at home,” says Liu. “He explained a lot of ingredients that weren’t as well known outside of a Chinese audience at that time.”

While Chinese-Canadians delighted in Yan’s familiarity, other Canadians were learning that Chinese food was not just egg foo yung or sweet and sour chicken balls, a step towards the multiculturalism the country would more fully embrace. But then one day in 1995, after more than 500 episodes, Wok with Yan ended, and the chef was not seen on television or in other media again – well, until he briefly surfaced the year before last.

Born and raised in the Toronto, Ontario suburb of Scarborough in the 80s, one of Yan’s biggest fans was Steve Gaskin. Before he was old enough to go to school, Gaskin’s Guyanese father and Chinese mother would drop him off at his grandparents’ home at 7am before going to work, and pick him up 12 hours later.

“I found it very hard to connect with my gung-gung [maternal grandfather] because my parents never spoke Cantonese, and he didn’t speak much English. I took Cantonese lessons, but I didn’t retain any of it,” says Gaskin. His grandfather, who ran a laundromat business in his adopted home, brought his family from Hong Kong to Canada via Guyana more than 50 years ago.

“My gung-gung only communicated in Chinese,” says Gaskin, “but just from grunts and facial cues, I knew what he was saying.”

The pair managed to bond over Wok with Yan. “I would sit next to him on the La-Z-Boy and just without even talking, we would laugh at the jokes and he would just kind of nudge me when something funny came on, or he wanted me to watch the technique.

“In the 80s, Stephen Yan was probably the only Chinese-Canadian celebrity. I was probably six years old, and the only Asian person on the big screen was Bruce Lee or Jackie Chan, so to see somebody like Stephen Yan, who’s in Canada, who was so approachable, was really important.”

In 2018, Gaskin and a friend launched Retrokid, a company that, through T-shirts and accessories, recalls childhood memories for Gen Xers who grew up watching Canadian television shows such as Mr Dressup, Polka Dot Door and Degrassi. Gaskin was determined to track down his hero.

After years of dead ends, in 2022, he finally got a response. But it wasn’t until a year later that Yan agreed to meet him.

Gaskin is coy about how he finally got in contact with Yan, divulging only that the former chef wanted “to work with a company that understands everything he’s done”. And with the success of Retrokid and the wider appetites for online nostalgia spun into products, Yan the savvy businessman must have seen that the time was ripe for a revival.

“Stephen Yan always said that he appreciated that there was this personal connection I had with my gung-gung as to why he wanted to do this with us.”

Together, they turned out “Wok with Yan” T-shirts, hoodies, tote bags, badges and fridge magnets, bearing the chef’s likeness from his television days. And, of course, a range of aprons with witty Yan-isms has proved to be the bestseller.

To help launch the collection, Yan agreed to fly from Vancouver to Toronto in August 2024 for a meet-and-greet with fans.

“It was pretty shocking to see him just come out of the arrivals gate,” says Gaskin, who picked Yan up at the airport. “Like, oh my God, it’s Stephen Yan. I didn’t know if he was going to come off a plane in a wheelchair or on crutches, right? But no, he’s super strong and mentally healthy for 85.”

While Yan was in Toronto, Retrokid gave Liu a chance to interview the chef for the Star, and, like Gaskin, the reporter was transported back to his childhood.

“It was really surreal,” says Liu. “He was still making jokes, he was just like a grandpa, where you ask one question and then his answer is, like, 10 minutes long because he’s lived such a full life.”

According to what he said in the interview, it was Yan who decided to pull the plug on his show in 1995.

“One day, I asked my accountant how much money I needed to survive,” Yan told Liu. “He said I already had a house and I didn’t need a dollar more. I wanted to contribute my time to those less fortunate, so I helped out with orphanages and schools in places like Thailand and China. I had enough earthly belongings.

“Back then, I had three restaurants [in Vancouver] and I had three disciples, including Martin Yan [no relation; a Hong Kong-American who worked with Yan in the 70s],” he explained. His protégé’s own television show, Yan Can Cook, also first aired on Canadian television in 1978 (initially as Yan Can), before having a highly successful run in the US, on PBS.

Stephen Yan also told Liu that, after quitting the show, he spent more time with his family and became much more active. “I ran 11 marathons, four times at the Boston Marathon and won the masters division. I also climbed Mount Everest.”

For someone so beloved, there isn’t a lot of biographical information available online about Yan, and he guards his private life closely. His birth date, for example, is not widely known, only that he was born in Hong Kong in 1939.

Not long after, in December 1941, the Japanese occupation of the city began and basic ingredients such as rice, flour and oil were rationed.

“[As a child,] I was poor and went to people’s stores where they would give me leftover food,” Yan told Liu.

“I was spending my time on the streets next to a theatre that was starring a Chinese actor, who was Bruce Lee’s father. Bruce and I became friends, and we used to play in a nearby warehouse, but I needed a job.”

When Yan was nine years old, a restaurant cook gave him work in exchange for food. One of his most laborious tasks was to take thousands of lotus seeds from a pot of boiling water, without gloves, and use a toothpick to push out their bitter cores. After three months, Yan was allowed into the kitchen, to learn from the cook, who taught him how to kill and pluck chickens, and use every part of the bird, as well as shop for the best ingredients.

Yan claimed to have been the fastest dishwasher at the restaurant. “Humans are adaptable and can do anything if they have the opportunity,” he told Liu.

He became a fully-fledged cook, and when he was around 15 years old, the chief cook of the restaurant arranged for him to go to school. Later, Yan said, he was one of two students chosen by an American senator to study business administration in the US, to which he sailed on an 18-day voyage to San Francisco.

Fearing being called up to the military as the US fought in Vietnam, Yan crossed the border to Canada in the late 50s or early 60s, he told Liu, one of 20,000 to 30,000 draft dodgers to have done so, according to Canadian immigration statistics.

By the late 70s, Yan was already managing his own restaurants when he was noticed by a television talent scout while leading cooking demonstrations in a shopping mall in the run-up to Chinese New Year.

The weekly Yan’s Woking debuted on Vancouver station BCTV in 1978. Two years later, national broadcaster CBC bought the show, rebranded it as Wok with Yan and shifted formats to present a daily afternoon cooking series.

Gaskin says some 230 people showed up at Toronto’s storied Royal Theatre for 2024’s meet-and-greet.

“It was great to give [Yan] a platform where he could just say thank you to all of his fans and the fans showed up,” says Gaskin. “Obviously, we could have packed that theatre to 500 people, but we also wanted to give the fans a chance to meet him, to actually go up and take a photo, and they loved it.”

Since then, Yan has remained elusive. All attempts to contact him by this author have been fruitless. The Retrokid team has been sworn to secrecy; Liu says he never got direct contact. And even now, almost two years after Yan’s rarest of public appearances, he shows no signs of emerging into the spotlight again, even to contribute to this article, to connect with his hometown, Hong Kong.

Vancouverite Billy Snaychuk wasn’t at the meet-up but considers himself a fan. “My most favourite part about Stephen Yan would have to be his aprons, and the way he always made the audience laugh,” he says. “He just captured the audience right away from the get-go. He definitely caught me as a kid, because I just loved watching him.”

Snaychuk’s father, a fisherman and entrepreneur, got to know Yan through Chinese friends who caught fish for the chef, delivering them to his restaurant, Yan’s Garden. From the age of six, Snaychuk watched Wok with Yan with his mother every day after school.

“My parents had the largest collection of Stephen Yan books, and I remember sneaking out of my room in the middle of the night and grabbing his books on the bookshelf and bringing them back. And I would just look at all the pictures and read the recipes,” he recalls, with a chuckle.

Once a month, his parents invited friends over and cooked dishes from Yan’s cookbooks, including Snaychuk’s favourite, gold coin beef.

“The flavour profile in it is just next level. And the texture of the beef, you can almost chew it with the roof of your mouth and your tongue, it’s just that tender,” says Snaychuk, who would follow in his hero’s footsteps and become a chef himself. He was promoted to executive chef at the age of 28 and went into restaurant consulting and even competed in the Food Network Canada cooking reality TV show Wall of Chefs.

As he got older, Snaychuk paid attention to Yan’s technique, particularly how he created flavour profiles by adding ingredients to the wok at different times.

“A lot of people, when they cook, they just kind of throw everything in there. If you do that, the whole dish is basically going to taste the same. But if you add things at different times and take them out and put them back in, you layer the flavours. And that’s something I really noticed – he layered his flavours with his cooking.”

While watching Yan was a joy for so many, working for him was not always so pleasurable, says former assistant Brenda Gonneville, who also has no idea where Yan lives now. “He’s not the face you see on TV.”

In 1981, Yan hired a 26-year-old Gonneville to help him in his office, which was above Yan’s Chinese restaurant, in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia. She had worked as an assistant to high-powered executives in the steel industry, says Gonneville, so was “well versed in dealing with high-powered, difficult people”.

Her job, as a native English speaker, was to look after Yan’s public relations, devise witty lines for the aprons and procure props and have them shipped to Ottawa, where his show was taped for two seasons before moving back to Vancouver. She recalls being the only Caucasian in an office full of Cantonese-speaking people but says she got on well with all the other staff. Gonneville was aiming to forge a career in entertainment, so worked for a low wage. After paying rent, she says, she was left with enough money only for a diet of white rice and boiled eggs.

“After three months, I’d had enough,” she says, “because he is a perfectionist, and nothing pleases him. He’s a hard worker. He expects more than 100 per cent from his employees.”

One day, she says, he was dictating content for a show and Gonneville was struggling to write it all down in shorthand, because he was speaking quickly.

“He had me read it back and I said, ‘I’m sorry, I didn’t get most of that.’ I decided then and there, and so did he, that we’d come to the end of the road.”

Fortunately, her brief stint with Yan led to a 20-year career in film and television.

When she returned to pack up her things, the office manager “took my hand and said, ‘Don’t you worry, you lasted longer than anybody’”, she recalls with a laugh.

“[Yan’s] an A-type personality, he’s driven. He expected everybody to put in the same effort as him, and if you failed, he wouldn’t put up with it.”

Difficult he may have been for those he employed, but, given the delight he’s brought to television viewers, one cannot begrudge his telling the hosts of Toronto daytime talk show The Social, in August 2024, that, “I was hiding; I want a simple life.

“I […] cannot believe that people remember me after 30 years,” he said on The Social. “And they want to know, am I alive? I am! I’m alive!”

And maybe that’s enough, to know that he’s alive. With Yan now well into his 80s, a quiet, simple life is perhaps just wok he needs.

item.title: [SCMP] Pentagon orders 30 US universities to scrutinise ties with Chinese research partners
item.description:
The Pentagon has ordered 30 US universities to conduct sweeping audits of their foreign research partnerships, including collaborations with Chinese institutions and organisations associated with former Confucius Institutes, or risk becoming ineligible for future federal funding.

The Department of Defence said on Monday that the unnamed universities must review their academic, financial and research relationships with foreign “entities of concern” and determine whether sensitive or export-controlled research had been exposed.

The institutions must report their findings and proposed mitigation measures – including the termination of partnerships deemed problematic – to the department by August 31, giving them two weeks to complete the reviews.
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon has ordered 30 US universities to conduct sweeping audits of their foreign research partnerships, including collaborations with Chinese institutions and organisations associated with former Confucius Institutes, or risk becoming ineligible for future federal funding.

The Department of Defence said on Monday that the unnamed universities must review their academic, financial and research relationships with foreign “entities of concern” and determine whether sensitive or export-controlled research had been exposed.

The institutions must report their findings and proposed mitigation measures – including the termination of partnerships deemed problematic – to the department by August 31, giving them two weeks to complete the reviews.

The department did not identify the universities or specify how many of the notifications concerned ties with China rather than Russia or Iran.

Responding to the announcement, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said China opposed “the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicisation or instrumentalisation of normal scientific, educational and academic exchanges”.

“Scientific innovation and academic development require open cooperation; restricting normal research exchanges will ultimately harm the interests of all parties, including US researchers and institutions,” the spokesperson said.

“The US side should abandon the Cold War mentality and foster an open, fair and non-discriminatory environment for educational, scientific and people-to-people exchanges between China and the United States.”

The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment.

The audits concern collaborations with institutions included on a list issued under Section 1286 of the 2019 National Defence Authorisation Act, as well as organisations the department described as being associated with “rebranded Confucius Institutes”.

The reference to Confucius Institutes – Chinese government-backed language and cultural programmes that faced mounting political scrutiny in the United States before many closed or changed names – places China at the centre of the latest research-security action.

“The Department of War has zero tolerance for academic partnerships that compromise our national security,” Emil Michael, undersecretary of war for research and engineering, said in announcing the audits, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Defence Department.

“Institutions that receive funding from American taxpayers must uphold the highest standards of research security, and these mandated audits will ensure accountability across the board.”

The department said the reviews were intended to protect taxpayer-funded research from unauthorised technology transfers, intellectual-property theft and exploitation by foreign adversaries.

Universities are “critical partners” in a broad range of Pentagon research programmes, said Joseph Jewell, assistant secretary of war for science and technology.

“The department must therefore ensure that our research investments are well protected from foreign exploitation,” he said.

In July, the Pentagon placed 130 universities and research organisations in China, Russia and Iran on its updated Section 1286 list, including 88 institutions in mainland China.

The list included some of China’s best-known civilian universities, such as Fudan University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, alongside institutions with more explicit connections to the country’s military and defence establishment.

Other additions included Shandong University, Hangzhou Dianzi University, Shenyang Aerospace University, the University of International Relations and the Chinese military’s Joint Logistics Support Force Engineering University.

The Pentagon previously told the South China Morning Post that the determinations applied to entire institutions rather than particular laboratories, departments or individual researchers.

US researchers were advised to exercise “strict caution” before entering collaborations, funding arrangements or data-sharing relationships with institutions on the list.

Under the department’s research-security rules, Pentagon funding is generally prohibited for fundamental research projects that involve collaboration with a listed foreign institution. Existing relationships may be subject to risk reviews, while some non-fundamental research can continue under limited circumstances if it does not involve collaboration or equipment supplied by a listed entity.

Monday’s announcement marks a significant escalation from warning researchers about the foreign institutions to requiring American universities to examine – and potentially end – their relationships with them.

It remains unclear whether the 30 universities were selected because the Pentagon found evidence of unauthorised technology transfers or other misconduct, or merely because they maintained relationships with blacklisted institutions.

SCMP has asked the Association of American Universities whether any of its members received notifications and whether the August 31 deadline gives universities enough time to conduct the required audits.

The Department of Defence said it was pursuing the initiative with the House and Senate Armed Services and Appropriations committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

The announcement came four days after the House China committee and the House Education and Workforce Committee released a report accusing Harvard University of failing to adequately scrutinise relationships with Chinese institutions associated with the People’s Liberation Army and China’s defence-industrial sector.

The Republican-led investigation alleged that Harvard-affiliated researchers had co-written work with scholars at the National University of Defence Technology, Beihang University and Nanjing University of Science and Technology, among other Chinese institutions with military connections.

It also accused Harvard of lacking the centralised infrastructure needed to identify and screen foreign research partnerships.

The report was co-written by a congressional committee that has consistently advocated tighter restrictions on US academic and commercial engagement with China. Its findings do not establish that Harvard is among the 30 institutions notified by the Pentagon.

SCMP has asked Harvard whether it received a notification and sought its response to the congressional report.

The congressional committees recommended that Harvard centralise its research-security operations, overhaul its due-diligence procedures and expand its screening of international partnerships. They also urged Congress to enact legislation imposing more extensive disclosure and research-security requirements on universities.

The Pentagon did not say whether that investigation contributed to its decision to order the 30 audits or whether the universities had been recommended for review by congressional committees.

The department said the audits would help it anticipate emerging threats and respond to “evolving adversarial tactics” while preserving the United States’ technological advantage.

Critics of Washington’s expanding research-security restrictions have warned that overly broad rules could discourage legitimate scientific collaboration, stigmatise researchers of Chinese origin and weaken American universities’ access to international expertise.
